subtopic: THE WOOD PULP INDUSTRY-PRESERVATION OF RESOURCES OF THE FOREST.
THE WOOD PULP INDUSTRY-PRESERVATION OF RESOURCES OF THE FOREST.
speechtext:
I wish to trespass on the time of the House for a moment to impress upon the Prime Minister and the government the immediate necessity of some action being taken in reference to the appointment of a committee of members of this House to ascertain the official facts as regards the forest resources of Canada and the United States. I do so at this time because of articles which have appeared in the public press and because of the action taken by the United States House of Representatives, the Speaker of which has appointed a select committee to investigate into wood pulp and print paper, and which committee is already at work. I wish to impress upon the Prime Minister certain editorials which have appeared in the Canadian press in reference to this matter, particularly an editorial in the ' Globe ' of April the 6th also editorial of * Industrial Canada ' for April, and an editorial in the Ottawa ' Free Press ' of April the 27th, from which I quote :
The Pulp problem.
As the year advances it is quite apparent that the seriousness of the situation which confronts this country as to the future of its paper supply, and as to the absolute necessity of putting an end to the wastage of the timber resources of the two countries principally involved is more and more impressing itself upon the public mind.
But as we secure additional information upon the predations of the pulp and paper industry of the United States upon our pulp wood resouroes, and as we learn, as we do learn every dav, that the situation in the United States is rapidly approaching the stage where they must procure their pulp from Canada, the question arises whether this issue has not approached the proportions of a national, and a vitally national, question. . . Why should Canada consent to allow these puip areas to be depleted without adequate return to the workers of this country in the future as has been our policy in the past?	.
There is one way to get out of the difficulty, and one only. The federal government should appoint a commission which shall go into the whole question and investigate its true bearings from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Such a commission would be able to secure official information which would be invaluable in enabling the government to deal with the problem from a national standpoint. Sir Wilfrid Laurier has already hinted that he has some such an idea in his mind, and it is to be hoped that the session will not close without the idea coming to fruition. . . .
It would be a new departure in Canada and we are sure that such a legislative committee would prove of untold value in the solution of the problem'.
I ask that the Prime Minister should grant a committee of the House for two reasons. First, a Royal Commission would make a cut and dried report, but the members of a committee of the House would be able to explain their report on the floor of parliament as is the practice in the United States. The second_ reason is that a committee of the House would not be as costly as a royal commission, because the members of that committee would be in receipt of their indemnity and would not receive anything further than their expenses. I would advise that a small committee of the House should be appointed to get the official facts, to sit during recess and report next session. This is not a new matter. So long ago as June the 7th, 1904, a prominent Canadian newspaper editor, Mr. John D. Grace, published in the ' Financial News ' of London, England, an article with reference to this matter. That article was quoted by the great English statesman Mr. Joseph Chamberlain in his fiscal policy speech of 1905, and in that arti-

cle, the statement is made that the United *States is almost at the end of its forest resources and that Canada, Norway and Sweden are the only three countries which can export pulp. Mr. Grace wrote :
When European experts are saying that a t*A0[DOT]' fauune 's within sight, the forests ot this country become a possession which cannot well be overvalued. Our timber will be as valuable as our grain.
I state that I believe Norway and Sweden are now at the end of their resources for export to any great extent and I ask the Prime Minister to question the geological surveyors of Canada as to whether 'there is an inexhaustible supply of timber in this country. For the last thirty years parties of from ten to thirty-this year I belieye there are thirty parties-have been exploring this country from one end to the other, and they are able to give accurate information. I do not ask for any speedy legislation. This is a large matter [DOT] it is a serious matter. But I ask that the Prime Minister will take some immediate steps to organize a committee so that we can get exact information. Another reason for action is this, that the president of the United States has called a congress or convention of the governors of the different states of the Union to assemble during the coming month of May for the purpose of discussing this question. I have had communication on the subject with the United States Consul at Ottawa, and he informs nie that he has no official information, but that he believes that the date set for the convention is May 13. I believe that it would be a very proper thing for Canada to be represented at that convention, where we could probably get invaluable information. The Owen Sound ' Times ' of January 9, and of March 19, 1908, has excellent editorials on this same line. So also the Seaforth ' Expositor ' of April 24, 1908. The ' Canadian Journal of Commerce ' of March 20, 1908. If legislation is enacted, as I hope it will be, on this question, it could be so framed as not to interfere with the rights or the profits of any of the farmers of Canada, as some fear it would.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE WOOD PULP INDUSTRY-PRESERVATION OF RESOURCES OF THE FOREST.
speechtext: Before my hon. friend takes his seat, would he be kind enough to state to the House the points that he would desire to have investigated by this committee ?

subtopic: THE WOOD PULP INDUSTRY-PRESERVATION OF RESOURCES OF THE FOREST.
speechtext:
The committee should have power, in the first place, as now is the opportunity for doing so, of finding out what are the timber and pulpwood resources of the United States-both of supply and demand ; also the resources of Canada, and as to whether the supply is inexhaustible, as has been stated for years ; also the visible supply to-day in other countries; also what would be the possible result of an export duty or the adoption of some other means by which the manufacture of our Mr. LEWIS.
crude product could be carried on in Canada also the best means to preserve our forests. A Royal Commission could be appointed, composed of members of parliament. They would be without pay except as regards their expenses. I contend that while we have only six or seven millions of people in Canada, the questions affecting this last great nation are just as great as they would be if we had eighty millions; and when we have only 214 representatives for this vast country, I contend that the full time of these men should be given to their legislative duties-not here, however ; because I think the lengthening sessions are interfering with the business of the country. They interfere with the business of the departments while we are here. Shorter sessions would be better ; but the whole time of a member of parliament should be given to the interests of this country. It takes very little to occupy one man's time ; and if he devotes that time to one great question-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: THE WOOD PULP INDUSTRY-PRESERVATION OF RESOURCES OF THE FOREST.
speechtext: I think the hon. member is rather wandering away from the question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE WOOD PULP INDUSTRY-PRESERVATION OF RESOURCES OF THE FOREST.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question to which my hon. friend has called the attention of the House is one which at this moment is engrossing the attention not only of the people of this country, but also of the people of the United States, and which should, in my humble judgment, engross the attention of the whole civilized world. Nothing is more important, I believe, than the preservation of the forests ; but unfortunately, we are all guilty, not in this country, but in all countries, with the exception of very few, of taking the forests too much as a negligible quantity. My hon. friend has stated that the opinion is entertained in this country that our timber resources are inexhaustible. If such tje the opinion of some, it is certainly not my own opinion. On the contrary, I believe that our forest resources are very far from being inexhaustible, and if the present waste goes on, it is not difficult to foresee that before many years pass over Canada will be very much in want of timber and of wood generally. If the committee which my hon. friend wants had for its primary object the seeking of means and methods whereby the waste of forest lands could be prevented, I would be very much in sympathy with it. I think there is no more important problem at the present day than to find ways and means of preserving our forests. In one respect the great enemy of the forest is the railway ; another enemy is the fire. Railways have to be built; but whenever a railway is brought into a forest it brings with it the danger of the destruction of the forest itself. I would not be adverse to the suggestion of my hon. friend to have either a committee or a commission appointed chiefly for the purpose of finding

ways and means to prevent the waste which is taking place annually, not only in this country but all over this continent. The government will be happy, on the suggestion of my hon. friend, to take the matter into consideration, and I may be able to give an answer at an early date. I notice that my hon. friend has suggested that we should be represented at the convention which has been summoned by President Roosevelt, and which is to sit at Washington during the month of May. I may say to my hon. friend that if we were invited we would be only too glad to accept the invitation. But as I understand that it is purely a convention of governors and officials of the United States, I do not suppose that we would have any standing in it. If we had, I would advise the government to send a representative.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, I would like to draw the attention of the right hon. leader of the House to an article in the ' Canadian Gazette ' of London, of February 6, 1908. The subject of the article is ' The Emigrant Bonus System,' and it states that application was made to Sir Marcus Samuel, judge of the Guildhall court, for the renewal of a license of an emigration agent and passenger broker. The judge was inclined to refuse the application, and Dr. Ginsburg, representative of the board of trade of London, appeared to oppose the application, and the Hon. Charles Russell represented the Dominion government and tried to induce the judge to grant the application for the license, which seemed to be in doubt. Hon. Charles Russell was about to address the court, when Dr. Ginsberg objected, saying that he failed to see his locus standi. The judge thought that the immigration agent caused certain advertisements to be published relative to the demand for immigrants in Canada, containing inaccurate representations. It was only by this action of the board of trade through Dr. Ginsburg that attention was called to the matter. It goes to prove that on the other side the system of bonuses incites the greed of graft and it is not to the benefit of Canada. This report continues :
Dr. Ginsburg. I say that the Dominion government have no more to do with it than any one in the street, and I protest against it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

Brantford public building-improvements, $500.

This vote is to complete the improvements and alterations, fittings and general repairs in the post office at Brantford. The total cost of the improvements has been about $13,000, of which $12,510.75 has been spent, leaving $489.25 to complete-or, say $500.

The amount spent seems to be large considering the changes Mr. PUGSLEY.
made and the work done. I do not see where they have put $13,000. However, this year the minister proposes to allow ns $500. This seems a very large amount to give out of a total of appropriations of $119,000,000. Does the minister really feel that he can afford this $500 for Brantford? And on what ground has he made the calculation? On that point. I would like to inquire on what basis the distribution of public buildings is made. Has it any relation to the requirements of the people, the amount of business done or the revenue received? If these matters, which, as a business man, I think are very proper to take into consideration, are the basis on which the department proceeds in these cases, I submit that the amount the minister is placing in the estimates for Brantford is totally inadequate for the requirements of that city. I do not think the hon. minister (Mr. Pugsley) has ever visited Brantford, and of course, I cannot blame him for that, for he has not been very long in his present office. But I can tell him that this is not a new question in this House, for we have drawn attention, year after year, to this post office building. This building, it should be understood, houses not only the post office but the Custome Department and the Inland Revenue Department in a city of 20,000 people. Let me give the figures of the revenue collected in that building according to the latest statistics I have at hand. These, I believe, are the returns for 1907, but whether for the full year or for nine months I am not quite sure. The postal department yielded $37,328, besides over $700 for rents of boxes. In round figures, the postal revenue of Brantford is about $40,000. The custom house collected $308,000, and the inland revenue collected between $70,000 and $75,000-a total of something over $400,000 paid into the coffers of this government from the city of Brantford. In return for this vast amount paid in by the city of Brantford and surrounding district, we have the munificent sum of $500 placed in the estimates this year to be spent in that city. This building stands practically as it stood twenty-five years ago, when the city of Brantford was about one-third its present size and the revenue was not 25 per cent of what it is to-day. We have asked, time and again, for a new public building. And I might call the attention of the minister to the fact that this is almost the only way in which the Dominion government can spend money in the city of Brantford. We have no use for the breakwaters and wharfs that are built in some other places-we have some water there, but we do not feel that a breakwater would do much good. We do not ask for dredging as do some of the sea and lake ports. But, surely, when the government has only the two avenues through which it can spend money in a community such as

Brantford-the armoury and the post office -we are not asking too much when we say that we should have a post office building commensurate with the business to be done and the revenue received. To properly house these three branches of the! public service, we should have in that city a building worth from $125,000 to $150,000. There are places in many parts of Canada giving a much less revenue than Brantford in which public buildings are put up costing from $75,000 to $150,000. And still, we are using the building which we have used for twenty-five years, and which is totally inadequate. Our people must walk up a winding stair to pay their customs duties. If there were any competition, no one would do business with the government. But there is no one else besides the government taking customs duties. But our citizens must climb this winding stair as they have been doing for about twenty-five years to pay about $300,000 a year into the coffers of the Dominion treasury. And they must climb a winding stair to pay $75,000 to the Inland Revenue Department. We are not asking for anything extravagant or anything but what is required by the public service. But we think that, when it comes to a city like Brantford, with its revenues, we should have a building more commensurate with the business done than the one we have to-day. I would ask the Minister of Public Works if. in deciding with regard to the location of public buildings, he takes into consideration the amount of business done and the revenue received?

I can assure my hon. friend (Mr. Cockshutt) that in considering the desirability of erecting a public building in a city or town, the importance of the place, the business done and the public requirements are all taken into careful consideration. As to Brantford, I take it that my hon. friend would not suggest that we should ask the committee to vote a larger sum than is necessary to finish the improvements that have been undertaken. When only $500 is required, to vote more would be a mere waste of the public money. So far as the erection of a new building in Brantford is concerned. I have not had the pleasure of any communication from the hon. gentleman who represents the rid-' ing in which the city of Brantford is' situated, urging that a new public building should be erected there. Although I have been for several months in the department. the hon. gentleman, as the one who is entitled to speak for the people of that district, has not made any communication to me in this direction, nor has any one else.
Perhaps the request was made in the House at a former session.

That may be, if so I was not here to receive it. I recognize the importance of the town of Brantford, I recognize that a large business is done there and a large revenue is collected. I can say to my hon. friend that I shall have much pleasure during the recess in looking into the matter and seeing what the requirements are, and will give the suggestion of my hon. friend a very careful consideration.

The minister rather criticises me for having failed to wait upon him or write him in connection with this matter. I have taken this, the earliest opportunity when the matter was under discussion, to bring it to his attention. His predecessor was asked on more than one occasion on the floor of the House, and was personally interviewed by myself, and if there are no records in the department of that kind, it is of little use for us to make these requests from time to time. I have made these requests on the floor of the House, and also personally, and the minister apparently now hears of them for the first time. I waited upon Mr. Hyman myself, and I think other citizens of Stratford have waited on him and I think considerable correspondence has been held with the government about this very matter, namely, the inadequacy of the Brantford postal facilities and the inadequacy of the inland revenue facilities. It is not a new question, and if the minister has not searched his files, or if these requests have not been placed on file, that is not my fault. X have made the request from time to time, and at every opportunity during my term in this parliament. The buildings have been inadequate for some years, and when these votes were made of $10,000 or $12,000 for repairs, I pointed out to Mr. Hyman that it seemed to me a comparative waste of money to tinker up an old building that was never going to be satisfactory, and that it would be better to take the matter up in a broad sense, as it should be, in order to satisfy the requirements of the city, and give us a public building worthy of Brantford and commensurate with the very large business that is done there. We do not ask for a lavish expenditure, but we do say that any business house in the city of Brantford doing a large business, would have premises erected a great deal more up-to-date than these government buildings. It is only because there is no competition in the revenue or customs business that so large a business can be done in these old premises. I trust the minister will carry out the promise he has made on the floor of the house, and that he will visit the city of Brantford at an early date and see for himself the great commercial and industrial activity prevailing there, and will give us a building suitable to the requirements of the city. I thank the minister for his promise, and trust that he will not forget it.

I feel it my duty to endorse what my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Coekshutt) has said as to the necessity of an expenditure for public buildings in the city of Brantford. I am much surprised that the Minister of Customs has not communicated to the Minister of Public Works in reference to the needs of Brantford in this respect. May I ask the Postmaster General if any requests have been made to his department for better service in the city of Brantford, and a larger building.
I could not answer offhand, but I think we have received a petition to that effect.

If the Postmaster General has received a petition to that effect, I suppose he would communicate it to the. Minister of Public Works. I should also suppose that my hon. friend the Minister of Customs, as an old resident of Brantford, and a representative of that constituency for many years, would have interested him-, self on its behalf. The hon. gentleman has been in this government since 1896. Now one of his colleagues says that no request has been made for a better service, and a larger post office building in the city of Brantford. Surely the Minister of Customs has not forgotten his old city that elected him to parliament for the first time. I would ask the hon. gentleman if any demands have been made upon the government for increased accommodation in the city of Brantford for the various services of the gover-ment, a city which is contributing so large a sum to the revenue. I certainly endorse what my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Coekshutt) has said. I have heard him myself several times on the floor of the House pressing the claims of his city upon the government for a more liberal expenditure, and suggesting that some of the money that is being wasted in other directions should be put to good use in the city of Brantford. On this side of the House we do not advocate a larger total expenditure by this government, but we desire to see the middleman dispensed with and the money wisely expended. A few years ago the government were proposing to inaugurate a pneumatic system of distributing the mails in Toronto and Montreal. Instead of wasting money on schemes like that, let some of it be expended in important centres like Brantford where there is so evident a public need of better facilities. I think the Minister of Public Works is not doing himself justice when he suggests that the member for Brantford has not directed his attention to the fact that a larger expenditure is necessary.
There is no suggestion about it ; it is a fact.

The hon. gentleman has given that as a reason why larger appro-Mr. COCKSHUTT.
priations were not made for the city of Brantford. I am sure that the people and his own friends in the city of Brantford will not appreciate that reference to my hon. friend who so ably represents them on the floor of this House.

I did not intend to say anything which would reflect upon the hon. gentleman who represents the city of Brantford. All I desired to do was to call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that, although I had been eight months, yesterday, in the department, I had not had the pleasure of having any communication from him upon the subject. Neither had I received any petition, or communication from anybody in Brantford urging that increased accommodation was necessary for post office and customs purposes. Now, the hon. gentleman makes the statement that he had, upon previous occasions, in this House, brought the matter to the attention of the then minister, and also that certain communications had been forwarded. I do not intend to reflect at all upon my hon. friend but only to state a fact which might, in some measure, at all events, explain why there is no provision being made at the present time for any new building for these purposes in the city of Brantford. As far as the present vote is concerned the improvements are quite considerable. We have provided for new fittings in the post office, new granite steps, new letter boxes and brass work, letter receiver, recuttiug of stone work, improved heating apparatus and an iron fence around the building. We have done electric wiring and improved the buildings by painting, graining and varnishing, we have made a number of repairs to the wood work, we have put in new furniture and we have done what seemed to be reasonable and necessary for the building.
Was it done by contract or day's work ?

Part by tender and part by day's work. I think that the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Coekshutt) did not need the assistance of the gentleman who sits in front of him (Mr. Blain) because the hon. gentleman took my assurance in good faith and with apparent good feeling that I would be very happy to make inquiry into the necessities of the city of Brantford in this particular and give the matter my prompt consideration. I recognize just as well as the hon. gentleman who represents that important constituency does that it is my duty, administering the Department of Public Works, to pay attention to the necessities of all parts of this country and that it would not be proper that I should neglect or overlook the reasonable wants of a place so important as the city of Brantford.

I do not wish to have it understood that I felt in any way hurt

at what the minister said, but I think that he was a little unfair in saying that X had not presented the claims of the city of Brantford because they had been forwarded to the department, and that the reason that I had not presented them again within the last few months was that I was awaiting the opportunity that arose to-day. If the minister carries out the promise that he has made it will be all right. The trouble is that this request has been made to the Minister of Public Works on two or three different occasions and unfortunately to two or three ministers. I think we began with the late Mr. Sutherland, we continued It with Mr. Hyman and now we are continuing it with the hon. gentleman who occupies the position to-day. The department changes its head so frequently that we are required to put in these applications a little too often. I think the records will show that the board of trade of the city of Brantford spent more than one evening discussing the inadequacy of the buildings in Brantford and that they placed their views on record and sent them down to this government. The hon. the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson), who is an old resident of Brantford, certainly knows the inadequacy of these buildings. He knows the immense amount of revenue that his department and the Post Office Department are obtaining from the city of Brantford, and I think it is nothing but reasonable that the Minister of Customs should back me up when I make the reasonable request that I am making, and when I say that the city of Brantford should have a little of this vast expenditure that this government is making annually. We do not ask for any extravagance, but we do ask that legitimate business requirements may be provided for in the city of Brantford. Instead of this small vote the department should make one job of it and put up a new building. I admit, as the minister has said, that they have improved the inside of the building considerably, that they have given us modern fittings and a certain amount of that kind of expenditure is all right, but it is only a temporary arrangement because the building is inadequate and it cannot be increased to the size which is necessary. I should say in justice to the hon. the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) that I do not think anything has been actually placed before himself at all but he will see that the very same argument that has been made with respect to the Department of Public Works also applies to his department. This matter was taken up when Sir William Mulock was Postmaster General. I think the records in that department will show that petitions came down to the department some four or five years ago and I may say they were endorsed by the citizens generally. I remember that an inspector was sent up by
the Post Office Department. I had the honour of being one of the committee that awaited upon him. We pointed out the inadequacy of the arrangements and we had a special committee that sat for weeks and months to endeavour to get the department to deal with this very matter. Although all of this had reference to the Post Office Department the hon. gentleman who occupies the position of Postmaster General is not responsible in that respect because the request was not made to him. We made it to his predecessors and we made it also to the predecessors of the Minister of Public Works. Now I renew it to-day to two of the ministers-to three of them for the matter of that, because the Minister of Customs should be included also. His department obtained $308,000 from the city of Brantford alone last year. The building is in the same condition, so far as I know, as it was twenty-five years ago. It was built in Sir John Macdonald's time, long before this government came into power, and we have had no addition to it from that time to this. There has been no change, I believe except some small changes in the interior fittings. The population of Brantford is three times what it was, the' business is probably ten times what it was and the revenue is probably three or four times what it was when the building was put up. If business is business it is right that the large amount of business which is done in Brantford should be housed in proper quarters. I am not going to find fault with the promise of the minister, only I ask him not to take too long to carry it out because it has been before the House on several occasions. We have pressed it upon the attention of the government and practically nothing has resulted. I have just had placed in my hand the answer which was given by the Hon. A. B. Aylesworth, then Postmaster General, to a question which I put to him in the House on March 19, 1906, and which will be found at page 339 of Hansard of that year. I shall read the answer in order that the present Postmaster General may see what has been done in Brantford within the last few years. The Hon. A. B. Aylesworth made the following statement:

Every single year during that whole term, each one of these sources of revenue from the city of Brantford steadily increased. The Postmaster General does $60,000 worth of business in the city of Brantford, not to speak of the returns from the customs and inland, re venue and all this business is housed in the one inadequate building. I think the minister must recognize tiie necessity for increased accommodation at Brantford and I trust that year after year I will not be compelled to bring this matter to his attention. When Mr. Hyman was minister and when he heard the statement I made in the House he said to me privately, but I think I may mention it : Cockshutt you ought to have a building in Brantford costing not less than $125,000. Mr. Hyman practically gave us to under-staiul that in the very near future this would be done, but to-day we have a paltry $500 in the estimates for Brantford.

I am surprised that the Minister of Customs sits silent without a word to say for the good old city of Brantford. When the Conservatives were in power, although he represented the constituency, they generously erected a building in Brantford which was sufficient for the business done at the time, but, the Liberals have studiously neglected that city. After hearing the statement of the hon. member (Mr. Cockshutt) I do not wonder that Brantford rejected the Minister of Customs because evidently since the Liberals came into power he has not. been able to get the claims of that city recognized. To-day when the hon. member (Mr. Cockshutt) pleads for the assistance of the Minister of Customs the Minister of Customs has not a word to say. The minister owes it to the city of Brantford to state whether there will be sufficient accommodation afforded that city and whether he will use his influence in that direction. Now, this item like all others includes a charge for architect's fees although one would suppose that if the Public Works Department were run on business principles it would have a sufficient permanent staff of architects and engineers to do all this work. There is a general impression that the Public Works Department has been running wild ; first one minister is brought in to improve it and then another until it is brought down to the present minister. I was much astonished the other day when I heard that contracts for dredging were to be given without tender.
Why not discuss the item before the chair. As a matter of fact the contracts were not to be given without tender; it was only an extension of the time of the old contracts.

I mentioned this to show that the Public Works Department wants reorganization worse than the Marine Department. Here, as was shown by the hon. gentleman from Simcoe (Mr. Ben-net) the other day, the Public Works Department paid in nine months $27,500 to one outside architect, when one good permanent employee at a salary of $5,000 a year could have done all the work. Either the department has not competent men to do the work or else they are farming it out amongst friends of the government so that large profits may be made by them.
They are afraid of their own architects since the Laurier tower fell.

That may be and probably they are afraid of their inspectors as well. It would be much better in every way to have a well paid and competent permanent official who would look after this architect work, and he would not be likely to be so susceptible to graft as the superintendents who are indiscriminately employed throughout the country. I believe that we should have, a permanent officer of this kind and that he should be paid a sufficient salary. Take the case of the little armoury at Belleville and an Ottawa architect has to be called in and everybody knows he is the son of the chief architect. He may be as good a man as any other, but it strikes me that if the chief architect should have a man in his department who is qualified to make plans for a building such as this
Why discuss everything under the sun on this item ?

I do not think that I am out of order in giving this as an instance of what is being done in the department. I object in the strongest possible manner to the Public Works Department spending $100,000 to employ architects outside of the department. I claim that the minister should employ a sufficient number of men to do the work in the department and not farm it out in this way to the disadvantage of the public.

I am sorry that my hon. friend should think it necessary, on this small item of $500 to finish certain work on a public building at Brantford:, to go over matters which have been already discussed again and again in this House. Let me say to my hon. friend, with all respect, that repetitions of this kind are actually costing this country more than would erect a new public building. With regard

to Mr. Taylor, the gentleman who supervised this work, he was acting as the clerk of works. My hon. friend must know that there must be somebody on the spot to see that the work is well done; we cannot leave it to the different contractors without supervision; and the item to which my hon. friend makes great objection amounts to $195.42, as will be found at page V-48 of the Auditor General's report. Will any one say that this was an unreasonable sum for looking after a work costing upwards of $13,000?

I find that a namesake of mine, L. H. Taylor-I do not think he is of the same politics, or he would not get it- was paid 2 per cent on $6,173.74 and 5 per cent on $1,014, and $10 for a special report, making $195.42; but I find that the Schultz Bros. Co. were paid for alterations in the post office $3,295, and for sundry repairs $433.12. The money spent does not represent the money on which the architect was paid the commission.
Part of the expenditure was made in previous years.

' If we Jo.k at Y-61, we will find Mr. Taylor figuring again on the construction of armouries at Brantford, on which he was paid $504.86. When a minister comes here and makes a statement, we ought to be able to put it down as being as true as the gospel ; but the hon. gentleman stated that there was only $10,000 paid to outside architects during the last year whereas we find that Mr. Perrault alone, on the new postal station on St. Catherine Street in Montreal and on the plans for the general post office on St. James Street, drew nearly $10,000.
The question was put as to how much we paid out each year for architects, and the chief architect told me he. thought it would not exceed $10,000. taking one year with another.

We find on almost every item we touch that fees are paid to outside architects. I venture to say that if you go through the Auditor General's report you will find that these payments will amount to several hundred thousand dollars.

In case I should be considered wanting in courtesy to the hon. gentleman who alluded to me, I wish to say that when I came in I did not know wnat this discussion was about. I understand that it is on an item for a further expenditure of $500 for some improvements in the existing building in Brantford, on which in the last two or three years there has been $13,000 expended. This expenditure manifests, I think, that the convenience of the people there is not being disregarded. Brantford is a city to which in the past I have owed a good deal; my home was there. Therefore, I would be very pleased to see a
fair measure of justice done to it. I cannot myself see that injustice has been done to it. The member for Grenville (Mr. J. I>. Reid), speaking without full knowledge of the fact, alluded to the Conservative government having erected the present building, and suggested that it might have been partly the cause of my temporary defeat there, because I had not accomplished more with the Liberal government. He is a little wrong there, I was at that time a humble member of the House, and I believe that it was on my recommendation that the public building was given to Brantford. It was given before our Conservative friends came into power the last time, so-if there be any credit for that, though I do not claim credit, as the place deserved the building, it was my representations that the building was put there. Subsequently a large armoury was put there in my time. That was under the Conservative government.
You were then in opposition?

I was in opposition as I was for eighteen years, which the hon. gentlemen will find to be a very long time. The old shed was dilapidated and had lost its roof, and on my representations the building was erected. The city of Brantford contributed one-half the cost, $10,000, doing more in that respect than other municipalities. Since this government came in the armouries have been greatly enlarged, $20,000 or $30,000 have been spent and they are now equal to any in the country. The hon. member for Brantford will admit that this government have not been disposed to slight Brantford simply because it was represented by an opposition member. It is a large and growing city, and we all know that the business has largely increased, possibly to such an extent that at times there may be a little inconvenience. As far as the custom house is concerned, we have room enough to do our business. Of course the climbing of the stairs to the customs house [DOT] and inland revenue office, which, as so often happens, are situated above the post office, is inconvenient, and I think it is right that the! government should ascertain whether the business of Brantford has so increased that the public interest would justify the erection of a new building, perhaps for the post office, giving the whole of the present building to customs and excise. I have no doubt that if representations are made to the minister, he will consider them. My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Coclcshutt) has been re-elected president of the Bell Memorial Fund, an honour which is only his due. That fund is national in one respect and therefore the government felt that they were justified in meeting the request of that committee and granted $10,000. I think

my hon. friend will be generous enough to say that since he has represented the riding the government have not turned a deaf ear to requests by him to which they felt themselves able to accede.
Have any new public building been erected in Brantford since the present administration came into power? -
I am not aware of new buildings but there have been great enlargements and improvements, notably in the armouries.

The revenue from custom duties in 1900 was $178,540.10, and by .annual increases it grew to $225,662.86 in 1905, showing a large increase. The complaint is that there has been no corresponding expenditure to provide better accommodation for those paying the duty, and ciizens in general.

The hon. gentlemen opposite do not want to have money expended simply because the revenue in a particular line has increased, if the existing accommodation will suffice. From the remarks of hon. gentlemen that is evident. My hon. friend has been in Brantford and I have no doubt that the citizens would show him the very handsome building erected by the Mackenzie government many years ago and improved by the present government.

I think the minister did not understand me and did me an injustice. I was not complaining about Mr. Taylor, my objection was not to the payment of so much to one architect, but to the practice of having so much work done by outside architects that should be done by the architects of the department. I do not believe that the work is done as well in the public interest or as economically as it would be if we had well-qualified and properly paid officials in the department to do this work.
Dominion publio buildings-renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., $20,000.

On this item of repairs, improvements and so on, i desire to call the attention of the committee to the fact that an enormous bill is creeping up for furniture and fittings for these several public buildings.

The figures seem almost incredible. There is only one explanation, and it is to be had by referring to the records showing who was the Minister of Public Works at that time. It is no wonder that this man could come to Mr. Hyman and take him by the throat, having all the evidence that he must have had in his possession. and there is a suspicion that some of the stockholders are there as representatives of others.
What is the total capital ?

I notice that it is becoming a habit of deputies, when they attend the House, to intervene very much in matters when any political question is coming to the front. Well, take this Newmarket Company, with Mr. G. M. Reid, of London election fame, as one of the directors -how did they get these contracts ?

If the hon. member (Mr. Bennett) will allow me a moment, I may say that there is not a single item connected with the Office Specialty Company or the Eclipse Specialty Company in the item under discussion. Surely the minister will not say that on a general item which covers the placing of letter boxes in post offices, &c., this discussion is not in order. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is a question of relevancy. This vote is for ' Dominion public buildings-renewals, improvements, repairs, &e.' I do not know what the ' &c.' means. There is another item later in the estimates for the Ottawa public buildings. Another item is $131,000 for public buildings generally. Then there is one for repairs, furniture and heating for Ottawa buildings, specially.
If the hon. gentleman really desires to discuss it upon this item, I will withdraw the objection.

Now this Office Specialty Company sells under these circumstances. Some repairs had to be made in the Barrie post office and tenders were called for. One would have assumed that when tenders were called to furnish public buildings, other contractors would have been asked to tender on the whole thing, but they were not. This Office Specialty Company must have a part out of every appropriation made by this department of Public Works. I am not laying this at the charge of the present Minister of Public Works, because he is innocent as to past transactions, and these are past expenditures that I have referred to. But I want to warn the minister that these two companies are on his heels, and will be on the heels of every Minister of Public Works, because they have been strongly entrenched in the past. Take the Eclipse Company, that is another political company. It is common talk here, if you talk with any person conversant with these matters, that A. W. Fraser, barrister of this city, is one of the large stockholders in that company, and is one of the leading lights of the Liberal party. These two companies have been allowed in the past to secure a monopoly to the extent of selling, in about eight years, no less a grand total than $538,000 worth of furniture. Take some of these returns and look at them. One would imagine that if, for instance, away down in Nova Scotia, the public building at Antig-onish wanted four desks, or four chairs, these could have been purchased from some local manufacturer. Surely the whole pro-



vinee of Nova Scotia can produce chairs, there are furniture dealers there. But under past Ministers of Public Works this furniture is all bought from this favoured company of Mr. Reid. Of course Mr. Reid was taking long chances to act as he did with the ex-Min is ter of Public Works. The evidence alone of this George W. Reid before the commission showed that he was the man who took thirteen men into the riding of West Elgin when the election atrocities were committed there, and among the thirteen men he took in there was Pritchard, the man who admitted on oath that he was concerned in the offending in that riding. Take another place in this return, Saskatoon, three desks, $150, nine chairs, $113.75. Surely furniture can be purchased at Saskatoon. ' There is another case at the Toronto post office. It is true they have a large office there where they seem to sell thousands of dollars worth. Then take another case, London.
I think this company has agencies in various sections.

I should not think they would have an agency in Antigonish. But take the city of London. Apparently Mr. Hyman was in the grip of Mr. Reid, when they had to send down to this Office Specialty Company to buy a $7.50 table. It is not a question of the country really requiring this stuff, but this company has the stuff to sell, and the department has to take it from them. Now how did the department deal with these two favoured companies when it purchased over $538,000 worth ? Under the Act the department is bound to call for tenders, and then there is a nice little game of love taps going on between the Eclipse Company and the Office Specialty Company which results in the Office Specialty Company getting one good job and the Eclipse Company getting another. The country is paying two prices for what it gets from these two companies. The minister has lying in his department an estimate from a firm in the United States for a certain lot of steel fittings to cost $17,000. They could be laid down in Canada for that, freight and customs paid, and actually they paid this Office Specialty Company $22,000 for the same articles.
That estimate was the cost at Washington, including transportation and duty.

Where the prices of labour and transportation are higher than they are in Canada. What was the result ? These American people were not invited to tender at all, and the minister replies by saying, oh well, here are two concerns in Canada who tender.

Is the hon. gentleman prepared to say, according to his memory, that the estimate given by the chief architect was not the cost at Washington, not Mr BENNETT.
of the goods laid down in Canada, but the cost at Washington with the duty and transportation added ?
I admit that it was the cost at Washington, but if they can make and sell the goods for $17,000 at Washington, why can we not make them at Newmarket or Ottawa for the same money ?

That is a very different thing. In a great country like the United States where they have hundreds of thousands of customers, we know that goods can be produced more cheaply than they can be produced in a country where the demand is comparatively small. Why do we find it necessary to protect our manufacturers ? How is it, even with quite a high duty, that we are not able to protect them, and foreign goods do come in ? It is because in the United States, in Great Britain and other countries, they are producing such enormous quantities aud are selling such enormous quantities, that they can cut the price very much below the price at which goods can be sold in this country where the market is comparatively limited. That is the answer I make.

Well, a company that can sell in eight years $322,000 worth " of goods to the government, besides the rest of the Dominion to supply, has not got a very limited market. But this is only on a par with the extravagance in every department of the government to-day, and it is only on a par with the same principle of *benefiting party friends at the expense of the country generally, because there is practically no competition. These are startling figures to go out from this House to the country, that two favoured concerns have, in the past eight years, succeeded in depleting the coffers of this country of $538,278 worth of these supplies. And mark you, there are thousands and hundreds of thousands of dollars paid out in addition to what is paid these two companies, because there are some members of parliament who, I assume, have stood on their rights and have told the Minister of Public Works that if he wanted to buy a chair or a table in their riding for a public building, the department was not to go to George W. Reid and Company to buy it, but they must patronize some local concern. Let any man go through these buildings at Ottawa within the past five or six years and he will understand what it means, they will see furniture thrown out on the snow in winter, splendid hardwood and pine, cupboards and cabinets that would suffice for every purpose of filing, but they have all got to be torn up and thrown out as waste, simply that Mr. Reid's company or Mr. Fraser's company may sell the departments at Ottawa hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of supplies. Now I hope that the minister, with this evidence before him, will call a halt on these two companies, and will

allow -the necessities of the case only to govern purchases in the future, and not buy great quantities of goods when really it is difficult to find a place in the departments to store them.

Is ho in accord with the sentiments or the views of the Minister of Finance?

I think that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance put the matter upon a very reasonable and very fair basis. I understood him to say that even in the case of small towns in a riding in which no public money was being expended; that is to say no money for public buildings, and more especially, if it were a county town-I think perhaps he limited it to that
No, the Minister of Finance did not limit it to a county town.

I think he said a county town. At all events he spoke of one town, and he said it was not unreasonable that a public building should be erected there. But, he further said at the same time that people must be patient, that these things could not all be done at once. While I am on my feet I may say to the hon. gentleman who represents the riding of Dufferin (Mr. Barr) that I am very much pleased to hear him speak so highly of the village in which he lives. I am glad to hear that it is a thriving village, but I may say ta the hon. gentleman that if the village which he represents is entitled .to a public building perhaps he is a little open to the criticism- I do not make it here as a criticism against
him-of not having in any way directed my attention to the necessity which existed for a public building in that locality.

The hon. gentleman must remember that he inis not occupied that position long. I can assure my hon. friend that I did bring it to the notice of his predecessor, and that he promised to give it careful consideration. I thought that consideration was being given to it. However, I will not fail to remind my hon. friend, the good-natured Minister of Public Works, that we are very anxious to have a post office in Shelburne and that we think we should have one.
I think that my hon. friend from Dufferin (Mr. Barr) was hardly to be blamed for not having brought this matter to the attention of the minister.
I did not blame him very seriously.

I had not the opportunity of hearing the minister when he spoke in Montreal the other evening, but I have had the privilege of reading the account of his remarks as published in a newspaper, and I see that he laid down the principle that public buildings were erected for the education of the people, that the people required something in the nature of culture and education in some parts of the country. He declared that where ignorance, stupidity and bigotry reigned, it was necessary that public buildings should be erected. We will see at once why the hon. member for Shelburne had no opportunity of procuring a public building for his town, and why villages of 1,000 inhabitants do obtain them. Up to the time the minister made the explanation. no man in Canada could understand why there was not a public building in Shelburne.

The Minister of Public Works is reported in the press recently to have said that a member from his own province had made an onslaught on him. I do not know to whom the minister refers, whatever suspicion I may have. The minister also stated that the gentleman who made the onslaught on him was not often to be seen in the House. If I had my suspicion in the first instance as to whom the minister was referring that suspicion would be dissipated by this latter statement, because if he was referring to me in his first statement he certainly could not be referring to me in his last statement, because so far as attendance in the House is concerned I have been a more regular attendant than the minister himself. If his remarks with regard to public buildings are not more truthful than these other remarks of his, they are not worthy of much credence.

I represent a large and important constituency and I think I

may say that there is not a single public building in that whole constituency.
What is the size of the largest town in my hon. friend's constituency?

My own town is larger than Glencoe, where you are erecting a public building; it has 1,200 inhabitants. I do not object to the erection of a public building where it is necessary and where the expenditure is not too great, but I have already made representations in this regard with respect to my own constituency and I would like to know why Glencoe in Ontario with 1,030 people should pay $1,250 for a site for a public building when I will guarantee that I will get a site in my own town of 1,200 inhabitants for half that amount. It is about time that the town of Boissevain should have a post office. If I were speaking about the man who has charge of postal affairs in that town for the past live years I would have something to say, but that is not at present under discussion. I rose to make as strong a jilea as I can to the Minister of Public Works to take active steps as early as possible to build a post office in the town of Boissevain, which is larger than the town of Glencoe.
My hon. friend comes from a town which has a population of 1,200 aud he urges very strongly that it would be a proper expenditure of public money to erect a public building in that town.
Yes.
My hon. friend is entitled to speak for his constituency and if he makes a proper representation to me I will be very glad to consider it between this and next session.

Let me tell the Minister of Public Works that for several years I have impressed on his department the necessity for erecting public buildings in the riding I represent. We have some large towns in that constituency, but yet there is not a public building within its borders. Delegations have come from one of these towns on different occasions asking that a public building be erected there, but no action has been taken and in the meantime little villages all over Canada, one-third the size of any one of three towns in my riding, and where there is no warrant, comparatively speaking, for the erection of a public building, have been favourably considered by the government. There is in my riding a town of 3,000 population, giving a postal revenue of $5,000 a year, and there are two others which give a slightly smaller revenue, and these towns deserve consideration from the government.
I.	have urged the matter on the attention of the government and delegations have Mr. SCHAF.VNEB.
come here to support my representations, but yet there is no sign in the estimates that any provision is to be made. Is there any underlying principle which guides the department in this matter? They seem to follow a happy-go-lucky method by which little villages get consideration and large towns are neglected. It is time some principle should be laid down which would guide those who are administering public affairs in this matter. We have gone on too long on this principle of spending public money without any consideration as to the requirements of the case.
What is the name of the town in which the hon. gentleman thinks a public building should be erected?
If you give me any encouragement to think that you will make use of the information to give the matter consideration I will name you three towns in my riding.
I will consider it carefully.
Bracebridge, Huntsville and Gravenhurst.

I came in as a new minister last summer and if I have not before heard from my hon. friend that there was necessity for a public building in any one of these places he can hardly blame me for not having provision made in the estimates. I have not hitherto, directly or indirectly, had any representation from my hon. friend that there should be a building erected in any of these towns. Of course, in considering whether we should at once erect public buildings in the riding the hon. gentleman represents, it must be remembered that there is a very urgent demand, which does not seem to be unreasonable, for the expenditure of money on public wharfs in that constituency, and it may be that the people of that riding have felt that it would be more desirable, at present at all events, to have money expended in affording facilities for transportation and trade rather than in erecting public buildings. That consideration may have had some influence. I may say that the question of giving increased wharf accommodation in the hon. gentleman's constituency is receiving my very earnest attention, and I hope I may be able to meet the very reasonable expectations of the people in that respect. With regard to public buildings, I will also say that I take the way in which my hon. friend has approached the question to-day as an expression of his desire that there should be more public buildings there, and I will give that matter my earnest attention.

The minister lays down the rule that we must make our applications to every new minister. I under-

stood that we made application to the department, and that that department had an official head and a deputy head, and that a record would be kept of the applications that were made. But if every time there is a change in the Minister of Public Works we have to renew our applications, it is as well that we should understand that. However, with regard to wharfs. 1 may say that there have been two or three built in my constituency since this government came into power, probably costing ail told $20,-
000.	As to that, I am not making any great complaint, as I have seen a deputation who waited on the minister a week or so ago, and they have stated that he distinctly pledged himself to put a sum in the estimates for a wharf at the town of Graven-hurst. I do not know whether that has been definitely decided upon, or has been merely taken into consideration.
Nothing is definitely decided on until it appears before the House in the estimates.
I do not know whether there has yet been a requisition for a post office in Aylmer, Ont.
Not to my knowledge.
I may tell the hon. minister that we have been promised a post office for the last fifteen years, and the promise generally comes just before a general election.
That would take it back to about 3893.

We had a promise of a post office from the old government, but did not get it. However, I am living in one of the nicest towns, as far as business is concerned, in Canada. I think the hon. Minister of Customs will bear me out in that; he has been in our town, and we are always pleased to have him. I have been living there about thirty years. I have no objection to any town getting a public building. Glencoe is a smart business town, but it does not compare with the town of Aylmer. The population of Aylmer is about 2,500. It is a manufacturing center. The post office is inappropriate to the town. We have also a custom house which is not in keeping with the character of the place. I would like to have a promise if I can get one from the minister to amend matters for us. We have not only a beautiful town, but a tine country. I do not think the hon. Minister of Public Works has ever been in that section. We would be glad to have him come, even at election time. We are always glad to see distinguished gentlemen come there, no matter what their politics are. During my campaign we were visited by five very prominent gentlemen who are sitting in this House the hon. Minister of Justice, the hon. Mr. Hyman, the hon. gentleman who has just left the chair, the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) and the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), and you know the result-to me it was very satisfactory. North Bay is a town that does not compare with Aylmer, and you are spending $66,000 on a public building there. Welland has a population of 1,863, and is getting a new post office costing about $27,000. Leamington is another place which 1 understand is to get a post office building. It has about the same population as Aylmer, and is a very beautiful little town. I would be very glad to have the views of the minister as to giving Aylmer a post office building, which we have been promised for years.

I may say that considering what a very nice, progressive town Aylmer is, its population, and the energetic representative it has, I am certainly surprised that although I have been here for several months, I have never heard from the hon. gentleman that there was the slightest feeling among the people that there should be a public building at Aylmer. It may be that the people of Aylmer have heard so much talk on the part of the opposition about the great extravagance which has been shown in the erection of public buildings in various cities and towns, that they have been rather timid in making application for a public building. But, from the discussion which has taken place to-day, I am very glad to see that there is such a consensus of opinion in favour of going to a reasonable expenditure in giving to the people in thriving towns accommodation in the way of public buildings. My hon. friend must not expect us to attend to all the wants of the people at once. We have to proceed reasonably, in a way which may appear to some people to be somewhat too slow. I am sure the hon. gentleman will not expect us to rush at once into the construction of public buildings all over the country. We must look to the wants of the people, and as these wants are urged upon our attention, endeavour to supply the reasonable needs of the people. I shall be very glad if I can have the opportunity of visiting Aylmer and shall be only too happy to take into consideration the wants of the town.	j

I wish to correct a statement of a few moments ago, as to the revenue of Glencoe and Shelburne. The revenue of Glencoe is $2,150.80 and that of Shelburne, $2,670.21. The expenditures in Glencoe were $816.65 and in Shelburone $991.18. We are not complaining about the progress that is being made in the country in the building of post offices and public buildings, all we complain of is that they are not distributed properly and we say they should be placed where there is the largest population and where the largest revenue is brought into the treasury, not in accord-

ance with some influence that may be brought to bear.
I understand you entirely approve of what we are doing but complain that we do not go far enough.
I neglected to state that I have the honour to represent a riding having 22,000 population and we have not a government building in that riding.

I wish to urge a suggestion which I have made unsuccessfully to several Ministers of Public Works, that a regulation should be adopted that all public buildings should be isolated from other buildings, that some safe distance, possibly 100 feet, should be left between public buildings and other buildings. In this case, for instance. I am sure that for the money spent in Glencoe the minister could have procured a square in which the building could have been placed

That is very desirable undoubtedly, but in cities especially it would very greatly add to the cost. As to the cost of land in Glencoe this is a comer lot, 100 by 165 feet; my information is that Glencoe is in the centre of a very rich and progressive agricultural district, and is quite an important railway centre. The price is $1,250 and I think my hon. friend is entirely mistaken in saying that the cost is too high.

I think it only fair to place on ' Hansard ' what the minister did say on the occasion referred to. He is reported in the Montreal ' Gazette ' of last Monday as saying :
In fact he believed that any government would also be justified in spending a limited amount on public buildings in quarters where other expenditure was not large, so as to cultivate public taste, to stimulate citizens and make the people contented and proud of the locality in which they lived.
I would ask him what amount of lethargy, discontent and lack of pride must he manifested before the minister will give a locality a public building ?

The report from which the hon. gentleman has read, while it gives a portion of the remarks I had the honour to make on the occasion to which he refers, does not profess to be a verbatim report. Some of the observations I made which are not contained in it would somewhat qualify the remarks quoted making my statement more in accordance with what I have said here to-day.
If the minister was mis-reported, would he repeat what he did say ?
I did not say that I was misreported, but some remarks were left out which would qualify those printed.

The minister might have answered that where the population of the district had shown discontent, lack of pride and lethargy by electing a Liberal representative, it would be necessary to give them a public building.

Again referring to the advertising, I stated that the newspaper having the largest circulation in the section of the country where the money we are now asked to vote is to be expended, Is the London * Free Press,' a morning newspaper. The London ' Free Press ' had a circulation-

I suppose my hon. friend would not for a moment think that I would wish him to justify the waste of the time of the House and the country beyond tbe extent to which he has wasted it this afternoon, by asking him for information as to the circulation of the London ' Free Press.' Do not let him excuse himself by suggesting any such request by me.

I am not paying any serious attention to what my hon. friend stated. I asked him the policy of his department in respect of advertising for public buildings. He was unable to state the policy and said in reply that when he was considering the advertisements that were to be published in newspapers for this public building now under discussion he would consider it. The London ' Free Press ' had a circulation of 20,012 on April 26, 1908. As to the London ' Advertiser,' although the figures are not published in the paper itself, I am informed on the very best authority that the circulation of that newspaper is less than 12,000 and it is an evening newspaper, the circulation being largely in the city of London, while the other circulates in every part of western Onario. The hon. gentleman is going to advertise for tenders for a building to be constructed at Glencoe. I am asking whether he will select the leading newspaper or will reject it for its politics. I do not expect an answer from him. Nor am I consulting the hon. gentleman particularly as to the waste of time he is causing tins afternoon. I am directing his attention to facts which are worthy of his consideration, if he intends to spend the public money appropriated for advertising in that way to do the most good. But, if he proposes to spend it in the interests of his political party, as he has been doing, the information I have submitted will be of no value to him, and will not be taken note of. Now,
I would like to ask out of what vote passed last year was $1,250 paid for this site ? Also has tbe site been paid for?
The site has been paid for, the money being taken out of an appropriation of $5,000 passed last year.
What will be the cost of the building ?

Something about $20,-
000.
Including heating and everything ?
Yes.
Is this a customs port of entry ?
Yes, customs as well.

Lest the minister should think me remiss, as he has suggested other gentlemen have been, I would call his attention to the fact that in the county I have the honour to represent there are three towns, more important, I believe, than Glencoe, and certainly more important than Knowlton with its 760 population wfrich has been given a post office building. These towns are known to him, but not so well, probably as to me. St. Andrews, in the county of Charlotte, is one of the most important watering places on our Atlantic sea-board, and one of the oldest towns in eastern Canada.
What is its population ?

About 1,300 or 1,400. Then, there is Milltown, an important manufacturing place, with a cotton mill employing about 800 hands, and St. George with large industries. All these are incorporated towns. If it is necessary for us to repeat our applications to every new Minister of Public Works who comes into office, and if the changes are to be as frequent as they have been in the last ten years, I think an officer shpukl be appointed and blank forms supplied so that these applications may be kept before the head of the department without undue labour. I observe that the minister has adroitly passed over the question suggested by the hon. member for Duf-ferin (Mr. Barr) and others as to the general policy of the government in regard to these buildings. I hope he will take note of the three towns to which I have called attention.

In my county I have a town which I believe is more important than Glencoe, the town of Kemptville, which has a population of about 2,000, and a postal revenue of $2,600 or $2,700. But we have other places where public buildings are more necessary than in Glencoe, though I am not objecting to this Glencoe public building. Take, for instance, the town of Morrisburg on the St. Lawrence, a place of about 3,000 people and a fine town. In view of these cases, I think there should be some statement from the minister as to his policy.

It is nearly six o'clock, but before the committee rises, I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. D. Reid) whether he is opposing this vote for Glencoe or whether it is that he thinks that others ought to be included ?

This appropriation for Glencoe has my approval, and would have my vote if necessary. But I say that there are other places requiring public buildings. whose cases should be considered. There was a case mentioned a little while ago of a towTn in Quebec with about 700 population, which is given a post office. These cases indicate that some special influence must be brought to bear to direct the action of the government in these matters. For instance, in the case of Glencoe, probably the chief whip of the other side (Mr. Calvert) must have brought pressure to bear on the minister in favour of that place, for I do not think this post office is given to Glencoe because of the great interest the Minister of Public Works takes in that village.

The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) must not go out and say that the members of the opposition are pressing for increased expenditure. It is quite plain what my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) is asking for, and I want to put myself right-and I am sure I speak for others about me. The opposition say that the government spends enormous sums of the public money uselessly, and that the government has no policy except a political policy in the spending of this money. A village represented by a Reformer is given a post office, but an important town represented by a Liberal Conservative receives no appropriation for that purpose. That is what we object to. And we object to the increased expenditure of this country and say that it ought to be reduced.

I would ask the minister if plans and specifications of this building in Glencoe have been prepared so as to show not only the cost of the building, but the cost of heating, fittings and furniture as well? The committee will then know exactly what this building is going to cost before we vote this money. The minister will remember that a few days ago I drew his attention to this point, that before any money should be voted for the erection of a public building the minister should state definitely the outside amount he proposed to expend so that the committee may know how the money of this country is going to be expended. I for one would object to this vote going through unless the minister is prepared to say that full specifications have been prepared, and that every dollar he intends to put into the building has been determined, and that it is the purpose of the government that this amount should not be exceeded. I hold that is the only way in which the expenditure can be controlled. If the minister is not prepared to say how much money he is going to expend on this building, I think he had better let the item stand until such time as he has arrived at,a conclusion. I am not very particular as to the amount, but I want a definite promise from the min-

ister so that those of us who may be here next year when another vote is asked for will know whether the government is prepared to abide by its estimates.

This is a re vote. There was a vote of $5,000 last year. The site has been purchased, and the chief architect has been instructed to prepare the plans and to limit the total expenditure to $20,000, and he assures me that he will see the expenditure does not exceed that amount.
