SUPPLY-CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION REPORT-Mr. JUSTICE CASSELS.
Mr. FIELDING moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I desire to make some observations to the House with respect to the report of the Civil Ser-

vice Commission. That report lias naturally attracted a good deal of attention, not only in the House but throughout the country as well. I was somewhat misled when I first took up a copy of this report, because in glancing over it hurriedly 1 imagined for the moment that I had in my hands some of the campaingn literature issued by hon. gentlemen opposite in the good old days before they were elected to office. At page 37 of the report I observed the following remarks :
It is true that the salaries of most of the civil servants are not equal to what they were thirty or forty years ago, in consequence of the greatly increased cost of living, the obvious and logical result of our wasting, impoverishing and demoralizing system of protection.
That phrase has a singularly familiar sound. I commend it to my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) as the report of one of his own commissioners who seem to entertain a different view of the present tariff from that which the hon. gentleman is so ready to place before us. There is this difference however in the character of this utterance as compared with that of similar utterances which were made by hon. gentlemen opposite in the days gone by. The utterance of Mr. Fyshe-as any man who knows him will be willing to testify-is absolutely sincere and would be the rule of his conduct if he were in power to-morrow. But the similar pledges of these hon. gentlemen opposite, though made with all the vehemence of Mr. Fyshe, were utterly forgotten when they attained the power to fulfil them.
Coming to the report itself, it naturally deals with the subject of civil service reform. I do not intend to speak of legislative reform to-day at any great length because I do not desire to forestall my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) who has had on the Order Paper a motion with regard to that particular subject which he intends bringing before the House, and which he dropped some time ago because the report we are now considering had not been printed. Civil Service reform had its commencement in England early in the last century. It hadits origin then in an attempt to reform the Indian civil service. Some advance was made later on in 1832 ; and in 1854 or 1855, the government of Great Britain, being unable to obtain the assent of parliament, took the matter into their own hands and determined by executive action that appointments to the civil service should be made upon merit alone and from men selected after competitive examination. Parliament shortly afterwards fell into line, and to-day the civil service of Great Britain challenges and commands the admiration of the world. Not only in Great Britain has the work of civil service reform made itself manifest to the Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
advantage of the country. Had not a similar service been accomplished in India, even before reform was brought about in England, we would in all likelihood see a very different condition of affairs in India to-day. Were it not for the reform of the civil service in India, I verily believe that the power of Great Britain in that country would probably have come to a termina-ation before this, and the fact that that great country is to-day ruled-ruled well and wisely I believe-by the British Crown is due, as much as to anything else, to the education, the status and the character of the men who belong to the Indian civil service and who have given just and equitable government to the people of that country.
In the speech which I made in Halifax on the 20th August last, I said that the Conservative party favoured a thorough and complete reformation of the laws relating to the civil service so that future appointments shall be made by an independent commission acting on the report of examiners. Some of the government organs say the government propose to bring in a measure on that line. I for one would be prepared to assist them in every way if they did, and I believe that the result would be a more enduring monument to their memory than anything they have accomplished during the twelve years they have been in power.
Let us consider one difference between the system which prevails in Great Britain and that which prevails in this country. In Great Britain the policy of every department is dominated by a political head, and its administration by a permanent head. Upon a change of government, the affairs of every department go on as before without any change except that which may be brought about by a change of policy, instituted by the political head of the department. That is a system which has not been so much in force in this country. In this country the political head of the department takes a greater or smaller share in the administration of the department itself. I believe that the British system is on the whole the best, although I am not insensible to some advantages which may be claimed for our system in a new country such as Canada, where the political head of the department may be very thoroughly in touch with the particular needs and aspirations of some interests under his special jurisdiction.
But even under the English system, what is the constitutional rule as to political responsibility? That rule is well known. I have quoted it many times in this House. Let me repeat it once again because it is very short. The rule will be found in Todd at volume 1, page 628. as follows :
As a necessary consequence of the division of the civil service into political and non-polit-

ical officers, and of the acknowledged supremacy of the members of the administration over all the subordinate employees, it is required by our parliamentary system that every branch of the public service should be represented, either directly or indirectly, in the houses of parliament. This duty is performed by the political heads, who are themselves solely responsible for every act of administration down to the minutest details of official routine. Having entire control over the public departments, they are bound to assume responsibility for every official act, and not to permit blame to be imputed to any subordinate for the manner in which the business of the country is transacted, except only in cases of personal misconduct, for which the political chiefs have the remedy in their own hands.
Surely no man can claim that in this country, where the political head takes a greater share in the administration than in Great Britain, there is any less responsibility upon the political head than in Great Britain.
I do not propose to deal at any length to-day with the subject of civil service reform by legislation. Let me, however, simply say that the requisites of civil service reform are that ability and industry must be recognized and must count, that there must be a sense of responsibility and that the civil service must not be a mere machine. Appointments upon merit and the recognition of merit in promotions must lead to a cultivation of individual initiative, which ought to tend very greatly towards raising the standard of the civil service in this country. This is recognized and expressed better than I have expressed it in the report itself, and I shall conclude my remarks upon this portion of the subject by expressing the hope that we shall bring about in Canada such legislative and administrative reform that Canada shall have not the worst, but the best system of civil service extant. Great corporations in Canada, dealing with this question upon common sense business lines and with honest and intelligent endeavour, have a splendid service where merit is recognized and receives promotion. If these great corporations can have such a service why cannot we have the same and why should we continue in the public service of Canada a system in which, according to this report, the evils of political patronage make themselves manifest at every step and upon every inspection?
Let us look for a moment at what the commissioners state in their report-and this is the report of gentlemen appointed by this government, gentlemen in whom they have confidence, and in whom they stili say they have confidence-and see what these gentlemen say as to the working of the political pull, of the patronage system, under the present government. At page 13 of the report, from which I shall be obliged to quote very freely for the purpose of making my points, as I prefer to
use its exact language instead of attempting to paraphrase it from memory, we read:
Your commissioners have so far dealt with the paragraph in the order of reference, stating that ' while the general principles of the Civil Service Act are regarded as satisfactory, &c., &c.' From the inquiries made by the commissioners and the evidence submitted to them they are constrained to declare that they are unable to agree with the expression of opinion contained in the order of reference, and they are of opinion that the repeal of the Act is really the best course to pursue in the public interest. What should be given in its place the commissioners will state when they come to that part of the report in which they make recommendations.
Let us now see some of the grounds at least upon which they put forward this statement respecting the present working of the Civil Service Act. Ou the same page they say :
The commissioners also find that in order to meet the pressure brought upon the several departments by influential politicians to take on assistants, officials who have not passed the examinations are employed temporarily and are called labourers. Patronage seams to run more or less through every department of the public service.	\
Again, on page 14, speaking of a particular branch of the post office, the commissioners state :
In that special branch of the public service politics was found, as a rule, to play an important part. The commissioners consider from the evidence submitted to them that on the part of responsible officials of the several departments, especially in the outside service, there is a dread of the politician, and every bit of strategy is resorted to to circumvent the carrying out of the patronage system.
On page 15 the commissioners say :
Your commissioners found in their rounds that a collector of customs, a city postmaster, a post office inspector and others were appointed politically. The recent appointment of a postmaster at Kingston was on the recommendation of the patronage committee ; the last appointment to the postmastership at Montreal, the most important in the Dominion, was given to an aged member of parliament, 67 years old.
And further on :
It is the political element in the Act which, from time to time, has become more aggressive and which has steadily tended to deteriorate the public service. It would seem to the commissioners that the great prosperity of the country during the last fifteen years has been such that able men, who were formerly attracted to the service of the state have now ceased to look to the rewards of that service and have turned their attention to other avocations in which they see prospects of higher emoluments, with' the result that inefficient and inferior men, unable to obtain better positions in the outside world, through political operations and other means, have been

brought into the service; whatever the cause the tendency is more and more to lower the standard of the civil service with the consequent detriment to the business of the state.
Again, at page 19, we find further evidence with respect to this :
In other instances of temporary employment people who have failed to pass the necessary examination, through political pressure or otherwise, have been unloaded on the departments when help is necessary, and to overcome the provisions of the Act are graded as labourers or some such designation.
These are sweeping statements, and if they are true-and they have not been denied up to the present-they are statements that show that the system of patronage carried on openly and avowedly by this government has seriously deteriorated the public service of this country during the twelve years they have been in power. But this is not all. On the same page of their report I find :
Your commissioners consider that in many cases promotions have been forced on the several departments owing to political influence; that the officials promoted do the same work as they performed in the lower grade, and, as has been mentioned before, promotions have taken place as a rule for other causes than the necessities of the service.
Can anything be more damaging, can anything be more of a condemnation of the government than a statement such as that ? How is the power of appointment to public office, or the power of promotion in public office to be regarded ? Is it not to be regarded as a public trust; is it not a trust as sacred as the duty of the government to deal fairly and honestly and wisely with the revenues of this country? When we find three men, political friends of this government, able men, representative men, men whose ability and wisdom and honesty have not been doubted, deliberately stating in this report as they have done, that not the interests of the service but political pull has dominated the appointments to and promotions in the public service, surely we would be justified in expecting that before this date-because this report has been before the House for more than a month- the government or some member of the government would have given some explanation or contradiction of the statement I have just read.
But that is not all. On page 27 of the report the commissioners state :
As a rule your commissioners found in the outside service that politics enter into every appointment, and politicians on the spot interest themselves not only in the appointments but in subsequent promotions of officers. While at Ottawa the departments generally are administered with a good consideration for the public interest, yet in the outside service the politics of the party is of greater importance in making appointments and pro-Mr. R. L. BORDEN
motions than the public interests of the Dominion.
I invite the attention of the right hon. gentleman and of every member of the government to this portion of the commissioners' report. The statement there made calls for observation from the government, and cannot fail, under present conditions, to arouse very great distrust among the people of this country. Again on page 28 :
In the outside service those who have the 'political pull' use it for all it is worth; they pass by their superior officers and bring pressure to procure anythin^ that may prove to their advantage.
On page 29 reference is made to the Department of Customs :
The chief positions in the outside service of this department are political appointments. Every collector of customs has been appointed from the ranks of the party in power at the moment.
Then on the same page, speaking of the same department:
Curious facts were brought to light in the inquiries into the outside service. At Montreal, for instance, there were found two binding waiters, one appointed in 1871 and the other in 1891, the one doing duty at the Bonaventure station and the other at the Dalkousie square station, both equally good men. The officer appointed in 1871, according to the last Civil Service list, after 36 years of service, obtained' a salary of $750. The officer appointed in 1891, with 20 years less service, obtained a salary of $1,000; and when inquiry was made the collector informed the commissioners that a most prominent influential citizen of Canada who could not be refused had been approached by the friends of the officer who was appointed in 1891, and having inquired into the matter, insisted that his protege should have an increase in salary.
So that not only does appointment to public office depend upon political pull and upon patronage, not only does promotion in office depend upon political pull and patronage, but the very salaries paid out of the public exchequer of this country are doled out to one or other civil service employee according to the amount of political pull he can summon to his aid. But that Is not all.
May I ask if that was not a circumstance that took place under the old government and not under this?

Well, I always was under the impression that the hon. gentleman did not regard the old government as the exemplar of all the virtues; and I have always been under the Impression that the hon. gentleman, when he paraded this country from 1878 to 1896, proclaimed loudly the reforms he would bring about. If the hon. gentleman, after a circumstance of that kind is brought to his attention, has

no better answer to give than to say that the Conservative party which he condemned from one end of the country to the other, did the same thing, then I think he ought to resign his office and get out of public life.

I am making no defence for anything I have done, I am asking the hon. gentleman a question. He says the public service has deteriorated under this administration, he cites this Act where political pull was exercised and I ask him whether the case occurred under my administration of the Customs Department or under the previous administration.
I made no comments, I simply asked a question.

I am not making these comments myself, I am reading the report of the commissioners appointed by the Minister of Customs and his colleagues. In order to make it perfectly plain I will read it again to the hon. gentleman.
No, read the evidence.

Am I not entitled to read the report of the commission appointed by this government? I do not know whether the commissioners have been paid by this government, but they were appointed by this government, and I presume they were paid for their services. They made this report
The report is supposed to be founded on evidence.
Does the hon. gentleman intimate that the report is untrue or incorrect?
As I read the report, I was under the impression that this particular case they refer to took place under the previous government. If I am wrong, I would like to be set right.
Ij. BORDEN. Well, in the name of all that is sensible what would the hon. gentleman argue if the evidence discloses that ?
I looked to see, and I think so, but I may be mistaken.
You had better look again. You want to get your work done for you.

I will read another paragraph :
In Toronto your commissioners ^ found that the senior officer in point of service who was appointed an 1896 was the fourth in point of seniority. The collector, surveyor and cashier were all his juniors, although drawing larger salaries than he receives. There is no question of the integrity and ability of the officer in question. The only suggestion which the commissioners can make in regard to the outside service of the customs is to
have the department absolutely divorced from political influence, and have all the appointments put upon the basis of merit.
Further on, on page 30 :
Of course, in the Inland Revenue Department, political appointments, as in other branches of the public service, prevail.
Further, on page 31:
Every postmaster is appointed politically, and the number of what are called city post offices is small. Hundreds of post offices are used for the benefit of politicians rather than the benefit of the state. Only recently has it been pointed out in the public papers that the postmastership at Kemptville has been vacant for six months, and your commissioners are of opinion that until the political system in use in the outside service is entirely abolished, notwithstanding all the business methods adopted by the department, efficiency will not follow.
On page 37, after referring to some of the evils which had been demonstrated in the administration of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the commissioners use this language :
The political pull has much to do with this; and no radioal improvement need ever be expected until the political pull is completely eliminated from all branches of the service.
On page 42, speaking of the public works service, they say:
In certain cases there may be over-payments of wages such as the notorious instance which was brought to light about a year ago, when a clerk of works appointed by political influences was found to have sublet his work to another person at a much lower rate.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have read from the report of the commissioners enough to indicate, not only the evil of the political pull and patronage system, but the fact that it has been in continuous activity since this government has been in power, and that through the active oper-' ation of that system much of the inefficiency, much of the extravagance, and much of the waste found by these commissioners in the administration of the public departments, are due. They further declare that the Civil Service Act which leaves full sway to the patronage system has often been evaded. They point out on page 13 that it is continually evaded by parliamentary votes:
That for the year ending March 31, 1906, during the last session of parliament, over 50 votes were passed with the saving clause ' notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act.'
And they declare :
It is known to the commissioners that many of the votes, not having that clause attached to them now, have had it in previous years.

They declare further :
It is the belief of the commissioners that hardlv a vote to pay the several classes of the public service has been passed, during one sesion or another, without adding the limitation already noted.
The opposition have called attention to this evil on many occasions during recent years, and they have pointed out the constitutional difficulty, which is not noticed by the commissioners. That is very obvious to any one who considers it for a moment. Both Houses have passed a Civil Service Act, and a repeal pro tanto of that Act is annexed every year by this House to the appropriation Bill which cannot be amended, but which can only be rejected as a whole by the upper House, and as a result the House of Commons repeals pro tanto an enactment made with the sanction of both branches of the legislature, and it does that against all constitutional usage and custom. Then they point out, at page 13 and again at page 31, that the Act is evaded by improper classification. They say:
It would seem that in the four post offices examined into by the commission, letter carriers were employed to do high grade duty and duties of clerks, that they are still designated on the pav-list as letter carriers; that in consequence of a desire on the part of the officials not to bring these letter carriers in their uniforms to the public notice, they to their loss have been deprived of their uniforms as well as their street car fares
On page 31 they allude to the same subject:
Your commissioners found that in all the post office branches, officials were employed who had failed to pass the examination laid down by the Act, and who were designated as labourers although in many instances doing clerks' work. If the Civil Service Act is to be of effect your commissioners are of opinion that this incongruous state of affairs should be brought to an end as quickly as possible.
Then they found a further evasion by means of what is called ' temporary employment,' and their remarks in regard to that are on pages 18 and 19:
So-called temporary clerks are constantly admitted to the service and remain in the service until their death. There are temporary employees at Ottawa who have been there for thirty or forty years. In other instances of temporary employment people who have failed to pass the necessary examination, through political pressure or otherwise, have been unloaded on the departments when help is neces sary and to overcome the provisions of the Act are graded as labourers or some such designation.
It goes back thirty or forty years. It is obvious that some of these men must have been taken on by administrations which preceded the present one, but the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) will remember

that we have brought this matter up over and over again in this House, particularly upon his estimates and.upon the estimates of other ministers as well, and have urged that there was every reason in the public interest why these men, if they are to be retained indefinitely, should be put on the permanent staff and brought thoroughly within the provisions of the Civil Service Act. Then, it is pointed out, at pages 14 and 42 of the report, that a very large number in the employment of the government are not under the Civil Service Act at all. I will not read that portion of the report as hon. gentlemen can consult it for themselves.
The commissioners deal with the question of suitable remuneration, and I agree entirely that it is a question of the utmost possible importance. The recommendations of the commission should be taken into consideration by the government at the very earliest possible moment. Although I have not had the opportunities of studying it that are possessed by lion, gentlemen on the treasury benches, my own opinion of the civil service, as we see it at Ottawa at the present time, is that it is over-manned and underpaid. I believe that men have been introduced into- the departments of the government by means of political patronage and political pull who are not wanted there, and that if the officers of the government, the heads of the different branches in these departments, were consulted and their evidence taken fully and frankly many of them would state that men have been brought into their departments whom they did not want, and whom they found to be absolutely useless. As far as many officials are concerned I believe they are underpaid and that men doing the same amount of work in the service of the great corporations and institutions of this country are better paid thaw the average civil servant is at the present time. This, however, is a subject that I do not intend to dwell upon. It will no doubt come to the attention of the House later on in the session.
The commissioners deal also with the necessity of a pension system, and their observations in that regard are worthy of being quoted. At page 21 they use this language :
At the outset your commissioners consider it a subject of regret that the Superannuation Act, which had been in force for over twenty-seven years, should have been repealed, and the present Retirement Act put in its place. To the commissioners the repeal seems most illogioal; when it is found that within a few years after its repeal Pension Acts have been placed on the statute-book providing for pensions to the members of the Northwest Mounted Police; the staff of the Intercolonial Railway, the members of the Permanent Corps and Headquarters Staff, and other employees under the Militia Department, as well as to their widows and families, it would seem that the

action in abolishing the Superannuation Act was not only illogical but hasty and inconsiderate.
So would think any person who has made a study at all of conditions as they prevail in this country at the present time. There is hardly a large corporation, such as a railway company or a banking company in Canada, that does not provide pensions for its employees after a certain age. Not only does it provide pensions for its employees, but it provides that there shall be an allowance under certain conditions to the widows and children of its officers after their death ; so that any man entering the service of one of these corporations has not only the assurance of a competence during his own old age, but he can feel absolutely certain that those who are dear to him and whom he may leave behind him will not suffer in want and poverty after he is gone. The government found a Superannuation Act upon the statute-book. No one pretends that it was perfect, but it might have been amended and brought up to the standard of the present day. Instead of moulding it in that way the government abolished it, and they provided a retiring allowance which these commissioners find to be absolutely inadequate and insufficient. They touch the subject further on in the report, at page It!. I will take the opportunity of quoting what they say there:
Your commissioners have in conclusion to point out that they are unanimously agreed that a comprehensive superannuation system should be placed on the statute-book; and- that this system in the present state of the Dominion should include pen sions to dependents of civil servants for there seems little doubt that with the exception of slight set backs the conditions of life in the Dominion are and are likely to be such that advances in prices of commodities will be the rule, and it will be almost impossible for the average civil servant to effect any savings from his salary. With that view your commissioners consider that the time has arrived when an efficient pension system should be put into force.
Now, I come, Mr. Speaker, to that portion of the report of the commissioners in regard to the administration of the different departments. Let me express my conviction that the government never intended that these commissioners should make any such examination of, or any such investigation into the several departments as that which they have attempted in the time at their disposal. In fact, we have heard rumours throughout the country, we have heard opinions freely expressed by certain stalwart Liberals, that the matter went wrong through the absence of the right lion. Prime Minister last May, and that if he had been here this order in council never would have passed in any such terms as would have permitted this investigation. But, if we had entertained any doubt as to the intentions
of the government in that regard, my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ayles-worth) with his accustomed caudour, has made the matter perfectly clear. He has pointed out that the government, never, for one moment, dreamed of the slightest investigation into the administration of any of the departments.
Well, Sir, we know from their record in this parliament that that statement of the Minister of Justice is absolutely true. When did they ever grant an investigation into any department? Two years ago when I moved for an investigation into the Department of the Interior with regard to the disposal of public lands, the Prime Minister declared that no investigation would be permitted; that if charges were made, they would be investigated, but in the meantime they would deny us such investigation and access as would permit us to make charges even if these charges were well founded. What was the attitude of the right hon. gentleman with regard to the Department of Marine and Fisheries ? After he himself had stated in this House that that department was not being well administered, he followed it up by bringing down a motion not to investigate the department but to find out whether or not the steamship 'Arctic' was physically capable of holding the stores which were said to have been placed in her. And when I moved in amendment that the whole Department of Marine and Fisheries should be investigated, the Prime Minister said that our words and our proposals were simply froth and wild talk. Does he now think the report of this Civil Service Commission froth and wild talk ? I venture to say that if he had permitted that investigation into the Department of Marine which we asked for two years ago in this House, all that is in this report and a good deal more would have been made known to the people of Canada long ago.
Let me bring to the attention of the House the charmingly candid words in which the Minister of Justice has made it plain that the Civil Service Commission took the government by surprise. In his speech on the 28th of April the Minister of Justice said :
I said on that occasion what I have no hesitation in saying again and what any hon.gentleman who reads the mandate to these commissioners can at one see for himeslf, namely: that they stepped altogether outside of that which was defined to them as their jurisdiction when they made a report at length which they have made with regard to the different departments of the governmental service. They were appointed to inquire into the operation of the Civil Service Act; they were not appointed to inquire into the administration of the general departments of the government service.
Further on he said :
I am simply pointing out, not in any way of attaok or even of criticism upon their work,

that they did undoubtedly go beyond the commission of inquiry issued to them in what they have reported.
And further on :

Let us read the conclusions of the commissioners with regard to the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
There are officers enough in the department, both inside and outside, to do all the work efficiently, if they were properly trained and organized: but there is no efficient organization.
Who was responsible for the organization ? The government of this country, especially the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; but every man who sits on the treasury benches is politically responsible for that lack of organization.
The only attempt at it is the appointment of men whose titles would seem to indicate what their duties are; but those duties have never been specifically defined. There is no record of anything of the kind, and there are no written or printed rules and regulations known in the service, which the commissioners think is lamentable.
Suppose that an investigation were made into the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway and that conditions such as those described in this report as existing in the Department of Marine and Fisheries were found, would it be proper for Mr. Hays or Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, as the head of the company to say: Oh, the responsibility is altogether with my subordinate officers and I will immediately institute an inquiry and take steps to have them punished ?
It is practically impossible to fix responsibility on anybody. The deputy is supposed to shoulder responsibility for everything as his signature shows; but that means that he speaks for ' the department,' and ' the department,' like the King, can do no wrong. There seems to be a huge redundancy of work which proceeds in a lumbering, haphazard way, giving rise to constant blundering and confusion. There is no sign visible of a single directing head, or an intelligent purpose, unless it be that of spending as much money as possible.
Who is responsible for the expenditure in that department? The government of

this country are solely responsible and the minister at the head of that department is, of course, especially responsible.
Zeal for economy and good management or pride in the work, is not visible. Perfunctory and mechanical discharge of duties is the rule, with apparently no perception of any need for improvement.	.
How long has this department been in that state, and is it possible that those conditions can have prevailed in any department of the government without being brought to the attention of the head of the department and, indeed, to the attention of every member of the government?
The lack of organization and of organizing power in the department has recently been very conspicuously and painfully illustrated by the fact that the accountant's or bookkeeping branch had apparently fallen into such confusion that expert accountants had to be called in to put things to rights, and create some intelligible system. After months of work by these highly paid experts the result has been at least greatly improved books, as far as mechanical form is concerned, but probably little else; and this achievement has been accomplished at an almost fabulous expense.
There is not only a lack of efficient organization and method in the department. There would also seem to be a lack of conscience. In connection with the enormous expenditures which are deemed necessary the word 'discount ' never appears. It is tacitly assumed that there is no such thing; but the whole commercial world knows otherwise. If no one gets any benefit from trade with the government except the trader, then it must be clear that in these great purchases made for the government, without discount, its officers must be assisting the trader to get better prices from the government than he can get anywhere else; for, everywhere else he has to give discount. In other words, some of the government's officers are serving two masters, and apparently succeeding with both-scripture notwithstanding.

We may have some good reason to believe that in so far as these two gentlemen are able to control and conduct the proceedings somewhat the same result might follow. ministration in any of the departments of he government, would you consider that the coroner's jury should be guided by men in the pay and in the employment of the assassins? That is exactly the position which the Minister of Justice is so stoutly defending. The men on the treasury benches today are responsible for the slaying of efficient, economical and honest administration in the departments. The report of 1892 shows honest, efficient and economical administration at that time. When the coroner's jury is to sit upon that which was once living, but which is now a corpse, we are to have the confidential friends and agents of the assassins guiding the efforts to probe into and investigate the cause of the decease. I think the proposition need only be stated in order to convince every hon. member of this House that the course which should have been taken was to select independent men, to go outside of the ranks of the political party which is responsible for this condition of affairs and to pursue the course which was pursued by Sir John Macdonald and Sir John Thompson in 1891 when they selected Mr. B. B. Osier and Mr. C. A. Geoffrion to probe into the Department of Public Works.
Now, Mr. Speaker, under these circumstances I think it my duty to place on record the views of the opposition in regard to the report of this commission. Let it not be forgotten that although this report was presented to the department on the 17th March, 1908, up to the present time we have not had from the government any statement of their intention to redress any of the grievances or abuses disclosed by this report, except that which was vouchsafed by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) on the day when the report was presented to the House. Although entirely apart and outside of the particular paragraph to which he directed atten/tion on that day, the most outrageous extravagance, waste, lack of economy and efficiency have been disclosed by this report, not one word has been proffered by the government to parliament or to the country in explanation or in promise of redress. I have omitted to metion one or two portions of the report which refer to waste. I have already referred at very great length to extravagance. At page 36 of the report I find this language :
There can be very little question that the lighthouse board has been the means of greatly increasing the expenditure of the department and that much of the increase has been wasted.
Under these circumstances it is the duty of the opposition to place itself upon record as to the necessity of reform and redress, as to the necessity of further investigation. In the first place, the resolution which I am about to move declares that the proposed inquiry before Mr. Justice Cassels is ab-239
solutely too narrow and restricted in its character. Can there be any doubt about that when it picks out one paragraph of that portion of the report which relates to only one department and when it deals with only certain incidents in that administration and not with the whole administration which has been so vigorously attacked. The next point I desire to emphasize by the resolution is that the investigation conducted by the Civil Service Commission was confessedly partial and incomplete. There can be no doubt about that after the extracts which I have read from the report. The next point which is emphasized by the motion is : That this extravagance, waste, inefficiency, and maladministration are deplorable and that immediate steps should be taken to reform and redress the same. And these being the premises laid down in the resolution, the conclusion is : That the public interest imperatively demands the appointment of a commission with full powers to make a thorough and searching investigation which would carry on to a conclusion the work already accomplished by the Civil Service Commission. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move :
That all the words after the word ' that ' be left out and the following substituted therefor:-
The investigation conducted by the Civil Service Commission was confessedly partial and incomplete.
That the proposed inquiry before Mr. Justice Cassels is unsatisfactory and insufficient inasmuch at is relates to only one paragraph of the report of that commission and. touches but a portion of the administration of one department.
That this House regrets the deplorable, extravagance, waste, inefficiency and maladministration revealed by that report and declares that immediate steps should be taken to reform and redress the same.
That the public interest imperatively demands the appointment of an independent commission with full powers to make a thorough and searching investigation into the several departments of the public service.
I may add in conclusion, that I have not mentioned the commissioners who have already acted simply for the reason that I do not know whether or not they would be willing to act again. If I named these gentlemen I might be met by the statement from the government that they had declined to prosecute their inquiry further, that their health, or the time at their disposal would not permit them to conclude the work they had begun. I have therefore left the words of the resolution general in their character in that respect, but I have no hesitation in saying that so far as I am concerned and so far as gentlemen on this side of the House are concerned we have'absolute confidence in the thoroughness, ability and integrity of these three gentlemen and we would be glad indeed to see them appointed to carry



on to a conclusion the work in which they have been engaged.
Rt. lion. Sir WILFRID LATJRIER (Prime Minister). I do not believe it will be difficult for the House, even after the very lengthy speech we have heard, to come to a conclusion as to how this motion should be disposed of and to decide that we should pass to the order of the day. I followed the observations of my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) with very keen interest for I was anxious to know what arguments he would present in support of this motion. The question is not new ; we have had it under debate three or four times already and I must say that I have not observed a very unanimous consensus of opinion amongst gentlemen on the other side as to how the question should be treated. My hon. friend (Mr. R. D. Borden) is of opinion that the inquiry with which we have entrusted Mr. Justice Cassels is too narrow and too limited in its scope and that it should be very much enlarged, while my hon. friend from Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron) is on the contrary of opinion that this investigation of Mr. Justice Cassels is altogether useless and that we have already enough information on which to come to a conclusion. I do not hope it will be possible for me to reconcile the different opinions of gentlemen on the other side. I am satisfied that whatever the government may do or not do it will not be possible for us to have their approbation. However that may be, we will be satisfied if we have the approbation of all conscientious men in this country who are honest and unbiased in their opinions. Let me call the attention of the House to the object of the motion presented by my hon. friend. He wants to have a commission with full powers to make a thorough and searching investigation into the several departments of the public service, and the reason upon which the hon. gentleman bases this new demand for investigation is stated in the first paragraph of the motion to be :
That the investigation conducted by the Civil Service Commission was confessedly partial and incomplete.
If by that word * partial ' my hon. friend means its ordinary acceptation and that the commission showed undue favour to somebody I do not know that the reproach should come from his side of the House, but the hon. gentleman went further and in his opening remarks he stated in so many words that when he opened the report of the commission he thought he was opening a campaign document. In view of the copious extracts he has read from this report I do not know how far it was proper for him to thus at the outset belittle the report of the commission, but that is a question on which I have no comment to make.
My right hon. friend evidently misunderstood me. I made that observation simply with regard to the extract I read from Mr. Fyshe's statement respecting protection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did not fail to observe that, and neither did I fail to observe that the ptlier commissioners rather have a slap at Mr. Fyshe and state they do not share his views. If we are to take the report of the majority and not of the minority I do not think the observations come at all under the description which my hon. friend gave them. But, Sir, this is of no consequence ; the commission was appointed in order to give information to the government upon the efficiency of the civil service and in the course of their investigation they found that in one department there had been not only inefficiency as they charged, but also something akin to dishonesty. That was no part of the investigation they had to make.	Still, I find no fault with
their findings.	On the contrary, if they
saw that the attention of the government should be called to a particular condition of things, it was most necessary that the government should be apprised of the fact, so that the proper course could be taken. Therefore, since we had the report of the commissioners charging something akin to dishonesty in a certain department, we thought it our duty not to let the matter rest where it was, but to have the investigation pressed, whatever the consequences, and the whole matter probed to the bottom; and this is the reason why we have appointed Mr. Justice Cassels to continue the investigation which has been left undone by the commissioners. It is to be observed on this point, as my hon. friend the Minister of Finance remarked on a former occasion, that the report of the commissioners states either too much or too little. It would have been better, if they found dishonesty, to have completed the investigation, and to have put their finger on the guilty parties, and reported them to the government so that the government could deal with them. They having failed to do so, we thought it our duty to complete the investigation, and, as I have said, we have entrusted the work to Mr. Justice Cassels. I am glad to say, so far as the selection of the commissioner is concerned, that no fault has been found with it. On the contrary, everybody agrees that no better selection could have been made than Mr. Justice Cassels. Everybody acknowledges his eminent judicial spirit, his honesty, and his impartiality. But, Sir, much fault has been found with the counsel who have been selected. It has been stated that the choice of the counsel was unfortunate, in this respect, that Mr. Watson was at one time the chairman of the Liberal organization in Ontario, and that Mr. Perron was at one time, a partner of Mr. Prgfontaine. So far as Mr. Watson

is concerned, for my part I never knew that he had been so prominently associated with a political organization, though I knew that he generally voted the Liberal ticket. So far as Mr. Perron is concerned, I must admit in all candour that I had forgotten that at one time he had been associated with Mr. Prcfontaine. Nor do I believe that this is a matter of much consequence. But, Sir, we have to view the matter in another light. Is it to be said on the floor of the Canadian parliament by gentlemen of the eminence of my hon. friend in the profession, or by other gentlemen who occupy very high rank in the profession, that when you select counsel you have to look to their political opinions? I belong to the legal profession, and I know something of its ethics; and I am sure I shall not be contradicted by the hon. leader of the opposition, nor by other hon. gentlemen eminent in the profession, when I say that it is not to be supposed that a man who is worthy of belonging to the bar ever carried his political opinions into court. It is the pride and the honour and a very elementary rule of the profession that the man who accepts a brief from anybody leaves his political opinions at the door of the court room. Who does not remember that in the many trials which George Brown had to undergo in his province, he was always defended by John Hilliard Cameron, who sat in this House opposed to him, and was one of the most eminent members of the Conservative party at that time? Did Mr. Cameron, though engaged in political trials and in defending the most eminent man In the party to which he was opposed, carry his political opinions into court? Or is it to be supposed that he did not do full justice to hie client because he happened to be opposed to his political party? Nay, more, is it not within the knowledge of everybody that my hon. friend and colleague the Minister of Justice, when in active practice, was often retained in election trials on the Conservative side? And is it not a fact that he always did justice to his client, whether he was a Conservative or a Liberal, without any regard to the consequences? Sir, I would be ashamed of the profession if it were to be supposed that a man who had the honour of belonging to that profession would be influenced in the discharge of his duty by his political proclivities. If a man belonging to the bar thinks that he cannot do justice to his client or to the cause with which he is associated, it is his duty to refuse the brief; but the moment he has accepted a brief, it is his duty to be true to the cause which he has accepted without any regard to the consequences. Sir, this is the ethics and the pride of the profession. Will any man in this House who belongs to the bar of Ontario or to the bar of any other province in this country take any other position than this? Why, Sir, because Mr. Watson happens to be a Liberal, 239*
or because Mr. Perron happens to belong to the same political party, though I am not aware that Mr. Perron ever took a very active part in politics, is it to be supposed that these men will be recreant to their duty or untrue to the cause that they have to defend, because forsooth it might happen that the political party with which they have been associated would suffer? Why did we appoint this commission? We appointed this commission in order to have the truth and the whole truth brought out in this matter; that is the purpose Mr. Watson and Mr. Perron have to serve. The order in council providing for the commission says:
The minister observes that some statements are made in that report which affect the honour and integrity of the officers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
On page 61 of the report the following paragraph appears:
There would also seem to be a lack of conscience. In connection with the enormous expenditures which are deemed necessary, the word ' discount * never appears. It is tacitly assumed there is no such thing; but the whole commercial world knows otherwise. If no one gets any benefit from trade with the government, except the trader, then it must be clear that in these great purchases made for the government, without discount, its officers must be assisting the trader to get better prices from the government than he can get anywhere else; for everywhere else he has to give a discount. In other words, some of the government officers are serving two masters and apparently succeeding with both-Scripture notwithstanding.
The minister further observes that it is assumed by that statement that commissions are received improperly, or enhanced prices paid through dishonesty on the part of officials of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. But, unfortunately, the report does not mention any names which would enable him to take definite action concerning these officials. It is,' however, in the interests of the Department of Marine and Fisheries and of the country that immediate steps should be taken in order to determine what officials (if any) deserve condemnation and to give to all an opportunity to meet the charges implied.
The minister therefore recommends that he be authorized to appoint the Hon. Walter Cassals a commissioner under part 2, chapter 101 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, to investigate and report upon the foregoing statements contained in said report of the Civil Service Commission reflecting upon the integrity of the officials of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, or of any of them.
This is the task for which Messrs. Watson and Perron have been appointed-to assist Mr. Justice Cassels ; and this is the task which, if they are true to the profession to which they belong, they will discharge faithfully, without fear or favour towards anybody. The strange suggestion has been made In the press that not only should Mr. Cassels be assisted with counsel but

that counsel should be appointed to represent the Civil Service Commission. I have not heard that suggestion made by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, but I have heard it made in this House and I have seen it in the press. Could anything be more preposterous ? The retiring commissioners are not on trial. Mr. Justice Cassels is not appointed to take issue with them, and there is nothing to indicate that his appointment is in any way contradictory to their report. On the contrary the object of his appointment is to continue and complete the investigation made by the commission, and therefore it is absurd to pretend that the commissioners should be represented by counsel.
The commissioners were appointed to inquire into the efficiency of the service and they have made a report. The gist of that report is that the service is inefficient and that its inefficiency is due to the fact that the service is recruited by political patronage. There is nothing very new in this. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition says we should have a third investigation. Why, this will be the fourth investigation. We had a commission appointed in 1881 which reported. We had a commission appointed in 1892 which reported also. We had one appointed in 1907, which has just submitted its report, and the hon. gentleman wants another appointed. Well, I have this to say that as regards the inefficiency of the service, it is the duty of the minister and the government to look into that matter and of no one else. We do not admit any necessity for an Investigation into that subject. We are responsible to parliament, and if there be inefficiency it is for us to devise a remedy.
The charge made by the commissioners that the civil service is recruited upon political considerations and none other is not a new one. The same complaint was made in the report of 1892. My hon. friend, who has made copious quotations, did not quote this part of the commission report which will be found on page 15 :
In the previous remarks your commissioners have pointed out that in their opinion the principles underlying the Civil Service Act are not in the public interest. In the report of the Royal Commission of 1892, the commissioners observe that: It is possible that public sentiment in Canada may not as yet he ripe for open competition generally, and it may not Ire possible as yet to eliminate altogether the power of politics in making appointments ; hut if the recommendations of your commissioners be accepted and strictly adhered to, the public service at Ottawa will, they are convinced, in the course of a few years be better for the change.
The commissioners at that time only took into account the public service at Ottawa. Thev. left in their draft Bill ,in the report the provisions of a former Act relating to the outside service. Your commissioners regret Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
to state that in their opinion the hopes of the members of the former commission have not been realized. The provisions of the Civil Service Act and its amendment have not made the service anv better. In fact the Act has been so amended, re-amended and whittled down that the public service, the commissioners believe, not only at Ottawa but elsewhere throughout the Dominion, has fallen back during the last fifteen years.
Well, If the service has fallen back during the last fifteen years, the party in office are not alone responsible because we have not been here ail of these fifteen years. If the evil goes back so far, we all may be held to an equal share of the blame. If the service has been rendered inefficient by political patronage, who is it who will cast the first stone? Can it come from the other side? Why, the service to-day is these gentlemen's own service. It is their service very largely as regards the personnel, and it is altogether theirs as regards the law. We have inherited the condition of things which now prevails and it ill becomes hon. gentlemen opposite to say that we are to blame.
While I am disposed to take the report of the commissioners as a basis of action, I am not disposed to grant that everything in this report should be taken as incontrovertible. In their disposition to blame the system that prevails, they have gone very far to find fault with some of the appointments. They have criticised the appointment of Mr. Harwood as postmaster of the city of Montreal, on the ground that he was an old gentleman seventy years of age and had been in active politics. That is true. But it is also true that the post office at Montreal has never been as ably managed as it has been by Mr. Harwood. For the last six or seven years, during which it has been managed by him, its administration has been perfect. No complaints have come to us and the public appear thoroughly satisfied.
It must not be forgotten that there are several aspects to be looked at before coming to any kind of a conclusion. We appointed a commission because the public were of the opinion that the time had come to have civil service reform. And what could we do better than appoint a commission to investigate and report and lay down a basis of reform ? There are in the report some things in which I am not disposed to agree altogether. There are some statements which I regret exceedingly and which I do not think reflect any honour on the commissioners. What they have said with regard to the Militia Department seems to me altogether uncalled for. And I am not disposed to congratulate my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, on the remark he made a moment ago concerning the speech by the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Bro-1 der) who, I regret, is not in his seat at pre-

sent. Some time ago, in a speech to a meeting of farmers, the hon. member for Dun-das said that the government spent $6,000,000 on militia and only half a million dollars on agriculture. Now, there is no man in this House for whom I have greater respect than my hon. friend from Dundas. He is a strong partisan, and for that I do not blame him because I am one myself. But though he is a strong partisan, he is generally very fair in discussion. When, however, before a meeting of farmers, he pointed out that the Canadian government was spending $6,000,000 on militia and only half a million dollars on agriculture, he was guilty of appealing to the worst prejudices that lie in the human heart.
I am sorry my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. D. Borden) should have been guilty of the same offence. Sir, the civilized nation does not live to-day that has not to spend more on militia than it can spend on agriculture and arts and many other useful things . That is our position. We are not in the condition yet, I am glad to say, and I hope we never shall be, of those nations of Europe, England, France, Germany, which spend no less than 50 per cent of their income upon war and preparations for war. But, Sir, we are in this position, though we are happily far from the condition of these nations, that we cannot ignore our duty to provide for the defence of this country. It is a part of the duty we owe to ourselves, it is a part of the duty we owe to our nation, and when an hon. gentleman in this House, like my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) stoops-stoops, I say, to try to create political capital out of such a question he plays a part, I believe, altogether unworthy of himself and unworthy of the position which he occupies in this House. We have to spend far more on militia than I would like; I wish we could spend far less, I wish we could spend $6,000,000 on agriculture and only half a million on militia, but unfortunately, if the time should come when my hon. friend occupies this seat to which he aspires, instead of heaping condemnation as he does to-day on our conduct, he will not be able to modify at all the policy which we have introduced. It is a part of our system of existence as a nation and cavilling against it is setting a bad example on the eve of what may turn out to be important events.
What does that mean, signs of war?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, I see signs of war. That is not only the petty war my friend is engaged in-if that was all I would not mind It-but Canada has a population of 6,000,000 of souls, it has a very large extent of territory, it faces on two oceans, and my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) himself remembers that when he was
in office, he had to provide for the preparation of war, which I hope is very far distant, although it may come at any moment. It is not probable but, Sir, if my hon. friend is ready to say that, situated as we are, we had better disperse the militia and abandon the preparation we have made, I will be prepared to say we have made a mistake -but he never can say that.
No, he will leave that to the Minister of Marine.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Sir R. L. Borden) wants to have another investigation. I repeat what I said that so far as the charge of dishonesty in the service is concerned, we have committed that charge to the investigation of Mr. Justice Cassels. So far as the efficiency of the service is concerned, we can keep that in our own hands, it is for us to deal with that, it is for the minister to look into that and provide for a remedy. We have no intention of shirking our duty, we have no intention of placing in the hands of a commission the responsibility which rests upon us. It is for us to administer the affairs of the country. So long as we have the confidence of the people and responsibility to the people we have no intention of shirking our responsibility and placing in other hands the duty that properly rests on us. If the service has deteriorated, it is for us to put it in a better position; if it has to be improved, it is for us to do it. But how is that to be done? First, by amending the law. The commission tell us that the law is deficient. Look at the report of the commission and what is their very first conclusion? The law is deficient and you must change the law. They regret that this was not done before. They call attention to the fact that in 1892 a similar commission reported in exactly the same way and nothing had been done up to the present time. If nothing was done I am not disposed, for my part, to be very severe with the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) who at that time was a prominent member of the administration, nor am I disposed to quarrel with the hon. member for North Lanark (Air. Haggart) who was also a member of the government at that time; they had before them the report which advised them to reform the civil service, to change the law, I am not disposed to be very severe upon them, because the reform of the civil service is a very difficult task and I do not know whether at that time public opinion was prepared for it. But, Sir, we have come to the conclusion that the time has come to tackle this reform. This was why we appointed the commission. We have now the report of the commission which was placed in our hands on the 17th of March last. The first thing we did was to look at the report, to study it, to investigate it. The next thing was to appoint a com-

mission which has been provided for by the appointment of Mr. Justice Cassels. The third thing was to commence the work of looking into the departments to see what improvements could be made, and the fourth thing was to prepare a Bill, which is now under consideration, to be brought before the House. When we lay that Bill before the House we may resume this discussion, but for the moment I have only to say that we do not intend to depart at all from the position we took at first. The duty is ours and we must face it. There is no reason to have another investigation. We have now had three Investigations, one in 1881, one in 1892, one in 1908 and with these we have information enough to do our duty. At all events this is what we propose to do, and I have to say simply this in conclusion that with the responsibility which is upon us we have certain things to do and we intend to do them ourselves ; they will be done not through a commission, not through others, but by the party now in oflice, the government responsible to the people. These are the observations I have to offer to the House on this occasion and I have to say that in my humble judgment, the best thing the House can do is to proceed with the orders of the day and to leave this matter in the hands of the government.

Mr. Speaker, whatever else the independent onlooker, if such there be, will have to remark with reference to the observations of my right hon. friend this afternoon in reply to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, I am quite sure he would come to the conclusion that the Prime Minister did not make an adequate answer to the case which was presented by the mover of the resolution. If he will permit a criticism from me I would say that his reply seemed to show, either a lack of appreciation of the condition of things as they now exist, or else so great an appreciation of them that he was not able to meet them, and so went off on what I consider to be simply a side issue. He undertook to divert the attention of the House by conjuring up a difference of opinion between the hon. member for Beau-harnois (Mr. Bergeron) and my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, saying that the leader of the opposition wanted more investigation whilst the member for Beau-harnois thought there was investigation enough, and quite as much information as was necessary. Well, this was an interesting piece of by-play; but I could not help thinking that my right hon. friend would have been better employed in ad- *
Sir WILFRID LAITRIER
dressing himself to meet the arguments in the case, rather than in giving us what was at best a figment of his own imagination.
I said that I did not think the right hon. gentleman showed an appreciation of the condition of things as they are to-day. I do not think I *would be making too strong an observation if I said that of late years I know of nothing that has produced wider comment and aroused deeper interest than the report of the Civil Service Commission. I do not say that such a report coming simply by itself would have had such effect, but coming as it does at this particular time, it certainly had an effect upon the country at large which is remarkable, and, whether my right hon. friend thinks so or not, has taken a very deep hold of the people of Canada. It follows a number of other incidents and transactions which year by year, for the last five or six years, have been gradually unfolded, and of which the people have taken due cognizance. The right hon. gentleman does not seem to feed that owing to laches, sins of omission and sins of commission by himself and his party since 1896, be has already lost and Is still losing in the respect and confidence of a great body of the electorate of Canada. After he came into power and for some years subsequently, he rejoiced in an almost complete adhesion of the provincial legislatures to his party and his cause. Year by year they have been slipping away from him, and have assumed a position of political antagonism. First he lost control by his party friends of the province of Manitoba; then he lost control by his party friends of the right arm of his party, the great province of Ontario; later still, he lost control, against a most determined campaign put up by himself and his colleagues and supporters, of the great province of British Columbia; later still the province of New Brunswick, which for eighteen years had stood behind him and his party, and during the last twelve years without shadow of question, the province of New Brunswick, although the fight on his behalf was engineered by his latest and one of his ablest ministers, has administered a well merited defeat to his Minister of Public Works, and to the federal party after all their intervention in that election. And only yesterday, in the good old city of Halifax, to which two of his party supporters left their places in this House and went down to conduct the fight on partly lines for the Dominion and In view of the next federal contest, the city of Halifax has, by an overwhelming majority, changed its political belief as shown in a civic election, and has defeated the Liberal candidates and elected the Conservative candidates for civic office.
My right hon. friend thinks there is nothing in all these signs. He has a compact majority behind him, for various reasons; does he believe that the country Is just as

compact behind him? And now, after all these signs of the times, after all the work that has been done by His Majesty's loyal opposition against great odds and great difficulties, after all the glimpses which they have been able to let into the departmental work and the methods of the government of my right hon. friend, comes this Civil Service Commission report. A commission of his own friends, appointed by himself, after a more or less exhaustive examination, has given to the government a report which has aroused more interest than any document that has been presented to this House of Commons for many a long year. Yet my right hon. friend seems to think that all is at peace in Zion, that so long as he can turn around and get ready applause from a large proportion of this House that sit behind him and support him he is safe in vouchsafing no answer, safe in taking any trifling position that he pleases on what is really a very large and very important question.
Some one in the newspapers, probably in the independent press, has remarked as a singular thing that this session at least the Prime Minister, who had a reputation for being politically astute, has been so unfortunate as to take the wrong side on almost every important question that has come up. I believe that will be found to be true. Prom the fight for the original documents on which my right hon. friend took the wrong side, and from which he afterwards had to retreat, down through a series of positions which he had to face in this House, my right hon. friend has been, for some reason or other, I do not know what particularly, forced to take, or has chosen to take, the wrong, the unconstitutional and the unpopular side.
In the matter of the purchase of supplies for the different departments of this government the right hon. gentleman generally agreed with the principle of the resolution which I had the honour to introduce, but when it came to the practical part of it, in the end, he finished by what ? Voting, himself and his whole party, for the continuance of the middleman's operations in the purchase of supplies. And so in reference to question after question. It has been remarked, and I think the observation is very true, that the right hon. gentleman appears to have been forced, for some reason or other, to take the wrong side on a great many of the important questions which have come before us. In the same manner I do not think he has appreciated the gravity of the question which is before the country to-day and I do not think, as I have said before, that he has appreciated the whole situation or met it adequately. In the first place my right hon. friend joins the procession of re-pudiators-shall I call them ? These gentlemen selected their own commission-Mr. Courtney, Mr. Fyslie and Mr. Bazin. They
were their own appointees. They declared them to be able men, they had their confidence, they set them to work, they gave them certain powers and these gentlemen acted under these powers and the spectacle is afforded to this House and the country of one minister after another, followed in the end by the right hon. gentleman himself, rising in his place in the House and repudiating his own commission. Why ?- because it had a surprise for them. It often does happen that a man has a certain thing in his head and he thinks that is the only thing there is in the universe, but he is surprised some day to find out that there are other things. The right hon. gentleman joins in the caustic criticism of these gentlemen, sneers at them, in fact, for going bevond their duty. Why this surprise ? Because it really happens to have operated as a flank movement which was not expected. The right hon. gentleman and his colleauges were devoting themselves to the frontal attack and as poor strategists they forgot that the rear and the flanks should also have been defended. Whilst they can, by their majority in the Public Accounts Committee, prevent investigation into public matters, whilst they can by their majority in this House, prevent information from coming down to members, whilst they can, by their majority in this House, deny any investigation and all investigation into alleged malpractices they forgot to fortify themselves upon the flank and the rear. And whilst they were successful by means of their majority in warding off frontal attack, their own friends, in the spirit of duty and of honesty and of thoroughness lifted the lid upon these governmental transactions and gave the people a glance at the inside. Hence this procession of caustic repudiators who, one after another, get up and flagellate the commission that they themselves appointed and sneer at the men that they themselves made their

own Royal Commission. Well, we will let that go to the country. The exhibition is one of bad taste, it is one, I think, of very poor policy, the average man in the country will easily see through it and it will not count to the advantage of the government.
The right hon. First Minister said that it was the duty of this commission simply to inquire into the efficiency of the Civil Service Act and that it was no part of their duty to investigate into transactions. But they did investigate some transactions in one part of one department and they came upon appearances of dishonesty and now the second commission has been appointed, as the right hon. gentleman with an odd failure to appreciate the meaning of language, declared to continue and complete the work of the first commission. It was not appointed for the purpose of continuing and completing the work of the first commission. What was the work of the first commission as under authority given to them and as understood by themselves ? It was to look into the Civil Service system certainly, to inquire as to its efficiency, and, as well, to make recommendations as to how it could be made more efficient, but when you come to No. 8 and No. 10 of the subjects mentioned in the order in council you see that there are other powers that are given them. No. 8 reads ' Efficiency and sufficiency of the departmental staffs.' How could that commission come to a conclusion as to the efficiency and sufficiency of the departmental staffs* unless they followed the work of these departmental staffs and found out how it was done, not only if it was efficiently done. Is efficiently the only characteristic of the civil service ? It was also important to inquire whether it was honestly done because honesty must be a characteristic of the Civil Service ; whether it was done in a businesslike way, whether it was extravagantly done, whether it was wastefully done, in fine, whether it was properly or improperly done. How were the Civil Service Commission, as appointed, to come to a conclusion as to the efficiency and sufficiency of the departmental staffs unless they followed their business from A to Z ? And in following out that business what did they find ? They found what they have embodied in the report, that instead of there being efficiency there was inefficiency, instead of there being any sign of a directive head in the Department of Marine and Fisheries there was no sign of

it, instead of there being any conscience in that department, not in the individuals in the department-that is not what the commission says-but in the department itself, they found that there was a lack of conscience, they found waste, they found extravagance, they found mal-administra-tion. In the very duty that they had to carry out to determine whether the staffs were efficient and sufficient they were bound to go into that kind of an examination. They went into one-half of the Department of the Marine and Fisheries, namely, the Marine part of it, and they did not get half through with that, but they found what has angered the government, what has somewhat astonished the country and what has proved up to the hilt the charges that His Majesty's loyal opposition have been making for the last five years.

I tell the right hon. gentleman that he must take back his words or else he must make Judge Cassels commission just as broad as was the commission of the three gentlemen who were first appointed. them for twenty-one years, the absolute exclusive right to fish commercially in the great fishing areas of the Northwest, and to sell the products.
