That is what I mean when I say that instead of appointing a royal commission to look into these matters in the public interest, the minister himself has appointed a commission to simply look into the deeds of subordinates and find out whether or not any of them have taken commissions or unduly obtained public money in the purchase of supplies or the payment therefor. That is the duty of Judge Cassels and his duty only ; but even that duty is circumscribed by the fact, according to the Minister of Justice that he is not expected to look into this whole matter himself. There are files to be gone through ad infinitum, years to be gone over, 1994, 5, 6, 7, 8-why it would take Judge Cassels years and years to make the whole investigation himself ; and that is why the Minister of Justice said he took the responsibility of appointing counsel. It is the counsel who are to look into these things. They will see what papers are to be scanned. They are to look over the files judicially and carefully. They are to designate the cases that are to be brought to light-and they alone. They are to steer the whole investigation, and they are to put the facts and cases before the judge who occupies a judicial position. So says the Minister of Justice. This commission is intended to have the effect of relieving the minister entirely of responsibility. And it is intended to have this other effect. Just as in the case of that deceptive and partial Investigation into the transactions connected withe the ' Arctic '. so in this case my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) stands before the people and exclaims : I have appointed a new commission to continue and complete the work which was begun by. the first commission. That is a fine song for the people. That will make elegant headlines in the Toronto ' Globe ', which is so zealous for the truth. That will be used ad infinitum by the party papers all through. See how our Premier meets the situation. When the first commission after seven months' examination made a partial report, our Premier appointed Judge Cassels to continue what the first commission had undertaken but had not finished. That goes to the people, that is read by the newspapers to the faithful, that is headlined and that is relied upon ; but when it comes down to the naked fact, he has estopped Judge Cassels from looking into a single transaction in any department outside of the Department of Marine and Fisheries and has estopped him from looking into any transaction there unless it involves the dishonesty of a subordinate in the Marine branch. That is what

the commission does. What this commission does, is simply setting aside by a rather bold hut at the same time transparent fiction, the real issue, trying to blind the people's minds while at the same time giving a semblance of a commission to get out what my right hon. friend so valiantly declared over and over again, he wanted, the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The last thing that my hon. friend wants in this matter is the whole truth. I am anxious that the country shall know exactly what this second commission is to do, what it can do and what it cannot do. People are getting wiser, systems are getting to be better understood, new ideas supervene, the experience of the world is constantly growing, and one age will endure what another age will not endure. So it is with reference to the civil service; and if my opinion is worth anything, Canada to-day is waking up to the importance of an improved civil service. Just here I beg to say that if my right hon. friend will bring in a Civil Service Act, prohibiting the features of influence, partisanship, and political appointments, he will have my most hearty support; and if he will press that to the very end of eliminating patronage from every purchase and every appointment by the government, he will have my support as well.
But my right hon. friend was not quite right. He says there was a commission in 1880. So there was, and after the commission of 1880 what was done? The Civil Service Act of 1882 was brought in and passed, and has been on the books ever since, adopting the principle of a civil service examining board, of a qualification and a promotion examination, and of a classification test. In 1892 another commission was appointed, I have the report of that commission in my desk. The report of that commission is worth studying by my right hon. friend, and especially by his Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance the other night tried to lead us to suppose that the report of the commission of 1892 was just as strong as the report of the commission of 1908. Any one who will read It will see the absolute difference. On the question of the operation of a civil service system, it was equally strong in 1892 as it is in 1908. In 1892 Mr. Barbeau and Mr. Hague, two members of that commission, went round the offices in Ottawa, looked them all through, made their comments on them, and with reference to this Department of Marine and Fisheries put in their report a statement which was read by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition to-day. That, Sir, was in 1891 and 1892. Then they said that with the exception of some obsolete methods of bookkeeping here and there through the departments, the departments were fairly well run, but in reference to that special department, they commended it because of its rigid oversight of its business and because of the fact that the supplies were economically bought. On that part of the report contrast 1892 with 1908 which has to do with the efficiency and sufficiency of the departmental staffs and methods of business; this commission's report is absolutely new and is absolutely clear on that point. In both you have the patronage system declared and execrated, but in this one it is ten. yes twenty times as strongly declared as it was in 1892.	.
But, may I call my right hon. friend's Mr. FOSTER.
attention to one thing? He and the Finance Minister declared that nothing was done. Nothing done? In 1893 we introduced, on the top of that commission, three Bills. The commission reported in favour of a civil service board to consist of a permanent chairman and four deputy heads, appointment by competitive examination, *>
clerks to be selected from the roster as established by competitive examination by the board, the superannuation system to be continued and an insurance system if it could be applied properly. In 1893 our government introduced an insurance Bill for the civil service, placed it on the statute-book and it remains there yet. We introduced a Bill strengthening the superannuation system by propounding and establishing fund No. 2 on a more equitable basis to the employees with six per cent interest allowed by the government and that was largely taken advantage of. And we introduced on February 3, 1893, a civil service Bill providing for a civil service board and for the strict supervision of the appointments to office and of the methods of conducting the business of the civil service in all the departments. Where was my right hon. friend? He rose and objected to it. Mr. Mills rose and objected to it. Both of them objected to it on principle and my right hon. friend moved the six months' hoist. Yet the Minister of Finance declared that we did nothing and my right hon. friend declared that we were quits as bad as they were. Well, we will see now what they do. I just leave that as a corrective of something which has been stated in the House and which is not quite correct.
One thing that amused me-and that expresses it exactly because it did not frighten me-was the forced denunciation of my hon. friend (Mr. Broder) by the First Min-ter. It was really a fine dramatic act. I and others sitting here and facing the chief actor could not help but admire the way in which enthusiasm and indignation were worked up and the splendid denunciatory tone in which the invective was launched against Andrew Broder. What was it that my right hon. friend found fault with Mr. Broder for? Mr. Broder, he said, went before a meeting of farmers-tinder, you know ! Farmers and farming questions are something like tinder ; you are apt to get a great, quick, and mighty prejudice aroused amongst a lot of farmers on a farming question! Mr. Broder actually went before the farmers and ventured to tell the farmers that the present government was extravagant in its expenditures for the militia and parsimonious in its expenditures for agriculture ! That was the whole thing. He did it of course, by an object lesson-so many millions for the militia and only half a million for pure agriculture, so many dollars for war and so many dollars for peace. It was the object lesson method of present-
APRTL 3ft. 1908
iDg the fact to the irascible and excitable farming audience that he had before him and he actually worked upon their prejudice to the detriment of the defence of this country, and my right hon friend blossomed out into a full grown champion of war and all the trappings of war. Why ? The one distinction that crowns the brow of the First Minister in Europe as well as in America is that he is a peace-at-any-price man. He hates militarism. He has vehemently denounced the militarism of the old country and fought against its being introduced into this country. He swept aside all the inducements for the colonies and Great Britain to get closer together because the spectre of militarism was above him day and night and frightened him. To-day he rather insinuates that some big thing is going to burst upon us in the shape of an unknown and contingent war and that Mr. Broder has been exciting the prejudices of the farmers against the proper defence of Canada. But, oh, Mr. Speaker, I did believe that it was a very fine play when I saw a portion of the audience that listened to him, said portion being the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries, for, in 1896, when I, as Minister of Finance proposed a vote of $1,000,000 in order to get some large artillery for this Dominion, absolutely defenceless,, in so far as that arm was concerned at that time, the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries denounced the project In this House, went down to the province of Quebec, toured through that province, got together audiences of his fellow-countrymen, wept tears and made them weep tears as he portrayed to them the foul iniquity of the Tories at Ottawa in putting up a vote of a million dollars for war in this country, the ultimate result of which would be that the French woman's sons would be torn from their arms and sent out to defend distant portions of the empire. Did my right hon. friend administer any rebuke to his friend and supporter, the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries when he appealed to the prejudice of race against the defence of Canada and against proper arming as regards large artillery at some of the ports ? Not at all. He gloried in it and lie thanked God for every vote he got by that kind of mechanism. Oh, these strange me-tamorphisms that at the last moment even gentlemen like my right hon. friend will be led to exhibit before the House and the country ! But my right hon. friend ended up by saying : We do not want any more investigations. That was one thing that I believed if I believed nothing else that he said during that speech. He and his party have shown that they do not want investigation. They have shown it in the Public Accounts Committee, shown it in this House, shown it in refusing us information before we voted supplies, shown it In refusing to
us investigation as to how supplies were expended after they had been voted and, time after time, has called his followers here to stand up against any beginnings of an adequate investigation into any department. Two years ago my hon. friend (Mr. R. I,. Borden) moved for an investigation into the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Then they all said :	It is a pure
and honest and efficient department, you shall not have any investigation. We trotted out the Merwins, we trotted in the Strubbes, we trotted in all the Brookes and the others, and we showed how they were fleecing right and left the Marine and Fisheries Department, and yet they would not allow us an investigation. My right hon. friend does not want any more investigations, but I venture to say that the people of this country do, and that they are bound to have more investigations. And so it is that the motion of the leader of the opposition, asking for what the Prime Minister says he has provided for, but which he has in reality estopped a continuation and completion of the work commenced by the first commission, is a motion which this side of the House can support and one which I believe he country will endorse. But, Sir, the man who wants the truth and the whole truth appoints a gentleman like Mr. Perron from the city of Montreal-I am saying nothing as to Mr. Perron's ability as a lawyer ; what I am saying is that for nine long years Mr. Perron was the partner of the minister whose subordinates are to be brought up before Judge Cassels in this investigation ; that he was not only a business-in-law partner with him but that he was a partner in Mr. Pre-fontaine's private and other concerns, and it is stated upon the streets of Montreal that he had a great many dealings with parties who had dealings with the minister and the departments. That is the kind of man -outside of his legal abilities entirely-a man who was the partner of the incriminated one for nine years, of the same political belief, engaged in the same schemes, profiting from the same enterprises ; that is the man that my right hon. friend has had the grace to interpose between truth and the public of this country in the investigation to be held by Judge Cassels. I miss my guess if the people of this country do not condemn that kind of thing. They like to see the game played fairly and they would have som'e idea that it was being played fairly if my right hon. friend had forgotten for a moment political bias and had placed a strong independent lawyer, or if he wanted two lawyers, a strong Conservative lawyer on that investigation and allowed the people some chance. The government by theory represents the people-this government by practice if not by theory represents its own selfish party interests an&

looks after those interests. And, to qualify these two gentlemen as being counsel for the people of Canada Is a misnomer. They are created "by and paid by and they will be rewarded by the party who has called them to thus interpose between a certain investigation and the people who demand it.

I rather regret and I am a litle surprised at the course of the speeches of the hon. leader of the opposition and the hon. member for North Toronto. I had supposed when we were going to have a discussion on the report of the Civil Service Commission that we would have a discussion on the best way to improve the civil service of Canada.
We will have that later.
I am glad to hear that. I remember that a little while ago the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) had a motion ou the paper for that purpose. He dropped it.
The hon. gentleman knows why I dropped it.
Certainly.
The hon. gentleman might state that.
I intend to. My hon. friend need not be so impatient.
I want to keep you from falling into difficulties.
You need not be alarmed; it is not my habit.
What about that letter-
Order.

Will my hon. friend have
patience ?
What about that letter the hon. gentleman got from Japan that he never got, and that he told this House he had when he never had it ?

My hon. friend dropped that motion for the purpose of discussing civil service reform. I had hoped he was going to discuss that question to-night, but instead of following his better bent he has taken up the role of a partisan and indulged in one of his usual speeches of that character. The leader of the opposition in his opening remarks said that when he read the report of the Civil Service Commission he thought, from a certain phrase in it, that it was a campaign document.
,. BORDEN. Of the Liberal party.

Of the Liberal party. I suppose my hon. friend had his mind so occupied with the idea that he intended to make a campaign document of this for the Mr. FOSTER.
Conservative party, that he thought it was intended for that purpose.
It spoke for itself.

It speaks for itself and if my hon. friend tries to he can find a great deal of good in it. But he prefers to try to make a campaign document of it and to turn it to his party political purposes rather than to draw from it anything for the benefit of the Civil Service of Canada. The hon. gentleman mentioned the fact that in a speech at Halifax last summer he laid down civil service reform as one of the planks of the Conservative platform. I believe he did on that occasion, but while I followed with some interest his tour throughout Canada I saw but little, after he left Halifax, of many things he had in the Halifax platform and I do not remember-subject to correction-that he dealt very insistently in other parts of the Dominion on that plank of his platform.
On 90 per cent at least of the occasions on which I spoke I addressed myself to that subject.

I accept the hon. gentleman's statement, but judging from the press reports of his various speeches I fear that part of them did not make so great an impression on the public or on the newspaper reporters who heard him as other parts of his speeches did. At all events, to-day the hon. gentleman is attempting to make a campaign document out of the report of the Civil Service Commission. I regret that. I spoke from the heart when I said that I would have hoped that we might discuss civil service reform and not party politics. However, my hon. friend is free to take whatever course he pleases. Now, the civil service reports which have been before the public of Canada from that of 1881 to that of 1908, are all full of strictures upon the political aspects of the civil service and of remarks about the evil effects of politics upon the Civil Service of Canada. I have no doubt whatever- speaking for myself and I think speaking for the inmost thoughts of everybody in the sound of my voice-that political influences are a serious detriment to the civil service, and that the result of political influence in this country is the same as it has been in England and in the United States in years past before civil service reform had been forced upon the people.
My hon. friend quotes these strictures in the report of the commission of 1908 with the evident intent of trying to hurt the present government, as though those strictures were only and entirely levelled at the civil service under the administration of the present government. I have here the report of 1881, which says this:
While there exists in the public mind a very general belief that the civil service is

not been sufficiently guarded against the evil effects of political patronage.
They wind up with this statement.
Politioal patronage is responsible for other evils, and we do not hesitate to express the conviction that many unnecessary civil offices have been retained, and that new places have been created, for no better purpose than to provide for the followers of influential politicians.
The recommendations in that report were directly in the line of competitive examinations under an independent civil service board. A law was passed in 1882, based largely on this report, but the essentials of the report were not carried out in that law, inasmuch as no independent board of civil service commissioners were appointed, and no competitive examinations were inaugurated. The result was that the civil service went on from 1881 very much in the same way as it did before. But we come to the report of 1892, made when the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Poster) was a member of the government, and what do we find in that report? We find the same condition of affairs described exactly as it was in the report of 1881. Referring to the report of 1881, the report of 1892 says:	[DOT]
Following this report a new Civil Service Act was passed in 1882, which provided for examinations to test the qualifications of candidates for positions in the public service, and also for the examination of candidates for promotion. This Act, although not going so far in its provisions as was recommended by the commission, has been amended year by year, with one exception, from the time of its being first placed on the statute-book until the year 1889, and so far as the commissioners have been able to observe, the amendments in general have tended in the direction of the relaxation of the provisions of the original Act, and the consequent prevention of its intention from being carried out.
They say further:
The principal recommendations contained in the Bill are (1) the appointment of a Civil Service Commission, and (2) the adoption of the principle of appointment by open competition.
They wind up thus:
It is possible that publio sentiment in Canada may not as yet be ripe for open competition generally, and it may not be possible as yet to eliminate altogether the power of politics in making appointments; but if the recommendations of your commissioners be accepted and strictly adhered to, the public service at Ottawa will, they are convinced, in the course of a few years, be better for the change. Intelligence and capacity will meet with their due reward, politics and favouritism will cease to dominate, the service will soon become attractive to many persons who now seek other avenues of employment, and in general the title of publio servant will be an honour to be coveted. The

doors to appointments and promotions in the service will open only to capacity and honesty, and no man or woman who aspires, as all have a right to aspire, to any such position, will have occasion to seek or use any influence less honourable than his or her own merit and fitness for office.
That was their recommendation. My lion, friend from North Toronto has stated to what extent his government carried out that recommendation. He says that they passed a Bill for insurance of civil servants. That was not a reform of the civil service; it did not embody in any way the removal of political patronage. On the contrary, it simply aided to a certain extent those civil servants who were already in office. He says that they approved of the Superannuation Act. I dare say that is true, but that does not in any sense imply a reform of the Civil Service Act or the carrying out of the recommendations of the Civil Service Commission regarding political influences. But my hou. friend says that they introduced a Bill and that the right hon. the First Minister moved the six months' hoist of that Bill. But why did he do so? Because the Bill was inadequate and inefficient, and did not carry out the recommendations of the Civil Service Commission. I have here the ' Hansard ' of that day. Mr. Costigan, in moving the second reading, said that the Bill perhaps did not contain all they intended to put into it. Mr. Laurier then went on to say that the Bill had been introduced without a word of explanation, but we now had its provisions and he added:
If I understand the Bill rightlv, what the hon. gentleman proposes, under the name of oivil service board, is simply a detective agency to look after the civil service. Look at section i of the Bill, and see what are the duties it is proposed to place upon the supervisors of civil servants. ... At all events his duty is to see whether or not the clerks are properly discharging their work. I submit. in all conscience, that the minister under whom the department may be, or the deputy minister, or the chief clerk of the department, are quite competent to do that.
That is the doctrine of the ministerial responsibility which this government have always advocated and endorsed, and it was because of that reason the leader of the opposition at that time moved the six months hoist. He said :
The Bill did not introduce an independent board of commissioners and did not carry out any of the recommendations of the commission of 1892.
Mr. Casey then made a speech. Mr. Casey was one of the first who advocated civil service reform in this parliament. In 1880 or 1881 he introduced a civil service Bill, and it was largely in consequence of the speech he made on that occasion that the government appointed the commission Mr. FISHER.
of 1881 and that the statute of 1882 was placed on our statute-book. In this debate Mr. Casey aslo spoke. He said :
As to the official proposed to be created, to be called the supervisor of the civil servants, my leader has apparently expressed all the objections to such an appointment, and I will not add anything to what he has said. As to the creation of a civil service board to examine candidates for admission, promotion and so on, so far I can go with the government. But I intend, at a later stage, to propose an amendment carrying out more efficiently what one would understand to be implied by the appointment of an impartial and non-partisan board to manage the affairs of the civil service. I believe that the conduct of the civil service should not be on partisan lines but that appointments and promotions and other proceedings should be dictated by a board appointed as judges are appointed and as the civil service board in England are appointed, during good behaviour, and not responsible to any political minister of the day. I believe the service should be conducted on business principles, that appointments, promotions and all other matters connected with the service should be carried on as in a bank or insurance company or any other institution of that kind.
The result was, not that a vote was taken and the Bill defeated, but that, after the discussion, Mr. Costigan said :
If the House will allow me. I will withdraw the motion for its second reading.
Mr. LAURIER, Certainly.
I can move the second reading another time when the amendments are prepared.

Will to-morrow ever
come?
To-morrow never did come. The Bill died a natural death. It was an abortion when introduced, and it never came into being.
I wish to say a few words with regard to the report of 1892. I have alluded to some of the recommendations of the commission of that day and to some of their statements regarding what they found in the service. I find here an interesting letter from Mr. Le Sueur, one of the best known and oldest civil servants in Ottawa who has since left the service. In this these words lie characterizes the service at that time :
Politics I need not define. We have it with us always, and we know what it means. The present question is, how does the intrusion of politics affect the public service? It affects it in many wavs: '
1.	By crowding it with unnecessary hands.
2.	By introducing into it, at times, inefficient or other unsuitable persons.
3.	Bv interfering with the due course of promotion.
4.	Bv interfering with the exercise of necessary discipline.

5.	By interfering with the due course of departmental procedure.
These are the Drimar evils of some of them. The secondary (in the sense of derivative) evils are to be found in the moral effects upon the service at large of these attacks, if I may so call them, upon the integrity of its organization and methods. How can industry be enforced in an overcrowded office? How can a proper standard of work be maintained where same are markedly inefficient? How can the moral of the service be kept at a high point if justice is trifled with? How can an officer who is not supposed to be a political partisan enjoy the highest measure of selfrespect if he is compelled, or thinks himself compelled, to act as a partisan?
That was dated January 2, 1S92. Sir. Le Sueur was then secretary of the Post Office Department and well qualified by his experience and honesty to pronounce upon it.
Sly lion, friends have quoted a lot from the present civil service report. But there Is a word or two in it which they were careful not to quote and to which I would refer them. Referring to tile commission of 1892, the commissioners say :
Your commissfoners regret to state that in their opinion the hopes of the members of the former commission have not been realized. The provisions of the Civil Service Act and its amendments have not made the service any better. In fact the Act has been so amended, re-amended and whittled down, that the public service, the. commissioners believe, not only at Ottawa but elsewhere throughout the Dominion, has fallen back during the last fifteen years.
Fifteen years took them back to the report of 1892 ; and it is curious to relate that since 1896, when this government came into power, we have not made any amendments to the Civil Service Act. It is the same Act, whittled down and made so poor and useless by the party opposite that it was ineffective.
The expression ' whittled down ' probably referred to the repeal, in individual cases, of the Act from session to session.
I do not think so. Coming immediately after the quotation from the report of 1892, I took it to be an endorsement and corroboration of what was said in that report.
Was there any Act between 1892 and 1896 whittling or cutting down the Civil Service Act ?

I do not know that there was, but there was nothing to improve it, and the late government had the opportunity of improving it.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) and his colleague (Mr. Foster) talked a great deal about the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the strictures thereupon. I shall not go into 249}	,
that matter except to point out that in the report of 1892, while the language is not so extreme or violent, the same thing is actually referred to. In my opinion violence of words and extreme language do not add force to strictures or make them any more applicable or true. Tre report of 1892 contains this remark about the purchases:
This is fully treated pf in the separate report on revenue and expenditure, but generally it may be stated that there has been a tendency in some cases to purchase in such a manner that the government pays retail prices for wholesale quantities.
In another part of the report it goes into that much more fully and deals with it almost as extensively as the report of 1908, but not in such extreme or violent language. I wish to deal with some of the things my hon. friend from North Toronto has said tonight. But first, let me say that I will try to keep to the question of the civil service and the Civil Service Commission. I do not think it is profitable in this or any other debate to drag in and dilate upon and picture in glowing words questions-that have been discussed and threshed out and disposed of in this House years ago. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) talked about the Department of the Interior. He said that no doubt certain things would have been discovered if the commissioners had gone on and devoted their attention to that department. He instanced certain questions in regard to the disposal of public lands and timber limits in the Northwest. He knows, no one better, that these very questions have been discussed here one or two or three years ago, have been disposed of by votes of this House that all his accusations and insinuations and those of his colleagues in the opposition have been completely answered and disposed of, and that since that time, in byelection after by-election in the country, these same questions have been paraded before the electors; the electors have been appealed to on these questions to defeat the government candidate and the series of government victories has been almost unbroken. What is and what can be the object of the hon. gentleman bringing up and resuscitating these things ? Is it simply to give himself the pleasure of the glowing word-painting he so often indulges in ? Is it simply to give himself the pleasure of gloating over imaginary scandals which he thinks may affect the country and that by constant repetition he thinks these things will come to be believed and so affect public opinion ? There is no fair or decent politics in such a course, but the hon. gentleman returns to these matters over and over again and deals with them in a xvay which I am disposed to characterize in words that would hardly pe decent or proper to use in parliament.
It was properly characterized In the Public Accounts Committee and declared to be a lie.

The hon. member for North Toronto reproached the First Minister because he had spoken briefly in answer to the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Borden). It is not always by any means the length of the speech that proves its effectiveness, in fact it may be said in general terms that the effectiveness of a speech is in inverse ratio to its length and that instead of quoting details of all kinds, instead of repeating over and over again, it is better to go to the heart of a question, to put the salient points before the House and the country and to deal with it on broad, statesmanlike lines, and I venture to think that the half hour of the right, hon. the leader of the governmet (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) was quite sufficient to reply and effectively reply to the two and a half hours of the leader of the opposition. I believe, too, that a reply can be as effectively made to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) in a much less time than that hon. gentleman spoke. He said the leader of the government had been on the wrong side. We have heard that for 12 years, we heard it when we first came into power, it was blazoned by the Tory speakers in the House and in the country that the Liberals had not the instinct of government and that it was impossible for us to have more than one term in power. Tbe results of 1900 clearly showed the error of that argument. We had the same thing for the succeeding four years from 1900 to 1904, and again we went before the people, and again these hon. gentleman's lucubrations, again their aspersions were declared to be absolutely without foundation. Since 1904 the same kind of thing has been going on and there is absolutely no indication that my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has in any way lost his cunning, or lost that keen, comprehensive ] tower of seizing the essentials in great public questions and being on the right side, the side which the people will endorse and support every time.
The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) then began to criticise and discuss the remarks of my right hon. friend. He caught him up on the statement that Mr. Justice Cassels was appointed to complete the inquiry. He knows perfectly well, every one knows perfectly well that it was not the general inquiry that it was suggested Judge Cassels will complete ; it is simply the question of the dishonesty of officials in the Marine Department which he is to complete. The commissioners made their report in general terms, they did not even make a direct accusation, but they indicated and showed they believed there was dishonesty on the part of certain officials Mr. FISHER.
there. It was to complete that part of the investigation, to finish up that question of dishonesty, to either acquit these officers of the aspersions upon them or to prove that they were guilty and enable the government to punish them In accordance with their guilt. In that sense and in that way Judge Cassels is to complete and round out that portion of the work of the Civil Service Commission ; but upon the other question it is not intended and nobody suggests that he should supplement the other parts of the report either in regard to the investigations in the department or recommendations as to civil service reform. In respect to these matters the Civil Service Commissioners completed their report. The hon. member for North Toronto said that the appointment of Judge Cassels was for the purpose of contracting the Minister of Marine and Fisheries out of his responsibility. If Judge Cassels was to undertake to investigate the management and the efficiency of the organization of the Department of Marine and Fisheries it might be said that he was appointed for the purpose of contracting the minister out of his responsibility. But he was not so appointed and it is not his business to do any work at all in connection with that part of the administration of the Department of Marine. The Minister of Marine, assuming his full responsibility as a minister, is quite prepared to do that, is doing that and is quite competent and able to do that, and I have no doubt whatever that with the help of the information which may be supplied him in regard to the dishonesty of officials and with the details as to the organization of the department which have been to a certain extent supplied him by the report, the Minister of Marine will be the better able to carry out his reorganization of that department and will succeed in doing it at no distant time.
The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) spoke of the government having discussed what we were to pay Judge Cassels for his work. I can say to the hon. member absolutely that there was no discussion as to what Mr. Cassels was to be paid or whether he should be paid at all. He was simply appointed because we believed him to be the proper and right kind of man to carry on the work for which he was appointed. It was not a question of payment. If he had wanted pay there is no doubt that the government would have been ready as the country would have been ready to pay him a fair amount for the work. He undertook to say he would not do it unless it was done without reward. All honour to him for that. All honour to him for it, I am glad he has done so. But the government have never proposed or suggested to Judge Cassels what reward he should get, or whether he should get any reward at all. Sir, in the appointment of Judge Cassels the government did

not discuss the matter with him, because we did not wish him to think for a moment that we were making any bargain with him. Judge Oassels was selected by the government because he was thought to be a suitable man and competent for the work, and I have no doubt he will carry it out in the way intended by the government and the way it ought to be carried out. But the hon. me'mber for North Toronto, without any evidence on which to base his opinion, without even having had the decency to ask the government a question on the subject, coolly jumps to the conclusion that the government have discussed and agreed upon the reward they should give Judge Cassels, when as a matter of fact nothing of the kind was discussed or even thought of. Sir, that is the way in which the hon. member for North Toronto builds up a fabric out of his own imagination, and by his word painting makes it seem almost real; then it goes out to the country, as It will be reported tomorrow, that the government have arranged to bribe Judge Cassels by appointing him to this work and giving him a large reward when, as a matter of fact, nothing of the kind was thought of. But it is the habit of the member for North Toronto, followed unfortunately by many hon. members opposite, to make baseless charges, and for the Conservative press to state them as facts, even though they are immediately denied afterwards.
Sir, the hon, member for North Toronto and the leader of the opposition have spoken of their desire to help us carry into effect amendments to the Civil Service Act. I am glad to hear it, I hope they will loyally fulfil their promise when the opportunity arises. But when they choose, in a discussion of so important a subject, to mix up the question of civil service reform, which ought to be discussed without partisanship, with a political attack upon the government in a formal motion of want of confidence, I can hardly believe in their sincerity or in their desire for civil service reform. I hope they are sincere, and when the government brings down a Bill to amend the Civil Service Act so as to make the service more efficient, I will be glad of the cooperation and endorsement of hon. gentlemen opposite. Sir, I do not intend to go into the question of civil service reform tonight beyond saying this, that I hope before the end of this session the government will be in a position to introduce a Bill to amend the Civil Service Act. I hope and trust that that Bill will make the Act more workable, and will improve the public service, and 1 believe that can be done on the lines of the reports and recommendations of the three Civil Service Commissions who have made reports to the government of Canada. I would be glad indeed if the present government were able to do what former governments did not do, although they had before them the reports
and recommendations of commissions of their own appointing. But they never acted upon them, and the result is that today the civil service of Canada is no better than it was 25 or 30 years ago when the Act of 1868 was in force. X hope that before long this government will be able to carry out a great reform of this kind, and thus justify its name as a reform government.

I would not have risen to speak on this occasion were it not for some remarks that the leader of the House saw fit to direct against myself when I was unfortunately absent from the House.
I have taken the trouble to find out what he said, and I desire to make some reply. He referred to me as having made certain statements before a farmers' meeting. I want to say to the right hon. gentleman that the statements he refers to I made, not before a farmers' meeting, but in this House, and in his own presence. X made those statements here, and I will take the liberty of repeating them again to-night, as I shall repeat them again in the country. I was very careful to quote the figures from the government blue books to prove my statement. I have yet to learn whether it is appealing to the lowest sentiments of any class of people when you ask them to compare the expenditure of one department of government with that of another department. That is the position I took, and if the right hon. gentleman sees fit to accuse me of using indiscreet language, perhaps I could remind him of an occasion, even in this parliament, when the most indiscreet language ever used in this parliament was used by the right hon. gentleman himself, and in my presence. If I may be allowed to refer to a past debate-the right hon. gentleman himself has referred to it-I allude to the statement he made in the discussion of the Japanese treaty, when he drew on his imagination to picture the combined fleets of England and Japan facing a common enemy in the Pacific ocean. Now, Sir, that speech was adversely criticised in the English press. Everybody knows that at that particular time there was a good deal of friction between the United States and Japan. If my statement was indiscreet, what are we to thiDk of the statement of the right hon. gentleman who is at the head of the government, and with whom your humble servant cannot be compared? Now, when I referred to the expenditure in the Militia Department, I made no criticism whatever of that department further than to say that this government was spending $11 on that department to $1 that they were spending on the great avocation of agriculture. I say that is true, and I will give the figures. I quoted from the government blue books of 1906. because that was the last full year of which we had any record. Turning to page 34 of the Public Accounts,

you will find this statement: Arts, Agriculture and Statistics, $003,500.34. Now, I have deducted from those figures the items which have no reference whatever to agriculture. For instance, Archives; would the right hon. gentleman tell me what these have to do with agriculture or produce of any kind that is raised on the farm ? The ' Patent Record '-what has that to do with the farming interests of the country? Census and Statistics-does that belong to the Agriculture Department any more than to any other? Criminal Statistics-does the hon. gentleman want to say that the criminal class are found among the farmers of this country? That is what his book says, the criminal statistics are charged up to the farmer. Here is the Year Book. I do not know that any man can say in whose interest that book is issued. It is not in the farmer's interest. For general statistics there was an expenditure of $14,-111.S5. Is that in the interest of the farmer any more than in the interest of any other class of people? Then, we find ' historical data re Acadian families.' Is that in the interest of agriculture? 'Quinquennial census, Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan ' called for an expenditure of $4,980. Is that in the interest of agriculture? After deducting these items I find that we have spent, in 1906. $518,976.56 in the interest of agriculture. As against that you take Militia and Defence and you find that there was an expenditure for that service of $4,294,124.62 chargeable to income and of $1,299,875.65 chargeable to capital account. Taking these figures it is within a few cents of $11 for war to $1 for agriculture. I say that should not be so. The right hon. Prime Minister said that he hoped we would never have the conditions of Germany, France and other European countries which have such heavy expenditures for war. Well, let us see. I hope we will never be in that position and the fact that we are not in that position and are never going to be in that position is a justification for my statement. Now, we will take France and these other European countries which have to be on a w'ar footing all the time. The peace of the world is in the balance and it would be jeopardized if these nations did not keep upon a war footing. Nothwithstanding that France is kept on a war footing, what is her expenditure for agriculture ? I am taking the figures which were given in a report to the president and Senate of the United States and which are thoroughly authenticated. Nothwithstanding the statement I make about these countries, France spends on agriculture yearly $9,200,000, as against an expenditure in Canada of $518,000 ; Austria spends $9,270,000 ; Hungary, $9,400,000 and Russia, which has had a most strenuous war, spends $25,280,000. Russia is our future rival in the sale of agricultural products. Japan spends $3,-Mr. BRODER.
750,000 a year, the United States, $10,000,000, and Canada. I repeat, $518,976.56. While the expenditure of other departments has been increased from one to threefold, the expenditure in the interest of agriculture has stood still. The commission, whose report is under discussion this afternoon, have criticised more severely than anything else the Department of Militia and Defence. What do they say ?
The expenditure in this department is going up by leaps and bounds.
I want to ask this House if the militia of this country is any more effective than it was ten years ago? You have machinery enough for an army of 125,000, but you have only 38,000 men. You say that this is the framework of an army but there is no permanency in the rank and file because you drill them once a year instead of for three years which is a mistake. You have done away with the three year rule.
No, that has not been done. The term of service has never been changed from three years to one.

I stand corrected. The commission proceed to say that:
In the estimates lately submitted to parliament for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1909, appropriations are asked for aggregating $6,500,000.
Is there a justification for that? With an expenditure of $518,000 for agriculture I say that my criticism is a fair and just criticism and it is a criticism that ought to be made. So much for that
I want to say before I sit down that I am pretty careful in the statements which I make and that I do not make statements without taking the trouble to verify them. I propose to give the expenditures for a few years in the Militia Department. I am quoting from the annual report of the Militia Council published last year and what do they say? If you take the men in the field, as detailed in this report for 1906, you will find a large preponderance of officers-an officer for every two and a half or three men. That is the bones of an army with a vengenee. The statement of the expenditure by the Department of Militia and Defence since 1896, is as follows:

My figures are taken from the public documents and I am usually pretty careful to see that they are verified before I state them. The right hon. First Minister has expressed his regret that I should have stated these facts but all I can do is to tell

the truth. X am not going to say anything I should not say even to please the right hon. gentleman.
Will you speak before the farmers any more?

I will if they want me. I never force myself on any meeting and I do not intend to. I wish to say that I am not going to be responsible for what the press say about me. I see that one paper says that I said there were less people in this country than there were in 1896. I am not accountable for that and X never made such a statement. I am simply accountable for what I say in this House and elsewhere. With regard to civil service reform, we hear a lot about the sinner who used to live in this country ten or fifteen years ago. It does not make any difference about who that sinner is or where that sinner is now. It is the sinners we have here that we have to deal with. That there are sinners the report of the commission has made plain. In 1891, when there was trouble in one of the departments, several civil servants were expelled, a minister of the Crown was sent into private life and some prominent party men were prosecuted in the court. Now, will these hon. gentlemen go that far and deal with those who are guilty? If they say they will we will see a very curious condition of things in this country. It will not strike one department only. Irregularities may grow up under any administration and with the large business of this country there may be an incentive to men to go wrong, but the men who are at the bead of affairs are chargeable with the responsibility of keeping things right side up and if they do not do it they are guilty and not the other people. They are the men who are responsible. If everything were in a flourishing condition in these departments you would hear hon. gentlemen opposite taking a lot of credit to themselves. Now, since things have gone, these gentlemen say: These things do not belong to us; this is an heirloom that we got from the old Tory party; we have inherited this trouble. You have inherited it but the child has grown on your hands and when you talk about rascality-shall I use that word?-it is pretty severe-the Conservative party may have sinned, but, as compared with hon. gentlemen opposite, they were in the primer when these gentlemen were in the fifth book. That is the plain . English of it. The interests of the country and the interests of public life demand that a thorough scrutiny and investigation should be held under the control of these gentlemen who have the right to see that the public departments are cleansed of what is not proper, and that the public service of the country should have that honest deal which it is entitled to from any government no matter what its party
stripe may be. I have not criticised anybody very much in this House, and perhaps that is a good thing for myself as well as for the opposite side, but there may a time come when I shall consider it my duty to discuss certain men and certain measures, and then I shall say what I have to say fearlessly and above board. I have never yet taken undue advantage of my opponent no matter who he may be, and I shall not do so in future, but I am going to have fair-play even if I have to fight for it.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).

speechtext: Oh.

Yes, he will never dare to do that. He will make insinuations but he will not have the courage to make charges and to expose himself to the consequences. Let him make charges against

me; we will have an investigation and we will find out which of us shall retain his seat in parliament; we will find who will be branded as a slanderer, and who will stand before this country a man who did his duty.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question ? Did or did not the hon. gentleman in 1896 pursue the same policy which I regret to-day is pursued by certain gentlemen now, of endeavouring to make capital out of the expenditures of the Militia Department? Did or did not he appeal to the fanaticism of the people of his province by stating that Canada was spending money for the purchase of arms for the defence of the empire?

Let me at once say that when the hon. gentleman speaks of the fanaticism of the people of my province he speaks of something which does not exist. There is no fanaticism in my province, and I believe the hon. gentleman knows it. We are broadminded in the province of Quebec. AVe are not ruled by prejudice, we are working for our country and for the advancement of our country. AVe are glad to serve under the British Crown to which we are devoted. And, Sir, when at different times in our history British connection was in danger it was the French Canadian who were there to defend it. AVho in 1775 stood up in defence of the British Crown if not the French Canadians? Who in 1812 fought the battle of Chateauguay and repulsed the American troops, if not the French Canadians? And. Sir, in 1849 when, because of the repeal of tne corn laws in England certain Canadians signed a document in favour of annexation to the United States, who were the signers? Let the hon. member (Mr. Sam Hughes) look at the signatories to that document and he will not find five French Canadians among the number. I tell the hon. member that there is no fanaticism among the French Canadians. The French Canadians are devoted to their country. I resent the insult flung at them to-night by the member for [DOT]Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) and I regret to say that such insults have become a habit with certain members on the opposite side.
Mr; SAM. HUGHES. Would the minister be good enough to answer my question, and I will substitute the word ' prejudices ' for the word fanaticism. He has given us a nice little speech now, but let him answer the question.

I have never appealed also to the prejudices of my countrymen. I know that my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) is probably living upon such appeals which he makes against the French Canadians. I know that he has been in the habit of insulting my fellow countrymen.

What Is tnat,
again?
I say that the hon. gentleman is in the habit of insulting my fellow countrymen.
The hon. gentleman cannot show an instance in my whole history where I insulted the French Canadian people. However, I shall reply to the hon. gentleman later.
Let me for a moment discuss the question before the chair.
That is a good idea.

It is certainly a good idea, and had I not been interrupted, I-would not have digressed. Now, Mr. Speaker, what is the motion before the chair ? Let us read the first paragraph of it, and we will see that hon. gentlemen opposite do not want an investigation made ; they do not want that the truth should be known; they do not want that Judge Cassels should be called on to make an investigation. Here is the way the motion reads :
That the investigation conducted by the Civil Service Commission was confessedly partial and incomplete.
That the proposed inquiry before Mr. Justice Cassels is unsatisfactory and insufficient, inasmuch as it relates to only one paragraph of the report of that commission and touches but a portion of the administration of one department.
So I understand that hon. gentlemen opposite are going to record their votes in favour of the declaration that we should not investigate the charge that is made in the report of the Civil Service Commission that there are men who have no conscience in the Marine and Fisheries Department. Let them read this motion. They do not seem to have read it, because they are laughing now. What does the report of the Civil Service Commission state ? It states that there is a lack of conscience amongst the officers of the Marine and Fisheries Department. I proposed to my colleagues to have an investigation made as to whether that statement was true or not, and I think it was the proper step to take ; I think that the country will commend the action that we have taken. But now we find hon. gentlemen opposite saying ; No, don't make an investigation ; we do not want an investigation made. That is the position which they are going to take. Well, I expect that the House will not agree to such a motion ; I expect that the House will stand by the government in declaring that an investigation must be made, and that we must find out whether there is a lack of conscience amongst the ' officers of the Marine and Fisheries Department or not.

But, Mr. Speaker, let us take from the Civil Service list the names of the officers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries appointed by hon. friends opposite. Is it because they are appointments of the late government-recommended by some members 'who are now sitting in this House- that the hon. gentlemen do not want an investigation ? I think so, Mr. Speaker. Let us take the names. The deputy minister was appointed in 1896 by hon. gentlemen opposite. Take the three chief clerks in the Marine Correspondence Branch; they were all appointed by hon. gentlemen opposite-one in 1879, one in 1873, the other in 1882. Take the Fisheries Correspondence Branch ; the two principal officers there were appointed by the Conservative government-one in 1892, the other in 1869. Take the Accountant's Branch ; the chief accountant was appointed in 1881, the next in 1879, and the assistant accountant was appointed in 1904 under this government. Take the Chief Engineer's Branch ; Colonel Anderson, the head of this branch, was appointed on October 23, 1874, by a Liberal government, and he is a man against whom there is absolutely nothing in the report of this commission. Mr. B. H. Fraser was appointed in 18S9, Mr. W. Bell Dawson in 1894. Take the Hydrographic Survey Branch; the chief was appointed in 1884. Take the Commissioner of Lights' Branch ; the commissioner was appointed in 1893, the assistant in 1883. Take the agents, of whom we have five-one in St. John, one in Halifax, one in Charlottetown, one in Montreal, and one in British Columbia ; of these five officers four have been appointed by the late government. Well, I am sure that our hon. friends opposite are not asked by the officers of the department, to oppose an investigation, as they do by their motion. No ; they want the truth to be known ; they are anxious that the truth be known, and it is only hon. gentlemen opposite who do not want the truth to be known. Are they afraid of something ? But hon. gentlemen opposite say: Oh, but the minister is entirely responsible ; if there has been some stealing in the department, the minister is responsible for it, whether it took place some time ago or many years ago. While the administration of the department may not have been all that it should have been, I repeat that the system in existence there is the system which has existed not only since the Liberals have been in power, but even when the Conservatives were in power, and I am going to prove it immediately.
The hon. leader of the opposition has quoted a great deal from the report of the Civil Service Commission, but he has failed to quote some paragraphs which are very interesting. He was very anxious to condemn me ; he was very anxious to prove that the existing Minister of Marine and Fisheries was responsible for everything that was found in that department. He did not quote page 37-oh, yes, he made a quotation, but stopped short. I quote it again, and this time I will complete the sentence which the hon. leader of the opposition commenced but left uncompleted :
Your commissioners have to confess that the general conclusions which they have formed regarding the administration of the department are most unfavourable. It seems to have a few redeeming features, although there are some, one of which is the presence in the department of some good men, chiefly but not wholly in the lower ranks. With a better organization and better methods these might form the nucleus of a good staff.
I think my hon. friend stopped there ; but there is another phrase which it might be interesting to know, and here it is :
The trouble is not of recent origin but has been long continued and is the result of evil methods and practices persisted in for many
years.
Was the hon. leader of the opposition afraid to quote this part ? The hon. member sitting beside him (Mr. Foster) has been Minister of Marine and Fisheries; he was perhaps one of those responsible for these evil practices ; what did he do to stop them? I might quote something to my hon. friend on the subject of arrears of payment. I need not go very far ; I will take the last report of the Auditor General during the time the Conservatives were in power, and what do I find there ? I find that there have been in those last years some arrears of payments. But if hon. gentlemen opposite want to do me justice, let them read the evidence given by Colonel Gourdeau. If they will read that evidence, they will find that there has been a great change made in the administration of the department. Let them read at page 649 of the evidence, vol. 1, and they will find the following evidence given by Colonel Gourdeau, the deputy minister:
Q. When you have a supply granted by parliament, do your officers try to live within that supply?-A. Yes, under the present minister. There is an order which has been adhered to. First of all, an account is received. That has to go to the clerk who looks after the estimates. If it corresponds with the estimates, he attaches his initials to it. Then it goes to the accountant who checks it. If it is an expenditure for a new boat or lighthouse, it has to stand until next year.
Q. You are trying to keep within the estimates of the year?-A. Yes. The present minister said he would hold the accountant responsible if anything was paid for that was not estimated for, he would take strict measures to prevent recurrence of that.
Q. The present minister has taken steps to keep the expenditure of the department within the appropriations?-A. Absolutely, and is particular in exacting a monthly statement showing how the appropriations stand.

I would like to know if the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) exacted that monthly statement when he saw how the r (fairs of the department were administered.
Q. There was a certain amount of laxity previous to his assumption of office?-A. It was a continuation of what had been the practice under every government. When they had to spend money, they spent it.
There is the best answer to the insinuations of hon. gentlemen opposite. Here is the evidence of a man who has been connected with the service under all the governments since 1867, and who states under oath that the present minister is the one who has made such an important change in the administration of the department. Even under the administration of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), this man says that the old system was existing and there were accounts which were not paid. But I have got here in the Auditor General's Report for 1S95-6 letters showing that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster)-who, I regret, is not in his seat now-was in the habit of making payments for one appropriation out of another appropriation, without any legitimate excuse. Here is the correspondence interchanged between the department and the Auditor General. It will be found on page 115 Part T of the Auditor General's Report for 1895-6. Mr. McDougall called the attention of the department to the fact that they were taking money-were I to follow the example set by some hon. gentlemen opposite, I should use the word * stealing '-from one vote and applying it to another. I shall not, however, use the word ; I am not the kind of man to use expressions and insinuations absolutely uncalled for. But what are the facts ? Here is Mr. McDougall complaining of the action of the department in ta' ing money from one vote and applying it to another. And I may observe that these irregularities were sanctioned by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). Would any one believe it ? It was this great administrator. It was not that crazy man, as he described me the other day. That is the language which the hon. gentleman uses with regard to myself, but here is what Mr. McDougall says. The deputy minister thought, of course, that when he could tell the Auditor General that it was the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), then Finance Minister, who had sanctioned these payments, no further difficulty would be made, but here is what the then Auditor General, Mr. McDougall, said :
Now if it were proper to charge these cheques to maintenance, it would have been equally so to charge them to any other vote covered by your credit; so that you see if such transactions are allowed to pass unnoticed, the subdivision of the annual sup-Mr. BRODEUR
plies into separate and distinct appropriations would be a farce, and, so far as keeping expenditure under its proper vote is concerned, parliament might as well vote the whole supplies in one lump sum.
And the deputy minister replies by sending to the Auditor General a letter of the hon, member for North Toronto (Mr. Fos-terl in which he said that this way of making payments was a proper thing to do. There is ample evidence to show that the practice of spending under one vote the moneys belonging to another vote was quite common under the administration of this paragon, the Ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Foster). Now, let me quote the evidence of another person. Bet me quote the letter of Mr. Gregory, on page 78, in which, writing about the Auditor General's inquiry regarding prices, he says:
I beg respectfully to state that the prices charged by J. J. Murphy, Samson & Filion, Terreau & Racine, are all fixed and agreed upon in advance. If lower rates are expected, I have no idea how you can obtain them. There has been no other system in the service before or since confederation, and it remains with the department to establish means of effecting a change.
I am trying to make a change, and if my hon. friends who, since the two years I have been in that department, have kept on criticising it day in and day out and making insinuations, will give me enough time to make those changes, I will see that the mistakes of administration which were made, even when the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) was Minister of Marine and Fisheries, will be corrected. It appears that I am to be responsible for everything set down in this respect, even for things which happened when this government was not in power. And we are told that we should not have an investigation made by a judge but by an independent commission. Here are officers of the department, charged with being derelict in their duties, charged with having lack of conscience, and who are asking for an investigation. Well, we have appointed Judge Cassels to investigate. But hon. gentlemen do not want a judge to make the investigation. What is it they want? I know what it is. If they were in power they would probably do what they did in 1892, and perhaps my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, who was not then a member of this House, will find extraordinary the procedure which was then adopted by his political friends. Would he believe me when I say-but he would not, I will quote the order in council.
I always believe you.

Charges similar to these were made against officers of one of the departments in 1891 and what happened ? Were they referred to an inde-

pendent commission as this motion states ? Were they referred to a commission absolutely independent ? Yes. The independent commission was composed of, do you know whom ? It was composed of the [DOT]minister whose officials had been found derelict in their duty, together with two other members of the government of that day. I am glad to say that my hon. friend the member for Lanark was one of those independent members called upon to investigate the actions of the Conservatives. Let us suppose for one moment that I had passed an order in council providing that I should myself make this investigation. You would see these hon. gentlemen rising in the'.r seats and saying: Look at the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the guilty one, the culprit! he is investigating his own actions ! Here is the order in council passed in 1893, appointing Mr. Dewdney, the minister whose officials were found stealing money. The member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) was also responsible as a Minister of the Crown for the actions of the officials, yet he assisted in investigating them ; and last but not least, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) was also on that commission. Here is an independent commission ; that is doubtless the one quoted by the hon. the leader of the opposition in his motion when he speaks of independent commissions.
Would the minister tell us what the finding of the commission was ?
Yes, I shall read the order in council, although it was rather long.
What was the finding ?

The point I wish to make is that the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has been complaining that the minister is responsible for the actions of his officers. The hon. member for Lanark claims that too, I suppose ?
Yes.

Then does the hon. gentleman think it was a fair thing for the men who were responsible for the actions of those officers to themselves investigate those actions ? Does he think it was a fair thing to do ?
It was our duty to investigate and we dismissed every one of them.
Oh, no, the hon. gentleman goes too far.
Every one against whom any charge was proved.

He did not dismiss them all. I think it is not fair. The hon. the leader of the opposition claims that the minister is responsible. Then the hon. gentleman should have dismissed himself, he should have resigned. But no, they cut the heads off the others, the small fry, but they kept their seats in the cabinet. However, the people dismissed them at the next election.
I did not think it would be proper for a minister or members of the cabinet to investigate the mctions of the officers. These officers were not appointed by us, none of those whose conduct will come before Mr. Justice Cassels were appointed by this government; and I thought it was fair and just that the investigation should be carried on by an Independent commission, not an independent commission such as my hon. friends opposite, but a judge, a commissioner in whom the country would have confidence in order that justice might be rendered to all parties. It is Interesting thus to read what has been done in the past and then to see the indignation of my hon. friends opposite. We have seen something of this to-day. We know that the hon. gentlemen had before them the report of the other Civil Service Commission, urging the appointment of an independent Civil Service Commission. They have done nothing, but to-day they are urging strongly such a change in system. When they were in power they never found it advisable to make the change which was recommended in that report.
Much has been said with regard to the expenditure of the Department of Marine. It is true that our department has spent money and we have been obliged to spend money. Why ? Because when the hon. gentlemen were in power they did not do their duty to the country. Take the case of Aids to Navigation. Will anybody deny the importance of having aids to navigation in order to help our shipping, in order to improve our trade, in order to add to the wealth of our country. Will hon. gentlemen opposite deny that ? We must judge them by their policy in the past; they were letting everything go to decay ; no aids to navigation were provided, no proper facilities were given and what was the result ? I shall quote some very eloquent figures which will show to this country that this government has done its duty with regard to transportation, with regard to aids to navigation, in such a way that we have reduced materially the rate of insurance on goods going to or from Canada. I have here the figures which will show the rates of insurance from Montreal direct to ports in the United Kingdom on provisions and merchandise and on grain, under the Conservative government and under this government:

When my hon. friends opposite were in power they had in charge the administration of the Montreal harbour, and what a condition it was in! It is this government who are building up the harbour of Montreal, and we intend to give to Montreal a harbour which will be a [DOT]credit to this country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I came into the department in the month of February, 1906, immediately after the opening of the session. Since that time I have been employed in that department at least .fifteen hours a day. It seems to me that a minister who lias devoted so much time to his department as that, should receive some commendation from the country, if not from the members of the opposition. I do not shrink from the labour. I have health and I have strength, and as long as I am at the head of this department I am willing to sacrifice my health and strength in order to make the department a credit to this country, and in order to remedy the evils and mistakes which were committed by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in power. Eleven ministers have passed through that department, of these seven belonged to the Conservative party and four to the Liberal party. Is it right that the responsibility for all the mistakes which were made in that department during all those years should fail entirely upon the shoulders of the present minister? I do not seek to evade any responsibility for which I am chargeable, but I refuse to be responsible for any acts committed by my predecessors. The undersigned observes that the Willson low pressure gas buoys are manufactured in Canada, while the welded compression buoys heretofore used were manufactured in foreign countries (G. B.?).

A few months after I took charge of the department, I saw that the system of accounting there was bad, and I thought that I should get somebody to make a thorough investigation, to find out whether the system of book-keeping we had there was good or not. Because I have done that; because I have tried to bring about some reform in my department; because I tried to provide the means of ascertaining every day what the expenditures in my department were, and of making comparisons every day and every hour to see whether the expenditures were too high or not, and whether they compared favourably or unfavourably with those of former years ; because I took these means of saving thousands and thousands of dollars to tlie department, I stand charged before the country by hon. gentlemen opposite as having been extravagant in providing that system of accounting. No, Mr. Speaker; it is the best thing I have done, because now we can ascertain whether the affairs of the department are properly administered or not. he did not do himself the credit of establishing a system in the department by which the books would show every day a trial balance. .1 thought it was absolutely necessary in such a department to have books which would show every day how the affairs of the department were going. I have heard it so often this session that I have come to admire it more and more every time I hear it, and I have no doubt that, surfeited as the hon. gentlemen are with the laudations he showers on himself, some one will rise and say something on behalf of the minister, for God knows he needs it, as no one has said anything in his behalf this session. He happened to be Speaker of this House and immortalized himself by being the most profligate spender of money ever in that office. He talks about juggling with accounts ; the accounts of the Speaker for that year were so enormous that he had actually to juggle them to the amount of over $8,000 into the account of the Minister of Public Works.

He sat in this House and in committees [DOT] and heard the Department of Marine assailed. He saw that in that garden of the grafter and that paradise of the plunderer they had been permitted to roam at large, that the department was approaching to the notoriety of the Public Works Department, he heard of its waste and saw it and on coming into power in that department he was the first man to extend the right hand of fellowship to the grafters who had been in that department for years before he entered it. He cannot deny that. Merwin and Brooks were the only men with whom he wanted to deal. These grafters who had pilfered, pillaged and plundered the money of the country were the first he dealt with.
