against the persons at whom they are aimed. The hon. member for North Toronto acquitted himself with that force which he usually exercises when he addresses this House ; but I must tell him that much clapping and slapping of the hands, much pounding of his desk, much gesticulation, does not add emphasis to his remarks, in the opinion of members on this side of the House, although such actions on the part of the hon member may and so call for loud applause from a band of his admiring followers. Now, what did, he bring up which the House was not already in possession of ? He went over the old land-deal scandals, or so-called scandals, the charges of impropriety in connection with timber and irrigation companies, charges which have time after time been investigated in this House and disposed of, merely to give what in his opinion was justification for a more extended inquiry than is proposed to be had before Hr. Justice Cassels. But he seems to forget that which we all remember, namely, that there had been the fullest, freest and fairest investigation of all these matters, from the original documents, in the Public Accounts Committee and otherwise, and therefore there is not the slighest necessity for any further investigation or discovery. But the hon. member for North Toronto said that the government were inclined to repudiate the commission, to find fault with it, to sneer at it. Now, I do not find, in any statement which has been made to-day by any one on this side of the House any such insinuation either on the part oi the government or on the part of any member sunnorting the government. On the contrary, the government realize that this is a report made by their own commission, am 1 am satisfied of one thing, though I do not know the minds of the government, that having received that report from a commission appointed by themselves, they are going to give its recommendations all the weight and authority that such recommendations coining from such men should have. They are not going to treat the report as such reports were treated by Conservative governments in the past. I have no doubt in my mind that if the administration of the various departments to-day is found wanting in any respect, though I do not admit that it is, the reason is that the Liberal .party did not take such action as they would have been justified in taking in the year 1S96 when they obtained power. The party which introduced into this country and into the civil service of this country that iniquitous system known as the spoils system was not the Liberal party. There was a civil service in this country before confederation. Under the Act of Union of 1841 we had a civil service, and it continued until the year 1867. In the year 1868 a new service had to be instituted;

there were new provinces, new requirements, and new services to he performed. So that in that year was passed the first Civil Service Act, and a very crude affair it was. In the following year was appointed the first Civil Service Commission. That commission was to find out what was requisite in the way of a civil service for the country. That commission made its report, and in pursuance of that report the first civil service was established under the coalition government, though the premier was the late Sir John Macdonald. The coalition system did not work very - well and did not stand very long; and shortly after confederation, instead of carrying out the idea of the fathers of confederation in regard to the civil service or the Senate, the spoils system was introduced deliberately, and appointments were only made to the civil service or to the Senate of political partisans of the government of the day. That was the first real introduction of that system into this country, a system which has for its motto, ' to the victors belong the spoils.' That system was continued. I do not say that the Mackenzie administration did not continue it as well as other administrations; but I do say that after the year 1878, after the Mackenzie administration went out of power, the system received fresh vigour at the hands of the Conservative administration which came in for a second time. It is well known that many of the Liberal appointments made at the close of the Liberal administration were deliberately set aside by the government of Sir John Macdonald and the places filled by prominent Conservatives. That surely was the maintenance of the spoils system. There was much outcry and much comment at the time, and it was on account of that that the Civil Service Commission of 1880 was appointed. How did the Conservative government of that day treat that commission ? They appointed it, I think I can safely say at this time, for the purpose of fooling or hoodwinking the public. They had no real intention of taking the civil service out of politics, but their commissioners had that intention, and the only real suggestion or recommendation which that commission made, the most pointed and most prominent, was that ail civil service appointments should he open to free competition. In 1881 there was nothing done. In 1883 there was very little done. It is true that there was a Civil Service Act passed and a board of examiners appointed, but there was no board of civil service commissioners appointed, as the commission recommended. It is true, the examination were prescribed, but not those that the commission recommended. The system of examination was changed, and although hundreds passed the examinations, only Conservative candidates could obtain ad-

mission to the service. That Act was amended every year up to 1889 and every amendment made to it was for the purpose of doing away with or relaxing conditions which the Act imposed. I make that statement on the authority of the commission which discussed the matter in 1892. They say there that the Act was amended from year to yefir for the express purpose of giving greater latitude to the government or relaxing its restrictions or conditions.
How did the next commission come to be appointed? It was appointed because there was a greater outcry throughout Canada probably than ever before. In 1891 this whole country was shaken and its people humiliated by the disclosures which had taken place before the parliamentary commission of this House. There was an outcry from one end of the country to the other that something must be done, that some reform must take place, and in order to meet that cry

but without the slightest intention of doing anything, except hoodwinking the public

another commission was appointed in November, 1891. That commission reported in the spring of 1892. Quotations have been made from that report on many occasions to-day, but there are some things in it which have not been brought out properly in this debate. The original powers given the commission were these. They were entitled to investigate any subject connected with the civil service which, in their opinion, required consideration and readjustment in order to attain the greatest possible efficiency. Their powers were similar to the general powers given the recent commission. Those powers are included under ten headings, and, besides the matters specially designated, the commissioners are authorized to inquire into any other matter relative to the service which, in the opinion of the commissioners, requires consideration. The commissioners in 18t>2 were four in number. Mr. J. M. Courtney was commissioner then as well as in the commission of 1907-8. The commission of 1892 made some express findings, which it is well to note. They found that there was political interference in the civil service; that the examinations were a mere mockery and the promotion examinations in many cases evaded altogether. They found that the departments were overmanned and underpaid; that they were overmanned through political influence and favourtism and that the purchasing system was very widely astray. They did not use the term ' discount ' or state that no discounts appeared, but the statement they did make in that respect is to be found page 58 of the report:
A still further subject your commissioners deem worthy of note, before treating of the expenditures themselves, is that relating to the purchase of supplies and the prices paid for articles purchased by the several departments. In his evidence before the commission, the Auditor General stated most distinctly that when goods were purchased without tenders, such as furniture and other supplies for the public buildings, as a rule, retail prices were paid for the same when wholesale prices should have prevailed.
Thus admitting that the same system was in vogue in those days as, it is charged, has been continued since. The attention of the late Conservative government was called to all these matters in that report. They knew that the departments were being overmanned through political influence. They knew that purchases were improperly made, and that retail prices were paid where wholesale prices should have prevailed. They knew that the examination system was a farce and that the spoil system was in full force. What did they do? 1892 passed and nothing done. So did 1893, 1894 and 1895 and nothing whatever accomplished. 1890 passed and with it the Conservative government, and then there began to be some shaking up of the dry bones in the various departments. It is perhaps not altogether accurate for me to say that in 1893 absolutely nothing was done. Among the recommendations of the commissioners was one with regard to superannuation, and there was a bill passed on that subject. But to the positive recommendation of the commissioners regarding appointments to the service, examinations, open competition and so forth, not the slightest attention was paid, so that I think the lion, member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) was not quite fair when lie said that the recommendations of that commission had been carried out by three separate Bills. The commissioners themselves drafted a Civil Service Bill, a most elaborate measure. Read it carefully because it would make the basis of a splendid civil service enactment. But it was disregarded almost in toto, and a Bill introduced by Mr. Costigan in 1893. You can search through the sections of that Bill- sixteen in number-and you will find them the most formal kinds of amendment to the original Act of 1882. One or two clauses of the draft Bill of the commission of 1892 were incorporated in the Bill No. 29 of 1893, but all the main recommendations of the commissioners, all the main clauses of their Bill were emasculated and deprived of any effect. Now these hon. gentlemen say that that Bill was not passed because of the stand taken by the right hon. gentleman who now leads the government. Nothing can be further from the fact. The Conservative government had then a majority of forty or fifty and they would have passed that Bill had they so desired; but what was objected to by the right hon. gentleman, then leader of the opposition, was that the government's Bill was merely intended to give the government the chance f maintaining the iniquitous spoils system which they had maihtained from confederation down to 1893. The Bill in any event was dropped and nothing

was done, and the Conservative government went out of power in 3896. What then happened? No sooner had the present government been sworn in than every Conservative newspaper in the land was crying out that the guillotine was at work and the Conservative heads of the various branches of the service were dropping into the basket. The late Mr. Tarte, then Minister of Public Works, did make some removals, and was caricatured throughout Canada with the guillotine beside him, as an unscrupulous tyrant. Sir William Mulock, then Postmaster General, made some removals, and he also was hounded and vilified. Certain removals were made In the Department of Agriculture, but strange to say the incoming government, having faith no doubt in the commissioners' report of 1S93, as regards the Militia Department and the Department of Marine and Fisheries, made no removals that I know of, but continued on the same old Conservative staff in each department without a single exception. There is one distinction between the report of 1893 and the report recently presented, which I desire to point out. The report of 1892 made under a commission given general powers to investigate just as broad as those of the commission of 1907, contains this statement:
The commissioners before entering into the consideration of the subjects laid down in the reference, desire to state, that it was not within the lines of their duty to follow up inquiries made by the Committee of the House of Commons in the session of 1891, which brought out certain irregularities, but rather to suggest such improvements in methods applicable to all departments as will tend to prevent irregularities in future.
They absolutely state they will not investigate these irregularities although their powers are almost identical with those of the commission of 1907. The commissioners at the very outset say they are not going to investigate irregularities which they considered were outside the scope of their commission. Certainly a certificate coming under such circumstances will have very little force, weight or effect throughout the country as there was no investigation into irregularities or anything of the kind, but the report of the commissioners states that they had visited the departments and that they found an extremely favourable condition of things in the Marine and Fisheries Department; they also make a complimentary reference to the Militia Department. Is it any wonder then that the incoming government should have made no removals in either of these departments ? If they had in view, as I believe they have had for years, a new civil service system, whereby the spoils system will be absolutely abolished in this country; in 1896, they set out properly to Initiate that system because the removals were few and under the circumstances should have been far more. How has it turned out? We had a com-

mission appointed in 1907 and where is the fault found? Is there any fault found in that report with the Department of Agriculture. where derelict officials were removed ? Hardly a word spoken of that department. Is any serious fault found with the Post Office Department, where objectionable Conservative officials were removed? There is hardly'a criticism of the Post Office Department. Is any serious fault found with the Public Works Department where Mr. Tarte cleared the way? Hardly a word, they did not see fit even to investigate that department. But when you come to the Marine and Fisheries Department and the Militia Department where there was no guillotine, where old Conservative officials were trusted and continued, there your trouble arises.
The old system has been, continued, until recently at all events, but I assume, although I do not know, that things could not have been going very well last spring. Some difficulty must have arisen and if any difficulty did arise, if there was cause for any suspicion, the government, I submit, did the proper thing under the circumstances in appointing a commission of three men in whom both the government and the public have absolute confidence, to inquire into the system. Why the government should now be condemned for that action I do not know. To my mind it was the only fair, honest, statesmanlike and businesslike course which the government could take. They themselves invited the investigation and they themselves, now that the report has been received, I think can be well trusted to remedy any defects which may have been reported in that system. I think, therefore, the motion which has been made on that subject by the leader of the opposition should fail. The investigation has been complete to an extreme, far more complete perhaps than any one anticipated, but it is well for the government and for the country that it ha'sl been so complete.	|
But there is a feeling in my mind andt I think in the mind of any unprejudiced man, that the commission either did go too far or not far enough in some of their findings, and it is for that reason that a judge, highly respected by every one who knows him, has been asked to point out or to place his hand upon the real culprit or culprits, if there be more than one, in the Marine and Fisheries Department. I have no doubt, although I do not know the mind of the government, that they will take steps to remedy the defects that have been pointed out. I do not know- just what lines of action they may see fit to take, but I am satisfied that when their measure does come down it will be found to remedy the defects and to satisfy the desires of every reasonable man in this country who wishes to see a better civil service system inaugurated and maintained.

The lion, member for North Toronto made what I would term a sort of wild election speech. He took his cue, no doubt, from certain remarks of his own leader when he spoke of the commission's report as being a sort of campaign document. It has been used as such a document by the Conservative party, there is no doubt about that. When the hon. member for North Toronto (Hr. Foster) took the floor, he immediately reverted to what he called the revenge which the people had taken on the present government in New Brunswick. He spoke also of what had taken place in British Columbia and then he referred to some small municipal election in the city of Halifax, yesterday. I believe that in some of the wards some aldermen were elected. These are the indications which present themselves to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), and evidently convince him that there is a brighter day coming for the Conservative party than there has been for many years past. If he accepts these as positive or conclusive signs he is easily satisfied and we do not quarrel with him, but I think he went out of his way to say some unkind and very mean things in regard to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. It was an unnecessary sneer for the hon. member to use in regard to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries when he said that the minister had gone down to the province of Quebec in 1896 to oppose military expenditures, in other words to raise a race and creed agitation in that province. I am satisfied that the statement of the minister in that regard is absolutely correct and the statement of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) is absolutely unfounded. I cannot say that he made that statement knowing it to be false, but I can say that he made it in such utter, reckless disregard as to whether it were false or true that it should be condemned by every right-thinking man in this House.
There is another peculiar circumstance to which I wish to refer. The hon. member who leads the opposition, on the 20th day of August last, proceeded to Halifax, there to enunciate his political platform and to announce to the citizens of Halifax, the capital of Nova Scotia, that he had placed in it a plank in regard to civil service reform. Why he should have gone to Halifax to make that announcement for the first time, I do not know. Was it in the spirit of bravado that he went there? I think it would have been more fitting if he had gone to the county of Carleton to make that announcement than to the city of Halifax. The hon. member for North Toronto always reverts to conditions in New Brunswick; time and again he tells us what has happened, what is happening and what will happen in the province of New Brunswick. Why, Sir, the strangest thing of all is to see these two hon. members
occupying the seats of the mighty in the opposition ranks of this House; the leader of the opposition himself, politically expatriated from his native province of Nova Scotia, driven to seek a seat amidst the preponderating Orange vote of the county of Carleton; the member for North Toronto, politically expatriated from his native province of New Brunswick, driven to seek a seat amidst the preponderating Orange Tory vote of the city of Toronto. And there they sit together, while Orangemen to the right of them, Orangemen to the left of them, and Orangemen behind them volley and thunder. I have no doubt, having regard to the constituencies which they represent in this House, that the hon. member for North Toronto finds it necessary occasionally to furnish some strong meat for his constituents, and he can best supply that by making sneers and jibes at something that transpired in the province of Quebec. The whole discussion of this question I think has gone rather far afield, having regard to the motion and the amendment which has been placed in your hands. However, at this late hour, I will not venture to trespass upon the time of the House by entering further upon the discussion.

Mr. Speaker, last night the hon. leader of the opposition called the attention of the government to a telegram which he had received shortly before from the town of Yorkton in the province of Saskatchewan, and which was as follows :
Yorkton, Saskatchewan, April 30, 1908. E. L. Borden, M.P., Ottawa.
Fort William contingent of vagrants presumably insane Doukhobors shipped here in charge of an official of Ontario government still in coaches on track here. Induced to come to Yorkton under /misrepresentation' that they were going to warmer climate. Doukhobors in villages refuse to acknowledge them. Citizens strongly protest against them being dumped here. Some twenty in a nude state iudecently exposing themselves. Provincial government inform us matter being taken up with Immigration Department of Dominion government. Matter extremely urgent. Please urge immediate action.
Secretary Board of Trade.

Secretary-Treasurer.
The reply of the Prime Minister was as follows :
As my hon. friend knows if these people have violated the laws of the province of Saskatchewan they are under the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities.
I consider that a most unsatisfactory statement coming from the head of this government. Let me recall to your mind the
facts of the case in regard to this special number of Doukhobors. They are well
known to the public, having been freely discussed in the public press. In the early part of last summer a number of Doukhobors started eastward on a pilgrimage on foot. They went by easy stages and reached Fort William or Port Arthur at the beginning of the winter. They took a house and stayed at Fort William during the winter. While they were there they committed several offences against public decency, and finally on April 9, this spring, nineteen of them were committed to imprisonment in the central prison for a term of six months, I believe. While they were undergoing punishment and before they had been removed from Port Arthur, the Dominion government stepped in and ordered their release when they had been in prison only ten days. The Minister of Justice stated in answer to a question of mine the other day, that it had been represented to him that these Doukhobors had come from Saskatoon, and as there was no room for the prisoners in the prisons of the country, it would be advisable to pardon them, and, to use his own words, ' let them be removed to the part of the country from which they came.' On these representations lie sent a telegram as follows :
April 14, 1908.
Mr. Police Magistrate Palling,
Fort William.
The Minister of Justice requests you will be good enough to send immediately report upon cases of ten male and nine female Doukhobors committed by you to Port Arthur jail.

For Deputy Minister of Justice.
The report was received and submitted to His Excellency the administrator on the 18th of April, and the release of the prisoners was ordered. Thereupon the Doukhobors stepped out from jail defiant and triumphant at having successfully defied the laws of this country. According to the newspapers, another telegram was sent at the same time that the Minister of Justice was telegraphing to the magistrate at Fort William, and was received by that magistrate before he had time to answer the first telegram. That telegram was as follows :
Please report pardon for Doukhobors now in Port Arthur jail preparatory to their being shipped back to Saskatchewan, where they come from.
I do not know whom that telegram came from. At any rate, the Minister of Justice repudiates it. But the fact that the two telegrams were sent practically at the same time showed that the Minister of Justice must have been a party to the intention to ship these people west to the province of Saskatchewan. The Minister of Justice says that, as far as he was concerned, the Doukhobors were at liberty to

come and go as they pleased like any other citizens and that he had no intention of sending them to the province of Saskatchewan. That is evidently a quibble. He knew all about it and was a party to the steps which were taken, and the Doukho-bors were released in order to be sent back to that province. I consider that the government of the Dominion have a considerable amount of responsibility for the release of these prisoners. I made inquiry as to whether the government would accept responsibility for having released prisoners almost immediately after conviction and before they had been properly punished. The right horn the First Minister rather smiled and said no, that the administration of justice was in the hands of the provincial authorities. I hold, however, that when the provincial authorities have done their duty and put these people in jail, the Dominion authorities assume a great deal of responsibility when they order them to be released. The Dominion government assume responsibility to see that these people do not offend the second time shortly after their release, and also to see that any expense incurred by another province, in case these people should again offend, should not fall on that province. Only the other day I saw a case reported in the newspapers in which the Minister of Justice had released a man convicted for stealing horses. The man was released before the expiry of the term, and shortly after he got out of jail he again committed a similar offence and put the provincial authorities to a great deal of trouble and expense. I am glad to say that the man was captured again and again committed for a long term, and I trust the Minister of Justice will not take it into his head to again release that man and start him on his career of horse stealing again.
The first thing that strikes me is that these Doukhobors were sent to Yorkton, instead of to Saskatoon if they came from there. On arrival at Yorkton it was found that some of them were travelling in a state of nudity and the people of Yorkton object to having these people turned out on their streets to parade in that condition. The people of the province of Saskatchewan are thus put to the expense of preventing these Doukhobors from committing any further offence against public decency. This whole business is a public scandal. These people, who were accustomed to parade in this condition iu the town of Fort William are released from the just punishment for their offences, put on board the cars, sent to another province and allowed to get out and offend the people there. It is time the government took some steps to look after these wretched creatures. They were brought into this country in the year 1899. They were placed in the province of Saskatchewan without the permission of the people of that province having been par-Mr. LAKE.
ticularly asked,' and yet that province is held responsible. That province has had a great deal of trouble with these people. It has been found impossible to make them obey some of our laws. They were brought in by this government with a great deal of eclat. They were the first fruits of the * splendid ' policy of immigration introduced by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sif-ton). Liberal organizations all through the country made a great hurroo about them. Special receptions were organized, brass bands and all that sort of thing, and they were received in a way very liable to spoil them and cause them rather to look with disrespect on Canadians. The cost of bringing them out was pretty considerable because they received a bonus of one pound per head, although at that time immigrants from the British Isles were only receiving one-half that bonus. For the first year they cost the government in bonus and keep, $7.47 per head for every man, woman and child of. them. Under the circumstances, I think this government are especially responsible, and should explain on what ground they were a party to shipping these people back to another province. These people remained there throughout the winter. In the early part of the winter we did not hear that they were acting in any very extraordinary way, but during the winter they apparently became demented. It is time for the government to take cognizance of this public scandal. The government are to be condemned for turning these people out naked into the streets of one of onr Canadian cities.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTII (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the answer I gave to the question of my hon. friend last week, I stated as fully as possible exactly the circumstances. I stated that in this whole business this government recognizes and undertakes no responsibility whatever except for the recommendation to release these prisoners. For that recommendation I of course take the fullest responsibility. It was made by myself in the course of daily departmental business and was a proper recommendation under the circumstances. It was made, as I have already stated, upon the direct request and recommendation to me of the Attorney General of the province of Ontario, who is the proper official and the proper constitutional authority charged with the duty of administering justice within the province. And I may say that in the twenty-three months experience I have now had in the Department of Justice. in dealing with applications for the release of prisoners, it has been not infrequent that for some special reason the pardon or release upon ticket of leave of some particular prisoner has been suggested or recommended by the Attorney General of the province from which that prisoner came or in which the offence was com-

mitted, and I do not recall any instance in which such a recommendation has not been acted upon. Certainly, it is a recommendation of the greatest potency, and one which, in all ordinary circumstances, I would think, should at least be regarded, if not followed implicitly. In the case of. these particular prisoners, there was an offence against good morals, an offence against society
On what date was tile answer given ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On April 23, as found in unrevised ' Hansard, page 7210. In the case of these prisoners, I say, the offence wras one against social order and one which had been dealt with by the local municipal authorities. The conviction had been made by the police magistrate of the city of Fort William, himself a provincial official. The application for the release of these prisoners was not merely supported by letter of the deputy Attorney General of the province in which their pardon was asked as something which he thought the best course to be taken in the circumstances, but the application was supported by the coming to Ottawa for that express purpose of two of the prison officials of the provincial government. These two gentlemen came bringing the letter I have referred to with them, and stating that the object of their application was in order that the whole of the colony of Doukhobors who had been living in Fort William for some months might return to the place from whence they came. It was stated to me that it was the wish of these people to rejoin their companions, their fellows, their family relations, I suppose, who remained in the province of Saskatchewan, and they were not willing to return if they were to be compelled to leave behind those of their unmber who had been imprisoned for the offence referred to. In the circumstances, I think, every hon. gentleman who hears me will concur in the feeling that the application came very strongly supported. I do not, at the moment, remember the length of the imprisonment to which these men and women had been sentenced, but I point out that, however much to be reprehended the offence is of which these people had been guilty, it is conceded on ail hands that it was something which they had done contrary to good morals and social order, but in which there was, on their part, no intent to commit crime, in which there was on their part, it may be, conscientious action dependent upon motives of a religious character, and an offence which, at all events, was induced according to every account of it, which I have seen or which has been made to my knowledge, by a sort of religious mania or frenzy which possibly amounts, as the hon. gentleman has suggested, practically to a loss of reason or to insanity. Well, if people are in that condition, those who are best able to take care of their fellows whose reason has been affected or impared, upon whom the care of such poor people to be pitied, unoffending creatures, may most properly be cast, are the very family relations or companions to whom, as I was told, they were desirous of returning. The responsibility for the care of the insane, equally with that for the care of prisoners under shorter terms and for the less serious offences, is upon the provincial authorities. And, in these circumstances, it was simply a case where people in prison for a comparatively venial offence were, by the constituted authorities of the province, asked to be allowed to go in order that they might go with their fellows to their homes, to tiie place from which they came. Though it lias been charged in the newspapers, and was in a sense endorsed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bake) who has just spoken, in the question which he put in the House, that the application to the convicting magistrate from the Department of Justice for a report in the case of these prisoners was immediately followed by a request, or direction, or suggestion, by telegram from the Department of Justice to the same magistrate that lie should report favouring a pardon, I took occasion to deny that very unequivocally in the answer I made.
I did not make the charge, but read the statement to that effect and asked if it was true.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Certainly, I acquit altogether my hon. friend (Mr. Lake) from any intention to make the charge. The language I have just used was that it was freely charged in the newspapers, and in a sense, endorsed by the hon. gentleman. I do not wish to be understood at all as saying anything to the contrary if the hon. gentleman wishes it to be understood that he did not at all share in the impression that this request for a report favouring a pardon had proceeded from the Department of Justice. As I have said, that was not the case at all, and I can only surmise from what source the telegram, which is quoted verbatim in the question I have referred to did proceed ; I supposed it must have come from the officials here in Ottawa at that time when they made the application for the release of these people and who were interested in getting them returned to the province of Saskatchewan. With anything that has taken place since the signing of the recommendation to His Excellency for the release of these prisoners, I have had nothing whatever to do, and I have no knowledge whatever beyond what has appeared in the newspapers, and from the reception yesterday of a telegram in identical words with the telegram read at the adjournment of the House by the hon. leader
7G27

oi the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). But whatever the situation in the province of Saskatchewan, or wherever these men may be, it is, I repeat, in my submission, a provincial matter, a matter in regard to which this government is under no resposibility whatever, and in regard to which any action that has been taken by the Department of *Justice in this connection is not one that leaves the department itself in any way open to fair criticism. I have acted with regard to these prisoners exactly in the way in which I would have acted if the same men or women had been Canadian born, in the same way as if they had been of any other nationality whhtever. The nationality of the people had not anything the slightest to do with the course taken with respect to them. And the number had nothing to do with it. It was simply a case with those convicted of this offence of going publicly without clothing, and an application on the part of the constituted authorities of the province in which that offence had been committed that these persons should be pardoned.
Once pardoned that person was absolutely free to go wheresoever he or she might see Qt, and so long as no law of the country was broken, that person was not to be restrained of his or her personal liberty. That appears to be exactly what has taken place. These people have gone, it may be in charge of a provincial officer, from Fort William back to where they came from. The hon. gentleman representing a constituency in the province to which they have gone (Mr. Lake) thinks that it was wrong that they should have gone there. He speaks of the Dominion government having stepped in. as though the Dominion government had officiously, of its own motion, without having been asked to do so, interfered in this matter and done something to put these people off the province of Ontario and on to the province of Saskatchewan. I disclaim any such representation of what has taken place in regal'd to this matter. There has been so far as the Department of Justice is concerned-and that department alone of any in the government so far as I am aware has had anything to do with this transaction-no siding with one province or with another province. It is a matter of absolute indifference, so far as the Dominion authorities are concerned, in which province of this Dominion those people may be. But there lias been a facilitating, if my hon. friend wishes to put it in that way, a facilitating of an intention expressed beforehand on the part of the officials of whom I have spoken, that these people should return to the place from which they came. It is in no other sense that there has been any sending of these men and women from one part of the country to another, and there is nothing in anything I have done in the matter which merits the application of the word ' quibble ' which I Mr. AYLESWORTH.
understand my hon. friend has used in describing what has taken place. I have stated from the outset exactly what I knew of the matter. I was told beforehand that the object in asking that these imprisoned people should be set free was in order ..that with those of their companions who were at large they might go away all together, and because those who were at large declined to go leaving behind their companions in jail.
I cannot speak of the other case to which the hon. gentleman has alluded, because I do not identify it in any way. He complains that in some other instance, some man imprisoned for horse stealing was improperly released. Well, it only illustrates, and I ask any hon. gentleman who will be good enough to take the trouble to consider this, something of the difficulty of the position in which any man is who has to advise on many hundreds of applications of this character in the course of a twelvemonth. It is manifestly impossible to please everybody in such things. My hon. friend thinks it was very wrong to have released that prisoner. The hon. member for Durham not so very long ago with some other hon. gentlemen in this House thought it was very wrong that I should not release somebody else convicted from Hie same neighbourhood. I can only say that each one of these cases has to be dealt with, with all the care I am able to apply to it, upon its own individual circumstances. I am perfectly conscious, only too conscious and only too sorry, that in many cases mistakes are made. I am afraid that in some cases men who ought in all honesty and justice to be set at large are not set at large, and I am only too well aware that in too many eases men who ought not to be allowed to go have been, by some misunderstanding of the facts or by some reliance that has proved unfounded, upon too frail human nature, allowed to go free. These things will always occur and there may be plenty more cases besides the one to which my hon. friend has alluded in which the event has demonstrated that it would have been better had the prisoner not been the subject of clemency at the hands of the Crown.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister of Justice is not quite accurate in the reference he made to the case brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Durham. In that case the prisoner expressly disclaimed any desire to have a pardon. He declined to be pardoned, because he claimed strongly that he had never committed any crime. What he did desire was that he should be afforded a new trial in order to bring forward evidence which was not available at the time of his conviction. He also desired that he should be tried by a jury of his fellow countrymen.

So far as concerns tlie matter which has been immediately brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Qu'-Appelle (Mr. Lake), the Minister of Justice disclaims all responsibility except the responsibility of acting upon the recommendation of the Attorney General for Ontario. No one can criticise the province of Ontario or any of the officials of that province for desiring to get rid of these people. It was a perfectly natural desire that these persons, having come from somewhere outside of the province and having conducted themselves in such a manner as to justify their incarceration either in prison or an asylum, should be taken out of the province as soon as possible. But when you come to the question of sending them back to the province of Saskatchewan, you must assume a condition on their part which certainly calls for action by some government and one would think it might merit the interference of this government which is responsible for bringing those people into the country. Those people, if they are in their right mind, have as good a right to reside in the province of Ontario or any other province of Canada as they have to reside in the province of Saskatchewan. Therefore, there was no possible warrant for sending them back to the province of Saskatchewan even if there were warrant for pardoning them of the effence for which they were convicted and setting them at liberty. It is perfectly clear that the pardon was granted with the idea that they would be sent back to the province of Saskatchewan. If these men are in such a condition that they are to be bandied about from one province to the other until friction arises between the various provinces, such as arises between the guardians of one poor district and those of another poor district in Great Britain, we shall have a very curious condition of affairs in this country. Suppose that the authorities of the province of Saskatchewan take proceedings against these people for that indecent exposure which is even now being committed by them in that province, suppose that they are again incarcerated, and that the Attorney General of Saskatchewan recommends to this government their discharge in order that they may be sent to a warmer climate in British Columbia, will the same play go on, will they be removed from the province of Saskatchewan to the province of British Columbia by means of the pardoning powers ' of this government, and then shall we have another performance of exactly the same character in the province of British Columbia? Persons who conduct themselves in this way are fit inmates for a prison or an asylum, and if they are mentally deranged, as the Minister of Justice suggested, then surely the government of the Dominion, responsible for bringing these people into the country, should co-operate in some way with the government of some 242
province and see that the public decency of the country is not any longer violated by such performances as those which have been going on in recent months.
Why did not the government of this country before exercising its pardoning power, make some inquiry of the authorities of the province of Saskatchewan to ascertain the circumstances under which these people hal left that province and come to a conclusion as to what the conditions would be if these people were deported from Outario to Saskatchewan ? It appears, notwithstanding all that has been said by the hon. Minister of Justice respecting the restoration of these people to family relations, that there are no family relations to be restored because the sensible Doukhobors, the majority of those people who are living, as I believe, quiet, decent, peaceable and industrious lives, refuse altogether to recognize this small section of the community which is bringing discredit upon the name of Doukhobors throughout the country. Why was not some inquiry made as to that before they were sent back to Yorkton ? Under the circumstances, it seems to me that the action of the government is not very, intelligent and that the Department of Immigration, or some department of the government, should get at once into communication witli the authorities of the province of Saskatchewan and see that such steps are taken as will prevent a recurrence of any such scenes as those which have been heralded throughout the press during the past three or four months in. eastern Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Department of Immigration has now a somewhat wide spread responsibility, and as having charge of that department at the present time, I must really protest against the suggestion of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. It. L. Borden) that, besides having the responsibility for all effort in regard to bringing people into Canada, it should be responsible for all people In Canada after they come here. I take it that we have a division of responsibility between the different branches of the one government and between the different governments of this country. A certain responsibility rests upon the Dominion government, a certain responsibility rests upon the provincial governments, and I do not think that there is any gain to be made by a provincial government assuming Dominion responsibilities nor by the Dominion government assuming provincial responsibilities. The Department of Immigration, to which my hon. friend has consigned these people, has to do with such effort as is sanctioned by parliament to bring to people outside of Canada the advantages of Canada with the view of securing their re-



moval here, and two years ago it was clothed with the further power to remove out of Canada to the country from whence they came people who, within two years of their coming, had transgressed the laws or rendered themselves obnoxious or undesirable here. But, these Doukhobors in question are neither in one class nor the other. They have been residents of Canada for a matter of seven, eight, or nine years, and during these seven, eight or nine years, as far as I am aware, they have been not only ordinarily law-abiding but they have been extraordinarily law-abiding as far, at any rate, as coming in conflict with the administration of the law is concerned. I venture to say that there are no other 8,000 people of any class, country or condition, who have come to Canada, who, during the nine years of their residence in Canada, have come as little in contact with the officers charged with the administration of the laws as have the 8,000 Doukhobors now resident in Canada. Therefore, Canada has not, either in its provinces or in the Dominion as a whole, suffered from the presence of these people in so far as the administration of law is concerned, or in so far as they have been a burden upon the enforcement of law in this country. These people, it appears, saw fit, some time during last summer, to change their place of residence. Having resided in the province of Saskatchewan for a matter of seven, eight or nine years, they for reasons of their own, saw fit to [DOT]change their place of residence and they exercised the right which is accorded to every person who is a resident of this country to remove from where he is to where he wants to be. They travelled through the settled portions of Manitoba, through its cities and villages and they were received with open arms wherever they went. The people supported them as they travelled along, gave them food, listened to their songs, admired their peculiarities, I presume, and sent them on their way rejoicing, until finally they arrived at port William. When they arrived there the people, or the authorities of Fort William, seemed to think that there was a possibility of occurrences that were not to their advantage. They communicated with the Dominion government here and asked the government to take some responsibility in regard to these people who had been residents of Canada for seven, eight or nine years, who had paid taxes and who were entitled to and had received the privileges and responsibilities of citizenship except the actual right to vote. Well, 1 can only say, Mr. Speaker, that the Immigration Department did not feel any responsibility and did not accept any, and I think the response which was sent to the inquiry from the authorities as to what the Department of Immigration was going to do with the Doukhobors was something in the nature of a general direction for them Mr. OLIVER
to go to work. The hint was taken, they went to work, they found employment and matters went on peaceably and quietly with them during the winter. But, it appears that as time went on, they saw fit to indulge in peculiarities which were in transgression of the law of Ontario. But, the authorities of Ontario did not take any notice of these acts. Whether they liked that kind of thing, or what their reasons were, I am not aware, but, at any rate, it was not until some time this spring that the authorities of the province of Ontario, charged with the maintenance of law and order in that province, took official cognizance of the actions of the Doukhobors, and when they did take notice of these actions and a proper penalty was placed upon them they at once appealed to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice for the release of these people who had transgressed their own law, who had offended against public decency in their own city and they asked that they be pardoned for the reason, as I am given to understand, that they simply wanted to be relieved from the burden of the cost of carrying out their own law-a law for the maintenance of public decency in the province of Ontario. Their request was acceded to and now these people are back in Saskatchewan. How they arrived there I have no knowledge. I want it to be distinctly understood that, in so far as the Immigration Department is concerned, it had no connection with the transport back to the province of Saskatchewan of these people, no interest in it and no knowledge of it.
If they went back as free agents and of their own accord I quite agree with the Minister of Justice that they had a perfect right to go back if they wanted to, and if they went back because of misrepresentation or by reason of undue force, then I presume that a criminal charge may be laid against those who kidnapped them. However, they are in the province of Saskatchewan now, the province in which they have resided-with the exception of their short excursion to Fort William-for the past eight or nine years. Whatever may be said as to the proper share of responsibility on the part of the province of Ontario for the conduct of these people I am at a loss to see what can be said by the people of the province of Saskatchewan. These people have been residents of that province, they have been subject to the responsibilities of residence in that province during all this period, and I submit it is the business of the province of Saskatchewan, when these people are in that province, to see that the laws of the province are maintained just as it was the business of the province of Ontario to see that the laws of that province were maintained when they resided there. The Dominion government has no responsibility with regard to these people in any way.

shape, or manner. The responsibility falls upon the provincial authorities and I assume the provincial authorities will discharge their duty and will deal with these people as is proper under the laws of the province. I might say that before provincial organization was given to Alberta and Saskatchewan and when the enforcement of the law rested upon the Dominion government, if any of these people then transgressed the law, the law was enforced upon them by the Dominion authorities. But now that the provinces have been organized and the responsibility for the enforcement of the law transferred to them I assume that the province concerned will discharge its duty and that the Dominion government will not be called upon, as it certainly ought not to be called upon, to exercise authority which it does not possess, and which if it did exercise in any province of the Dominion except in regard to these particular people, would be held to be a gross infraction of provincial rights and would be resented. I understand that these people are in a condition of mind which does not render them amenable to ordinary considerations, and such being the case it is not possible for this government which has no authority over them to deal with them effectively, hinder the present circumstances I do not think it would be sound public policy for this government to undertake to deal with these people on any principle that this government has the authority to exercise. As I understand, their condition of mind is such that they are only subject to coercive measures and it is only the provincial authorities who have the power to apply these measures. Therefore it is a matter entirely within the control of the province, it is entirely within the responsibility of the province and in my humble estimation sound public policy requires that the province should deal with the matter as it should be dealt with under the ordinary laws and administration of the province.

I thought as I listened to the speech of the Minister of the Interior what a wonderful revolution has taken place in his ideas with regard to those particular people. The time is not far distant when he himself referred in most uncomplimentary terms in this House to the Doukhobors, and not only did he do so from his place in the House but well do I remember reading the caustic articles of the Edmonton ' Bulletin,' of which he was proprietor, in which he scored this government for having in the first place brought those people to Canada, for having in the second place granted them special privileges, and for not having after their first pilgrimage dealt more strenuously with them. The Minister of Justice may have legal justification for what he has done, but still I do not believe that the sensible 2424
people of this country will justify his action in liberating those people and dumping them back on the province in which they are apparently unwelcome. He has stated that he has only complied with their own request that they should be returned to their friends in the province of Saskatchewan, but it appears since their return to the town of Yorkton, that they have no friends, that their fellow countrymen refuse to welcome them, and as a result we have had that telegram which was read last evening by the leader of the opposition. It is distinctly stated there that those people were induced to return by misrepresentation, it having been stated to them that they were being conducted to a warmer climate. The people of Yorkton justly protest against their being dumped on their town. I have no doubt that the representative of that constituency will, before this debate closes, rise in his place to uphold the citizens of his town as no doubt he received a telegram in common with others, requesting that immediate action should be urged upon the government to prevent the disreputable scenes that have already been witnessed in Yorkton. The Minister of the Interior has stated that those people are most law-abiding; that during their recent pilgrimage they were fed by the people of Winnipeg and of the various towns and villages along the route, and that they were well cared for in the town of Fort William. Well, the people of the west are noted for their hospitality and they certainly would not see those people die of starvation, and so their charitable organizations supplied them with food and clothing which unfortunately was soon discarded. The Minister of the Interior has also told us that those people ' indulged in their own peculiarities.' Well, if my information is correct, very strange peculiarities they are. A short time ago I met two prominent citizens of Fort William on the train and they informed me of some -of the peculiarities of those people which are certainly calculated to shock the moral sense of the community. So strange are those peculiarities which the Minister of the Interior has spoken of, that the municipal authorities of Fort William had to board up the windows of the house in which those people lived so that the boys of the town might not havp an opportunity of witnessing such peculiarities. And yet, those gentlemen from Fort William stated that the Minister of the Interior (to use their own expressive words) had the hardihood to rise in his place in parliament and to eulogize those people as being the most moral people in the world. If the hon. gentleman had witnessed some of their actions, as represented by some of the reputable citizens of Fort William, I am sure that he would not rise in his place to defend them and refer to them as moral people; because they conducted themselves

hi a manner to bring the blush of shame to people appearing on the streets of Fort William. I do not blame the people of Ontario for desiring to have those people removed beyond their borders. It is true, they came from the Northwest; but they were brought to this country by this government, and received special consideration, the government paying $5 a head for every man, woman and child. Had they been English, Irish or Scotch, they would have received only $1.75 a head, but being the peculiar pets of the government, they were given this special consideration. When they arrived at Halifax, they were met by immigration agents who were tumbling over each other to extend to them the glad hand of welcome, and to read addresses to them, eulogizing them as persecuted persons fleeing from the tyrannical wrath of Russia to seek homes in this new land of the west. They were conducted by those immigration agents on special trains to the west; and when they arrived in Winnipeg they were treated with special consideration by the municipal authorities and the charitable organizations there. They were given soup of a special variety, not made from animal food, lest it might not agree with their fastidious taste. Addresses were again presented to them and finally they were located on their lands in the west with the idea that they would settle down and become law-abiding citizens of this Dominion. From that time to this they have given constant trouble to the people of the localities in which they have been situated and to the people of the country wherever they appeared. Their first pilgrimage was to the town from which I come. They came there, not in dozens, but in hundreds. They were herded in the skating rink, and the people of the town had to provide for them until the immigration authorities appeared on the scene. When the immigration agent came, it was necessary to get a special train and put them on board by force and take them back to the town of Yorkton under guard of the mounted police, and return them to the lands on which they had been located. This would not satisfy them, and shortly afterwards another outbreak occurred. and from that time there have been repeated outbreaks of these fanatical people. Last fall they started out at great danger of losing their lives; men. women and delicate young children in inclement weather walking in a semi-nude condition, begging on the way to keep themselves alive, to the city of Winnipeg, where they stayed for a few weeks, and then on to Fort William, where they have been a burden to tlie town during the past winter. I remember the time when the Minister of the Interior spoke harshly of the Galicians and even more harshly of the Doukhobors, and I have here a clipping from the Edmonton ' Bulletin,' which gives in rather dramatic language the views held by the hon.

gentleman in those days. This article, which appeared after the first pilgrimage,
says;
The Doukliobor pilgrimage has ended without the tragedy that was confidently expected, and that would have occurred had it not been for the ' persecution ' to which they were subjected by the authorities in being forcibly sent to their homes. What the next move will be remains to be seen. They may stay quietly at home and attend to business, or their ' religious ' enthusiasm may take some other fantastic and possibly less harmless form. At any rate, the secret is out. They are not by anv means the people.they were represented to be. They cannot travel any longer on their reputation of being Russian Quakers, or of haying been persecuted by an intolerant church and government for conscience' sake. They have shown themselves to be nuisances personally, socially and politically. Such people as this, this country has no room or use for. The difference between those who went on the insane pilgrimage and those who did not is only a difference of degree, not of kind. The pilgramage was the logical sequence of their beliefs, A'l believed. but the difference was that those who remained at home resembled many other people to the extent that they did not live up to their beliefs. How soon they will arrive at a sufficient exaltation of spirit depends merely on the effectiveness of the preaching of the next crank who strikes their settlements; and whose missionary efforts will be helped rather than hindered by their having come oil their recent pilgrimage practically none the worse.
The question now is, shall such people be pandered to by the authorities in the future as they have been in the past? They have been dealt with and allowed to consider themselves, as a separate people. They have been aided financially as no other people have been or should be. Their disregard of law hag been winked at.
Yet the Minister of the Interior states today that there could not be 8,000 more law-abiding people in the Dominion of Canada than these Doukhobors.
All no doubt with the best intentions. But only with the result that Canada has been put to serious cost and trouble and has been made a laughing stock by their antics.
This pilgrimage is the limit. It puts them outside of reason or excuse.
If that was the case at the time of their first pilgrimage, when they retained their clothing, what must have been the case at the time of their last pilgrimage when they walked through the streets of Fort William absolutely nude.
The authorities will not hereafter be justified in dealing with them otherwise than as ordinary citizens. The law of Canada exempts from military service all whose religious beliefs prevent their taking part in the defence of their oountry. The Doukhobors can claim that exemption with the Mennonites, Quakers, Dunkards and others. But beyond that not a step-not a line. Their peculiar ideas regarding marriage have so

far been ' respected/ This is a reproach to our laws and a danger to our social system. For if a Doukhobor may defy the marriage laws, why may not any other persons? Their political beliefs are a combination of theocracy, socialism and anarchy. The fact that they wash themselves is a strong point in their favour. But the other fact that they do not believe in work beyond providing for present need and are liable at any time to turn into a horde of tramps and beggars, completelv knocks out the argument of their industrial value, which at earlier stages of the game was supposed to make up for every disadvantage.
There is a general objection to the importation of people whose presence, aspirations and votes tend against the proper social, political and industrial development of the country. The bringing of these Doukhobors was a mistake, but to allow them to remain on any other terms than as ordinary citizens would be a crime. They have made several attempts to find other locations. The sooner they find them the better for Canada, as removing a problem that, if it remains a problem-
These were the expressions of the hon. gentleman a few years ago. To be sure, he was not a minister of the Crown at that time, and was not called upon to defend the actions of the government in having brought those people of Canada; but to-day he feels obliged to defend not only the action of his predecessor in bringing them here, but the action of the Minister of Justice in giving them liberation and dumping them on the province of Saskatchewan. But it was not the hon. gentleman alone who condemned those people in past times. The Bible of the Liberal party, the Toronto ' Globe,' also advocated the removal of those people from our midst. I shall read a very short excerpt from it:
The Czar of all the Russias has never had much experience in welcoming subjects returning from foreign countries, and Canada should give him an opportunity to appear graciously and gracefully before the world in a new role. A Doukhobor Old Boys' Society returning to visit the scenes of youthful experiences, to renew friendships and revive happy memories, would be a felicitous occasion. on which the Czar could play the gracious host, and the returning pilgrims could bear the honours of distant successes with becoming modesty. They could sit by their old hearths and tell of the ways of immigration agents in distant Canada, of the kindly curiosity of the natives and the easy indifference of official authority.
We must admit that they have had sufficient to stimulate their curiosity. Anybody who has seen them on a pilgrimage will acknowledge that:
And the very easy indifference of the official authorities.
That is rather strong language for the Toronto ' Globe.' It goes on :
The homeward pilgrimage of a Doukhobor Old Boys' Society would lie a delightful reunion from all points of view, and should be encouraged. The Doukhobors could make modest disclaimers when old friends gave congratulations on the distinctions won abroad. They could protest that, although their names were on every tongue, and their portraits adorned the illustrated press, they had not set their hearts on the applause of the 'multitude. And when pressed to remain and once more make their homes amid the scenes of happier years, they could temporize, hesitate and at last reluctantly yield, returning again to the ways and associations of their former life.
This would be gratifying, says the ' Globe,' from the Canadian standpoint:
Taking, up the white man's burden is all very well in its way, but carrying it home is a far different matter. It is a practical move to send the assistant secretary of a charity organization to investigate a case of distress, but a far different matter to bring that case of distress home, and establish it in comfortable quarters. If the Czar did not mind, we could send out a force sufficient to impose the blessings of civilization as they have it in England on all the Doukhobors in his dominions. That would be a practical and systematic way to take up the white man's burden. But bringing the Doukhobors here to civilize them on the spot is positively inconvenient. The white man's burden is of the many things to which distance lends enchantment. If the Doukhobors will only return to their own home we will never lose our kindly interest in them. We will send them all the moral and religious admonitions that the censor will pass. We will subscribe to prizes for their annual pedestrian contests, buy tickets for their Christmas tea-meetings, entertain their walking delegates, send tourists among them, and reach out to them (across the ocean) the glad hand of friendship. We will give them the civilizing influence of our example at a distance. The personal freedom of this country does not appear to suit our friends of the lofty ideal. A Czar who would arrange their domestic and personal habits, determine their interpretation the Scriptures, set forth where they should live, and what they should work at, when they should travel and when they should stay at home, would fill a much felt want.
This is from the great government daily, the Toronto ' Globe,' about those people, those people of whom the Halifax 'Chronicle' has spoken in a similar strain. I do not know that it is necessary for me to take up any more time except to condemn, as a westerner though not a resident of the province of Saskatchewan, the action of this government. Evidently it is resented by the good people of Yorkton and by the people of Saskatchewan as a whole ; and I very much doubt if this continual game of battledore and shuttlecock unloading responsibility from one government to another and carrying on conferences ail the time this great exhibition is going on-while those people are kept in a car on a siding at Yorktown, guarded by mounted policemen to prevent their making exhibitions of themselves-is one which the people will

stand much longer. Our people will show their resentment against the importation of that class of immigrants and the special treatment accorded to them. Those Douk-hohors have refused time and again to obey our laws. Time and again they have protested to the government against having been brought here under misrepresentations, and because they have not been allowed to follow out their own views with regard to marriage laws, registrations, homestead entries and so forth. And while some of them have changed their ideas and become reputable citizens, there is a large element among them who cling to their peculiar views, only a portion of whom have been on the recent pilgrimage. Those people are liable to an outbreak of this kind every once in a while and to become a charge on the country. It was a huge mistake to bring them out in the first place and in the second place to give them special treatment.

I would suggest that the province to which these people belong and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) should join in making assignment of them to the ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sif-ton) in order that he might settle them on one of his numerous estates in the west and send for W. T. R. Preston to take care of them.

If there is no further discussion on this matter, I have one to which I wish to draw the attention of the House. I purpose dealing with it now in order that, when we get into Supply, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) may take cognizance of it. As the matter refers to two departments, and I know that you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, (Mr. Marcil) would rule me out on an objection sure to be raised by the Minister of Public Works, I think It better to discuss it while you are in the chair, in order that when we are in Committee of Supply, the minister may perhaps give some explanation. My hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid) asked the minister to give an account of what he had done with a number of the fire extinguishers which had been purchased. The minister replied that he would get the information and bring it down, and I presume he will have it when we get into Supply. On the 22nd January last I moved for a return showing how many fire extinguishers had been purchased by the government for the different departments since the 1st June, 1906, to the 1st January, 1908, from whom purchased, the prices paid, and the total amount paid. The Minister of Public Works brought down a return, and after seeing that return and finding a number of other fire extinguishers, not included in that return, charged here and there throughout the Auditor General's Report, I raised the point that Mr. W. J. ROCHE
the order for these had not been complied with. Then a further return was brought down from the Department of Marine and Fisheries. That return showed that since the 13th June, 1900, to January, 1908, 53 fire extinguishers had been purchased from Mr. P. E. Perreault, at $14 each, making a total of $742. This extravagant department which pays such extravagant prices paid in this instance less than the Department of Public WTorks. Mr. Perreault evidently worked on a similar commission, and Mr. Gregory got his goods cheaper than did the Department of Public Works. Here is the return of the Department of Public Works which the minister brought down. The total number of fire extinguishers purchased was 195. From Patton and Company 95 were purchased, and from Charles Patton of Montreal 100, at $15 each in both cases. The Minister of Public Works therefore paid $1 more for the extinguishers he got than did Mr. Gregory for those he bought at Quebec for the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and I shall show the reason why. Last evening we listened to the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) eulogizing himself for the course he has pursued since he became minister of that department. Let me draw attention to a letter which he wrote, following the lines on which his predecessor had worked. It will be found in the report of the commissioners on page 79. It was written by the minister to Mr. Gregory, at Quebec, and was dated July 27, 1900 :
I have to inform you that if you consider that chemical fire extinguishers are necessary on hoard the vessels of the Quebec agency you are to purchase them from P. E. Perreault 312 St. John street, Quebec. Mr. Perreault has been advised to call upon you in connection with this matter.
If Mr. Gregory could get a letter that indicated more clearly to him that he should purchase a number of these fire extinguishers than that letter written by the minister on the 27th July, 1906, I do not know what better authority he could have. This is the letter from the minister saying that a friend of his will call on him, and if he wants any fire extinguishers to purchase them from him. And now what do we find ?
October 8, 1906.-Gregory writes about fire extinguishers bought from Perreault, who is now an employee of the agency

Because the minister employed Perreault and put him in the agency.
Where does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) find that I ever signed such a letter ?
If the minister will bring down the files, I will point out the letter. He found the letter on the file and quotes it.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) says he has seen the file and knows there is a letter written by me ? Does he assert that I have signed it?
The commissioners have gone through the files and have given the House their report stating what they found. They found this statement on the files.
There is no statement that I signed this letter.
If the minister will produce the letter, no doubt his signature will be found at the bottom of it.
Does the hon. gentleman assert that I signed that letter?
I am making no assertions. The hon. minister appointed a Royal Commission, and I am quoting what the Royal Commission said.
No, that does not say that I signed the letter. Does the hon. gentleman say that I signed it?

The hon. minister will make his own speech. He made one last night-and of all the speeches I ever listened to since I came into this House over twenty years ago, that speech, as coming from a gentleman who ought to be a statesman, was the most extraordinary I ever heard.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) has stated that I signed that letter.
I did not make the statement.
I deny that I signed it.

I want to make my speech. The minister is not going to put me down. I am reading from the report of the Royal Commission. And I will give him the page-page 79. And any gentleman who reads that will say that it comes from the department to the agents at Quebec, and from the head of the department.
The hon. gentlemaD said I bad signed the letter.
I did not. The hon. gentleman cannot find that in ' Hansard.'
Then, that is all right.
I say this is from the head of the department, from the minister, for further down there is one from the deputy, and they quote his name.
There is no directing head of the department.

No. But here is an intimation to Gregory, as plain as can be, to buy some of these worthless fire extinguishers from Perreault. The report goes on :
October 8, 1906.-Gregory writes about fire extinguishers bought from Perreault who is now an employee of the agency and has a lot of fire extinguishers on hand which he would like to sell to the department. Under the circumstances, as he is a poor man with a family, and now unable to go out and solicit their sale. This was well understood by the late lamented minister, who was his friend, and fully recognized the worthiness of the said chemical fire extinguishers. I would recommend that the department take them off his hands, as we have several stations requiring such protection.
October 12, 1906.-Letter from deputy

The first was from the minister, but this is from the deputy.
Does the hon. gentleman assert that I signed it ?

I am making my speech aul the assertions in it will be pretty clearly understood. When I am through, If the minister wishes, he can make his speech.
October 12, 1906.-Letter from deputy-With reference to fire extinguishers purchased by you from P. E. Perreault, I find no authority on file in the department for the purchase of these fire extinguishers, and I notice that within the last couple of years large purchases have been made from this gentleman. In this connection, I may say that in 1904-5 the late minister purchased from Mr. Charles Patton fire extinguishers to the sum of $9,000. Of this number, 142 were sent to Quebec for the use of your agency lighthouses and Dominion steamers. Besides that, a number were stored in Montreal and are there still.
That is. they were still in store in 1906, though they were purchased in 1904. That gives you an Idea how the department is run :
If you had notified the department that fire extinguishers were absolutely necessary to put on hoard the Dominion steamers and to be used at lighthouses, the required number could have been sent from Montreal. Instead of this, it appears you made purchases from Mr. Perreault without any instructions or authority from the department. The minister would like to have an explanation in regard to this matter. He would also like to have a statement of how the fire extinguishers purchased in 1904-5 were distributed.
October 8, 1906.-Gregory writes to department^ in answer to their letter of October 4 and 5 returning P. E. Perreault's accounts for chemical fire extinguishers, and asking me to inform you upon what authority the purchases were made. He refers to a 'letter of July 27, 1906.
