That is the letter I have already referred to that came to him and was his authority; he took that letter of July 27 as a hint to purchase these fire extinguishers, and he did purchase them, and here the deputy Is holding him for his action. He goes on. in his letter of October 15, 1906 :
I shall have a statement prepared by the inspector of lights as soon as possible,

showing how the fire extinguishers purchased in 1904-5 were distributed, and forward the same to the department.
The statement is that 142 fire extinguishers were sent to Quebec for the use of the agency lighthouses and Dominion steamers, but Gregory contradicts that by his telegram which shows there were only fifty instead of 142.
I stated a little while ago that I would explain how it came that the Minister of Public Works paid $15 for these fire extinguishers, while the Department of Marine and fisheries paid only $14 at Quebec. Mr. Patton is a manufacturer at Montreal. He could not make so many sales up here at Ottawa as he wanted to. Mr. Grant, a lawyer in this city, suggested to Mr. Pattou that they would form a partnership, and he would get an agent who had some influence with the government and would make some sales for him. So, there was a company formed at Ottawa. It was called Patton and Grant, because as I say. Mr. Grant is a lawyer here and he did not want to have his name appear as a selling agent for fire extinguishers. But they borrowed a name from a fellow by the name of Crowe. And the firm was called Patton and Crowe. But Grant did the business. He assumed the name of Crowe for himself. They sold to the government through the agency of Mr. Auguste Lemieux, who also is a lawyer in the city of Ottawa. He wanted a commission of $3 instead of $2, they had to raise the price to the government, and so the government paid $15 here -while they paid $14 in Quebec. You will see how this was brought about. One hundred fire extinguishers were purchased from Patton in Montreal and 99 from Patton and Crowe in Ottawa. Patton and Crowe, of course, were Patton and Grant. Patton and Crowe put in an account to the Public Works Department and got the cheques which were made to Patton and Crowe. Grant handled the cheques. He himself personally paid Mr. Lemieux his commission to the amount of between $600 and $700 on the quantity he sold to the department here. Grant gave his own cheque to Lemieux, and marked on the cheque ' for commission.' These cheques were endorsed by Lemieux, put into the bank, and the money drawn, and the cheques were returned to Grant, and up to a certain time were in his office. But afterwards they were missing-they were stolen from his office for a purpose. A vacancy had loomed up in the representation for Ottawa
How does that appear ?
That is my information, and if there is anything incorrect about it

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) will pardon me. I am asking the question because I am not informed
Mr. TAYLOlt.
what took place here a year or more ago. Is there any evidence of what my hon. friend is stating now before the Public Accounts Committee?
No, it is not before the Public Accounts Committee.
Is it before any committee?

We will be in public accounts in a little while from now and you can ask any of these questions you like.
ill-. PUGSLEY'. The hon. gentleman may say if it has been proved.

I am giving the information I have. My information is that the proof is on hand. These cheques were taken from Mr. Grant's office and deposited in the safe of Mr. Lindsay. A vacancy was being created here in Ottawa by the transference of Mr. Belcourt to the Senate, and Mr. Lemieux, who sold these fire extinguishers, was an aspirant and thought that as his brother was the Postmaster General lie had the pull, and should he the coming member to fill Mr. Beleourt's seat. Mr. Belcourt had his eye on another gentleman and had made a promise that when he vacated the seat that other gentleman would be the candidate. Mr. Lemieux had to be got out of the way. These cheques made by Grant payable to Lemieux, having been taken out of Grant's office, were missing. Air. Belcourt was then down at Saranac Lake in the Adirondacks for his health. These cheques were sent down to Mr. Belcourt who would not trust the cheques across the ocean to the Prime Minister, but had them photographed and sent the photographs to the Prime Minister with an explanation. The Prime Minister wrote back: When I come home
Why did he send them.

To show that Lemieux had to be got out of the way. When the Prime Minister came back he said: There are the cheques already filled out for a commission to you, a lawyer selling goods to the government; you have to back out- and Lemieux quietly backed out and took no further part in the contest.
Would that not qualify him as a member?

I do not know but there were two of them who wanted it, and Mr. Belcourt and the Prime Minister wanted one man, hut Lemieux and the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) wanted another man. Cheques come in useful sometimes. I have heard a statement, I have never had it verified, but from the facts it appears there was some truth in it. We remember when the late Minister of Railways left his seat on account of the Transcontinental Railway proposition which was being introduced by

the government, it was supposed that he was going to take the stump against the Prime Minister, and the information is that the Prime Minister called on the late Mr. Blair, and asked him his intentons, and that Mr. Blair said: I am going to go to the country in opposition to this scheme of building au opposition line to tile Intercolonial and putting this country into $20,000,000 of debt. And the information is that the Prime Minister put his hand in his pocket and pulled out some cheques that a big contractor had made payable direct to Mr. Blair and with his name signed on the back of them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In justice to tlie memory of Mr. Blair I must say that there is not a word of truth in that.
I am glad to hear it, I thought it was my duty to tell the hon. gentleman. But the facts were there, Mr. Blair did not take the stump, the cheque shut him tip.
Mr. Blair is dead, he cannot reply of course.

But the evidence is here in these two returns. Perreault sold the government these same fire extinguishers down at Quebec at $14, and Lemieux sells them to the Minister of Public Works at $15. There is a dollar of extra rake-off anyway, and Mr. Grant paid his cheque to Mr. Lemieux for the commission on them, gave his own personal cheque and a gentleman who informed me saw the cheques, made payable to the order of Lemieux, and marked on the face of them ' commission.' That is the information I have in reference to it. If my hon. friend wants any information, this gentleman came voluntarily into my office and said he saw the cheques and gave me the information.
It is a great mistake to believe all j'ou hear.

I am stating this, and if the hon. gentleman appoints a committee he will find that I am correct, and that he and his people paid a dollar more than was paid at Quebec. Look at the thousands of dollars, $9,000 in one lot, and $2,000 or $3,000 by the minister himself, expended for what is practically no better than a bottle of vinegar for fire purposes.
Vinegar will not do any good.

Just as good as this, mixed with a little soda and water. Any way they were giving $15 for these, and the Department of Marine alongside was giving $14. If they had bought from the manufacturer they could have saved the $600 or $700 paid to Grant. I want the minister, before we go on with his supply, to bring down information as to where these were distributed, to bring down the reports
of the different engineers as to their value and all correspondence in reference to them. I want to know why $15,000 to $20,000 of the people's money have been paid in the last five years for fire extinguishers. I think it necessary that this information should be given before we go into the minister's estimates, in order that he might be prepared to answer the questions. The officials of the Marine Department will also give some information of what was done with this large quantity down at Quebec. I want to know particularly why the Department of Public Works paid $15 for the same article that the Department of Marine bought at $14, as shown by the two returns which have been brought down. There may be other departments that have not yet reported. I do not know how many have been purchased by the Department of Agriculture and some other departments. We have only two returns down, and when I moved for this return, the Minister of Public Works brought down the information simply for his own department, although my motion asked for all departments. I have since got the return for the Marine and Fisheries Department. Were there any others to which Lemieux has sold these fire extinguishers? I do not know, but we know he has sold, and has got his commission from Mr. Grant for 105 of these machines.

I cannot promise to have these returns to-day, but as soon as possible I will have all the information desired so that the matter may be considered when we are in Supply. I would like to say that so far as I am aware there have been very few of these extinguishers purchased since I became minister. Probably there have been some. I am nOt able to say why the price is $15. That appears to have been the price paid before I became minister. With regard to the usefulness of the article, I understood from the chief architect that they were considered valuable for the purpose of extinguishing fires.
Their name would indicate that.
Things are not always just what they would appear to be from their names, but I am told they are a pretty good article for that purpose.
Would the minister bring down the report of his engineer or officer upon which they were bought?
Yes, if there is such a report.
I suppose there would not be any bought unless there was a scientific report.
That was all before I went into the department.
They would not be bought without a report since you became minister?
I am inclined to believe not.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer for a few moments to a matter which I have brought up two or three times before. It is the matter of the timber reserve on Turtle mountain. I believe that the idea of preserving these timber reserves is a very laudable one but I think there should be some exception made when the conditions warrant it. I think there should be some examination made as to whether these are actual timber reserves or not, and further, I would like to inquire of the Minister of the Interior if he has had any information of late in connection with the special reserve to which I have referred. In speaking the other day I tried to show the Minister of the Interior that it woul l be absolutely impossible ever to make this particular reserve of any importance. The minister, in answering what I said, seemed to be labouring under the impression that I thought there was no large timber there and he said that the idea was not to produce merchantable timber but rather to produce what might be called climatic conditions. That is all good in its way, if the idea can be successfully carried out. But it will be absolutely impossible to make anything out of part of the timber reserve on Turtle mountain in so far as climatic conditions are concerned. I have made a personal examination of this reserve and I think that all the timber that is there-and when I speak of timber I really mean brush-could be put into two or three sections and it is a matter that affects about 70,000 acres of land. There has been a very small growth, some of the trees being but three or four years old. But, the point I want to make is that even what timber there is on this so-called timber reserve is being absolutely neglected. We have had a gentleman there whom the Minister of the Interior knows very well and whom I know very well, and, while I do not wish to say anything offensive, yet I think that a duty devolves, upon me at the present time in connection with this particular reserve. There seems to prevail here a condition that apparently exists all over that western country and that is that the men whom the government appoint as overseers, or timber guardians, or whatever name they may be designated by, are. if not political hacks, to say the least, political organizers and we find that the gentleman who is supposed to be looking after this Turtle mountain reserve absolutely spends his time endeavouring to get promises of votes for the Liberal party. He Mr. PUGSLEY.
is a man who has made an absolute failure of life in every other condition and as a last resort, he has applied for this government position and the people in that country have to suffer because they have to satisfy the political aspirations of one man. During this spring a fire has gone over the entire district and, according to a letter which I received last night and to an item which I have taken from a paper issued in the town of Boissevain, some eight or ten miles from that reserve, a great deal of destruction has taken place. I call the attention of the Minister of the Interior to the fact because he may not be cognizant of it. From the information which I have I believe that this district will never be made a successful timber reserve. There were a number of settlers in one township of this reserve and they were offered certain conditions if they would leave that place and go to a place which had been designated by the government. I understood the Minister of the Interior to say that no definite promise had been made to these men, but it does seem, from my conversation with a number of them when I was there only a few days ago, and from the letters which I have received and which are in my possession, not from my own supporters, but from men who vote against me that there is a great amount of dissatisfaction with the condition of affairs on that reserve. I think the dissatisfaction is universal amongst the settlers of that district, whether they be Liberals or Conservatives and I believe that, the Minister iof the ' Interior not being conversant with this matter, it was my duty to call his attention to it. As I have said, it affects some 70,000 acres of land. If this will never make a timber reserve under any conditions is it not practical business, is it not necessary in the interests of the department and of the district concerned, that the matter should be looked into ? I do not ask you to take my word. I would like you to make an investigation. I, claim that these settlers, even though they were going to have some parts of this as a timber reserve, were doing a great deal of good there. They were looking after their own sections and they were on the edge of the timber reserve and. being in that position, they were able to prevent fires. But, most of them have been sent away, some of them are there still, not very many, and the consequence has been that the timber has all been burned over. There is another grievance. During last spring the gentleman to whom I have referred and who is the timber agent there had a large number of men planting seed on this soil in order to produce trees. The Minister of the Iuterior knows just as well as I do that this is money wasted and thrown away. You cannot find a settler anywhere in that district but would tell the Minister of the Interior and this gov-

eminent that it is absolutely useless to plant seeds under these conditions. I will not call it graft, but it is simply a waste of money and I am positive that the Minister of the Interior is not familiar with the facts or he certainly would prevent that condition of affairs from existing any longer. The paper to which I have referred contains the following paragraph :
Several men are employed in the timber reserve planting tree seeds on the land that has been burnt off. It is very questionable if the seeds will grow, or, providing they do, whether they will not be destroyed by fire as the hush has been hitherto. It would he a great deal better if the Dominion government would open up this land for settlement instead of using it as an experimental ground.
I am in entire sympathy with that statement. I am also in entire sympathy with the reservation of timber areas when It is practicable, hut in this case where it is absolutely impracticable I say that the area should be thrown open to settlers, that those who are there should he allowed to return to their homes and that those who are there should be allowed to remain. I also received a letter last night from a gentleman who is familiar with the conditions in that district. Amongst other things he says:
Another thing which is something of vital importance, what is the use of keeping a man here looking after our timber reserve as you call it ? Why, the fire has went over the whole thing in the last few days and killed every green tree in the hush. All the young stuff ds killed.
Then, further down, he says :
Now, I hear	is out sowing
tree seeds and planting trees. What is the use of wasting the people's money in this way? The fire will kill everything again. If this land is given out to settlement it will be taken care of. Bach settler will take care of his own. As it is nobody is looking after it. Hoping what I have written may set the ball rolling, I remain,
Yours truly,
I have only one object in calling the attention of the minister to this timber reserve and that is to express the hope that he will give it a little more attention than he seems to have given to it up to the present time.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rather sorry and somewhat surprised to hear the expression of my hon. friend (Mr. Schaffner) with regard to this particular reserve. Of course it is well that we arrive at a final knowledge or a final understanding of a certain condition. I hope my hon. friend does not wish to blame me for a misunderstanding in regard to this particular reserve because I would remind him that this reserve has been
a reserve for many years. It was a reserve when my hon. friend was elected to represent the constituency in which it is situated. It was at first reserved by departmental order, then the Forest Reserve Act was introduced into this House and the provisions of that Act were approved of unanimously by the House. There was certain discussion as to the benefits that might accrue by that Act to the people who held timber limits within the reserves, hut there was unanimity of opinion in regard to the general principle of making certain reserves and of preserving them by legislative enactment in the terms of the Bill then before the House. My hon. friend would have been protecting the interests which he now assumes to protect had he then given the House the information he has given it today. That would have been the proper time to tell us that this timber reserve was not necessary, that it was not a proper place in which to make a timber reserve, that the settlers who were then on it should have remained on it, but my hon. friend did not give that information and so he will have to assume at any rate joint responsibility with me for the legislation by which the responsibility was laid upon the Department of the Interior to see that those who were in residence upon the reserve were removed from it.
I scarcely understand how the Minister of the Interior can hold me in the least responsible. He himself admits that this was a timber reserve before I came into the House.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was previously a timber reserve by order in council, and when the legislation was before the House to make it a_timber reserve by Act of parliament that would have been the time for my hon. friend to put in his protest.
If the hon. gentleman will refer to that occasion which is two years ago he will find that I certainly did put in my protest.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: At the time the Act was passed ?
Yes, and I referred to these settlers at the same time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is not. in my memory that the hon. gentleman did so, and if he did he is now in line with his attitude of that time. But apparently he was not able to impress the House with his views. Be that as it may, it was the will of parliament that there should be a reserve there and that the reserve should be cleared of settlers, and efforts have been made since to carry out the will of parliament. I have already expressed my regret for the necessity of action being taken which in itself cannot be other wise than a hardship. But it was not my action, it was parliament caused

it to be done. In accordance with the declaration of parliament we have secured the removal of several of these settlers, and if any promises have been made to them in order to secure their removal I can only say that my instructions are that every promise shall be fulfilled. If every promise has not been carried out it should be carried out, and I expect it will be. I appreciate quite as much as anybody else the difficulty of the situation of these people.
As to those settlers who are still on the reserve it is expected that they will remove possibly within the coming month and we are using all reasonable effort to facilitate their going and to make the conditions as little burdensome upon them as possible. Until parliament sees fit to rescind its action there is nothing left for the department but to endeavour to secure the removal of the settlers from the reserve.
I regret to hear that fire has swept the reserve. I suppose that having assumed the responsibility of taking care of the reserve we must assume some responsibility for fires that occur. But as we have only one man there to take care of the reserve which includes several townships, any of us who are familiar with conditions in the west will understand that there are times when an army would not be able to protect such an area from fire. It may have been our fault or it may have been the misfortune of circumstances.
In regard to the view of my hon. friend that it is wasting money and time and effort to plant tree seeds upon the ground recently traversed by fire, I can only say that my information is that in succeeding years after a burn has taken place a new growth comes up rapidly; and I assume there is no inherent reason why the same course of nature will not follow on the Turtle mountain reserve.
That growth comes up without any planting of seed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Precisely.
Could the minister tell where it comes from ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Unlike my hon. friend there are some things that I do not know.
I don't know either and that is why I asked.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We agree for once.
That is the strangest thing in the world.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a fact that a new growth does come up after a fire, and I assume that our planting of seed on the burnt ground will not be frowned on by Providence or by nature any more than if we did not plant seed there at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: But let me remind the Minister of the Interior that they were planting these seeds there long before the fire. They were spending time and money planting seeds on that soil which will never produce trees of any description.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, if it will not produce trees it is not very valuable land for any other purpose; and the idea in setting it apart as a reserve that it was not valuable for agricultural purposes, is confirmed by the statement the hon. gentleman has made. At any rate, I assume that we are not to any serious degree hindering the settlement of the country by keeping in reserve a tract which is not capable of even growing trees. However, I have better hopes of the case than my hon. friend.
I have some belief that the withdrawal of the land in the first place was fairly well advised ; and, being on the summit of an elevated and broken piece of country, the source of certain water supply for the surrounding country, both on the surface and under the surface, it seems to me that the Turtle mountain is the place of all others in the west where there is warrant for a forest reserve, and where every effort should be made to preserve and to perpetuate and increase the sources of the water supply for the benefit of the surrounding country. Our efforts may be mistaken ; we may be under a misapprehension ; there are many things yet to be found in the secrets of nature ; but we are using reasonable and legitimate efforts to seek what it is desirable to seek.
In regard to the political action of our officer there, I can only say that I regret very much to hear the statement made. I can assure my hon. friend that any such action is entirely contrary to my views or wishes, and the matter will be taken up on the representations which he has made, and will be dealt with.
It is quite possible that the reserve having been created a number of years ago, there has not been the fullest care taken in defining the boundary; that is to say, we have taken in more land than is perhaps suitable for the purpose. We have not had until quite recently a scientific organization, as it might be called, that would warrant us in revising these limits ; but we have been successful during the past year in securing the assistance of some gentlemen of eminence in forestry matters, and we hope, by investigations on the ground during the present year, to be able to readjust the boundaries, if such readjustment is necessary, so that we shall not be preventing settlement by holding land unnecessarily, and shall be doing the best we can to aid the surrounding settlements by securing the preservation of the existing forests and the reforestation of the deforested part of what is now the Turtle mountain forest reserve.

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Souris (Mi-. Schaffner) was not objecting to the principle of forest, reserves. I think that in common with all the other members of this House who have any knowledge of timber matters, he highly approves of the idea of creating forest reserves. The only fault 1 have to find with the action of the government with respect to this matter is that they have not set apart enough of the timber wealth of the country for the future-not only to preserve it for a time when it will be infinitely more valuable, because of its scarcity, than it is at the present time, but also on account of the water supply. There is one matter which has come up in connection with this subject that I think is deserving of some consideration on the part of the department, and that is the question of fire guarding. I understand that there are about 70,000 acres in this particular forest reserve, and yet the minister says there is .only one person to protect it from fire. It seems to me that it is very bad policy, after setting apart such a large tract of country as a forest reserve, to take such meagre precautions' to preserve it from fire. There are only certain times of the year when there is danger from fire, that is, early in the spring and late in the summer ; and it seems to me that the proper course would be at those times to have an efficient force to protect this property. It would cost something, it is true ; but you have a very valuable asset there, which it is worth expending some money for the purpose of protecting. It is valuable in more ways than one. It is valuable on account of the actual money's worth that is there ready to be turned into money, and also because, if fire sweeps over it. if you are going to continue it as a timber reserve, you will have to begin again at the seed, and it will take nearly a century for the timber to grow again. Therefore I strongly urge the minister. whose timber policy in this respect I have commended, to largely increase his force of fire protectors, putting them on, not the year round, but during the particular seasons when it is absolutely necessary to protect the forest from fire. If bo does this, lie will be deserving of the thanks of the House and the country.

I would ask the Minister of the Interior if he has made up his mind yet when to throw open to homestead entry the lands that have been taken out of the reserves that have recently been formed. For instance, in the Riding mountain timber reserve, as the hon. gentleman is aware, there were certain townships over which fire swept, destroying the timber : and an order in council was passed taking these out of the reserve and throwing them open to homestead entry. That
occurred over a year and a half ago. Many settlers visited the land office with the idea of making entry, in accordance with the newspaper advertisement, stating that on a certain date those lands would be thrown open to homestead entry, only to be disappointed. I have the same complaint to make as the hon. member for Souris, when he states that the timber inspector having charge of these reserves-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has exhausted his right to speak.

Then I ask the Minister of the Interior when it is intended to
have those lands thrown open to homestead entry ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. minister can only speak with the permission of the House, as he has exhausted his right to speak.
Mr. OLIVER I only wish to answer the hon. gentleman's question, if the House is willing. The lands which have been cut out of these reserves were announced as being open to entry by an error. They have been held under reservation for the purpose of accommodating squatters but we are moving them out of the reserve, and as soon as we are able to get the squatters out of the reserve and adjust it we will open the balance of these lands which were cut out of it. I regret that the officer who has been in charge of the work has been ill some months and the work has not gone forward as rapidly as I hoped. However we have succeeded in getting a large number of the squatters out of the Riding mountain reserve and we have every prospect of getting them all out by the end of this month.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
There is a matter which I think of sufficient Importance to bring to the attention of the House, and that is the providing of transportation facilities for that part of niy constituency which lies remote from railway accommodation. I know that it is no part of the duty of the government to provide transportation for new settlements, but I am satisfied that I shall convince the House that there are exceptional circumstances connected with the case I have to lay before you. Mr. Speaker, which justifies me in taking this unusual course. I refer to the construction of the Moosejaw-Lacombe branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway. A charter to build that branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway has held for some years. Two years ago they built fourteen miles from Moosejaw in a northerly and northwesterly direction, but they have not laid any steel since. Last summer

they graded fifty miles more. From time to time they have announced that they would proceed with the construction of the railway, and relying upon those promises, settlers went into a district remote from transportation facilities, but although they have been there two or three years they still find themselves without these facilities. These settlers have been hanging on by their teeth, so to speak, throughout these years, and I do not think X need offer any apology to the House for taking the stand that a company such as the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has held this charter for years and which is building railways in other parts where competition is keener, should be brought to book for their neglect in this matter. I have been across the Saskatchewan river where this railway is supposed to run, and in that section there are many settlers from fifty to one hundred and fifty miles away from any railway. It is very inconvenient for them to get fuel. For a time they were able to obtain fuel from the small timber around their residences or in the valleys, in the creeks and rivers, but that is almost entirely consumed and there are to-day perhaps seven or eight thousand people who have gone in there relying on the promise of the Canadian Paeiffic Railway to construct this line. You will find there tiie finest farmers you will see anywhere, who have taken up the best lands you can find in the west. These lands are second to none in Canada. I have visited them myself and I have reports about them from very reliable sources, and I think that in a few years ; ou will find my prediction verified that that land is going to be the most prosperous part of the Northwest Territory. I refer to that part lying near the elbow of the South Saskatchewan river, and north and west of that ooint. Last summer, in my capacity as representative of the district, I made an appointment with Mr. William White, and got from him the authority to announce that last year his company would construct a certain portion of the railway. I.est any one should take exception to my repeating the conversation, let pie say that it was strictly in an official way. I met the vice-president of the Canadian Pacific Railway by appointment. He agreed to receive a deputation composed of my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. McCraney) and Mr. W. P. Sutherland, M.P.P., and myself. Through some misunderstanding I did not get word to my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. McCraney) so that Mr. Sutherland and myself only saw Mr. Whyte. He authorized us to say last year they would lay fifty miles more of steel and grade at least seventy more miles, but from that day to this they have not laid one foot of steel or done any more grading. But they let last fall a contract for seventy miles and gave the people to understand the road would be built at once, and the people accepted Mr. KNOWLES.
that promise in good faith. Throughout these years these people have been practising the strictest economy, but in the most cavalier fashion without giving any explanation the Canadian Pacific Railway have sent out the announcement that they have seen fit to cancel the contract which they had made with Mr. J. D. McArthur to build these seventy miles. Although I cannot expect the government to build this road or do anything very severe with the Canadian Pacific Railway. T do think that this condition of affairs should be exposed and that the railway company should be censured for playing fast and loose with the settlers in that way. There are people out there who are being ruined financially-fine young homesteaders who cannot get their fuel, in or their wheat out and who are in the impossibility of carrying on with any success their farming operations. That is a very serious condition of affairs, to which I call the attention of the House, and especially the attention of the .Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham). I have in my hand a petition which is sixteen feat long by actual measurement. It is very closely signed and no doubt has about 1,000 names on it. I have another which, by actual count, contains over 300 names of people living in the vicinity of Tullisv.lle near the elbow of the South Saskatchewan. I tried to present these petitions to the House, but as they ask for the building of a railway and therefore call upon the expenditure of public money they could not be received, anything connected with the expenditure of public money having to come direct from the government. The petition is as follows :
We, the undersigned settlers in and around the district of Tullisville, hereby petition the Dominion government to use their intiu-ence on behalf of our neighbourhood in securing a line of railway. In order to market any grain, we are obliged to draw it from 60 to 80 miles to town. Some of us have even greater distances than this to go. We also have the Saskatchewan river to cross which makes it very inconvenient, and being without railroad facilities we find little or no encouragement whatever in raising large quantities of grain until such times as we can get a closer market. If in the near future there are no signs of a railroad, the half of the neighbourhood threatens to pull out on obtaining their patent. This would mean a great loss to this district.
These people went in on the direct assurance of the Canadian Pacific Railway that they would construct the line. A railway company should not be allowed to give a pledge of this kind to the people and then place the people at a most serious disadvantage because of their non-fulfilment of the pledge. I have a letter here dated Fertile Valley, Saskatchewan, April 15th :
Could vou let me have any definite information regarding the action of the Canadian

Pacific Railway in abandoning construction work on the Moosejaw extension? Also if you think it possible that the government or the Railway Commission could take up the matter and secure the completion of the line to the crossing on the South Saskatchewan river in township 29, range 8, west third meridian, this season. It is needless to point out that it is impossible to continue under present conditions. Hundreds, perhaps thousands, will follow those who have already abandoned the country.
KENNETH DUNBAR, Honorary Secretary Liberal Association.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles) if he has ever brought this grievance of the people in that part of the country before the Railway Committee of this House. These railways are always asking this House and its railway committee for additional legislation. I think that when they do that their attention ought to be called to any breach of contract of this kind. And I hold further that no road should get further legislation or further concessions from the government if there is a breach of contract on their part such as this appears to be. It may be that there are financial reasons why the company cannot construct the road at the present time. As to that, I am not informed ; although I do know that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has been able to procure large sums of money in the English money market within a short time. I have a strong opinion that these railways which constantly appear before this House and the railway committee for additional privileges should be told and told perhaps by the government, that no further concessions in the way of franchises will be given them until they make a reasonable effort to complete the roads that they have already incorporated, certainly to build the roads that they have given a pledge to build. If that is done, some kind of control will be held over these roads, and they will be compelled to keep bargains made with the people. The railways always talk of their vested rights And on those rights they insist. But the public also has vested rights ; and when the railways give a pledge they should seek in every way to carry it out. The only excuse I can imagine for not building this railway which will accommodate so many people, is, probably, the condition of the money market. But, so far, I have not heard that urged in this case. I think, if the hon. member (Mr. Knowles) and his friends from that part of the country go to the Minister of Railways and insist on his using his influence with the Canadian Pacific Railway and with the government as a whole, to have the government tell the Canadian Pacific and other railways that they shall not have further concessions until they complete the obligations they have undertaken, it will have a beneficial effect.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: With the permission of the House I may say that I have not brought this matter before the railway committee because it does not afford publicity enough. My wish was, I will not say to expose, but to reveal the position of this railway, and the railway committee does not meet my purpose.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: But the Canadian Pacific Railway Company appears before the committee-has appeared this session -asking for these additional advantages, and that would be a good time to ventilate the matter.

speechtext: Again with the permission of the House, I would say, with regard to Mr. Whyte's promise, that he explained that he could not get ties.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I desire to say a word in support of the position of my hon. friend from West As-siniboia (Mr. Knowles). I am familiar, to some degree, with the country through which he says this proposed railway would pass. The hon. gentleman and myself attended a picnic some forty or fifty miles west of the town of Hanley in the month of July last, and I must say that I never went through any portion of western Canada which appeared to be so fertile and so well suited to make the home of a prosperous people as that country is. There are many parts of the west in which our population is mostly foreign. (But I was particularly struck with the fact that in this section it was almost entirely an Ontario population, and I found amongst the people there a number of persons whom I had known in Ontario. I think that if any hon. gentleman from Ontario had been there he would have felt himself, perhaps, more at home than in any other part of the west. They were all full of hope, but they were full also of requests that we should do what we could to influence the the Canadian Pacific Railway in the building of the road. I was to have accompanied my hon. friend (Mr. Knowles) to Winnipeg to interview Mr. Whyte, as my hon. friend has stated. The announcement which he was able to make after that interview was one very well received in that portion of the country. We found, on the trip to which I have referred, that there were two great needs. One was that of getting out the grain. The nearest market from the point we visited was Hanley. It is necessary to cross the south Saskatchewan river, [DOT]and there is a journey of some fifty miles. The conditions make grain growing altogether unprofitable, but the people were in hopes that the railway might be put through in a very short time. There was also the other difficulty which my hon.

friend mentioned, one very apparent to us, and that is the necessity of making provision for fuel. I would point out to hon. members that, while we have heard nothing of the fuel question in the west during this session, we still stand in fear that, unless we get railway accommodation to some portions of the country which are almost wholly treeless, as is this part to which I have referred, we must look for a great deal of trouble in the future. The value which our land has is not derived from its grain growing qualities so much as from its proximity to transportation. What I have sometimes felt is that, in granting charters to railways, although there is no undertaking on the part of the railways to construct, we almost mislead people to go into a given portion of the country by the announcement that a railway may pass through. Unfortunately, our people seem to think that a charter is a railway. Of course, that is a great mistake. But when corporations like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, with the credit it has, makes an announcement and gives a contract, it seems to me that the influence of this House and of this government should be made use of to compel, or, at least, to influence the railway to go on and construct. I feel that these people have a great grievance against a corporation which has received every consideration at the hands of this House, and I hope the Minister of Railways will use his good offices in having this contract completed.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
In reply to the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Knowles) and the hoi), member for Saskatchewan (Mr. McCraney), Of course, it is regrettable that thickly settled portions of any part of the country should be so remote from the market and have no connection by way of railways or other rapid transit. It is a well recognized fact that the time consumed in marketing a product has much to do with the price and with the profit made in raising it. I can readily understand the disappointment that would result from a promise made by representatives of a great railway not being implemented. People, as my hon. friend (Mr. McCraney) has said, would rush into [DOT] that territory, believing they were shortly to have railway communication with one of the best centres of that country, the city of Moosejaw, only to find, after they had been there a few months that their hopes were not to be speedily realized.
I certainly appreciate the bringing of this question before the House. I am inclined to think, without wishing to be anything of a scold, that if we could devote more attention in the House to bringing these matters that are of direct interest to the people, before the country and before those Mr. McCRANEY.
interested, we would perhaps, accomplish more for the public than we do by some of the discussions we have. This is a question that directly affects a portion of the people of Canada, and what affects one part of the country affects us all. It is of the utmost importance, that just as rapidly as possible in all parts of the country the people should be brought into the quickest possible communication with the best market. That is the reason that parliament assists in the building of railways. It is not at all, to my mind, that they want to assist the companies, as some hon. gentlemen would think, but it is an effort on their part to encourage the companies or urge them on with greater speed to bring the people in closer communion with the outside world and thus make their living more comfortable and their occupations more profitable. It is on that ground that parliaments assist railways. When a railway, is assisted by parliament, it must assume an obligation in return for that assistance and I have no hesitation in saying that it is the duty of these companies, as rapidly as they can, to extend the facility of railway communication to all the people they can.' As I understand, the Canadian Pacific Railway have built a stretch of about fourteen miles, had let a contract for seventy miles more, and have constructed one hundred miles at the other end. The great disappointment has been paused by the fact that they cancelled the contract for the seventy miles.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The whole mileage is quite long.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: About five hundred miles in all.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It would be quite an extensive road if constructed. I am not here to apologize for the railway, but I think it fair to say that the past year has been very discouraging to railway companies. The Railway Committee this session has been very lenient with companies asking extensions from the very fact that they find it difiicult to finance their present undertakings ; and I think I can say with some assurance that in undertaking to finance any line they have to give a pretty direct account of what they propose to do with the money they obtain, and so the lines that are going to be profitable the quickest are the ones to which they are trying to devote their efforts.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Does not the minister think they will look rather to the lines where there is competition ?

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
That might be, but the men supplying the money may, to a certain extent, influence that too. The last year has been very discouraging to the railway companies in two ways. First it was very

difficult to raise money, and second, the receipts from the railways during the past few months have fallen off very materially, and if my hon. friend will compare the receipts of the large railways during the past six months, with those of the corresponding six months of a year ago, he will see there has not been much recently to encourage them to extend their lines.
Another matter of which I think it is fair to speak is that a year ago or a little more, there was a great congestion of traffic in the Northwest. There was a cry, and a reasonable one too, all over the land that none of the railway companies provided a sufficient amount of rolling stock. The hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) took the position, and not unwisely, that the railways ought to be compelled to supply the present lines with complete railway stock before they were allowed to build another mile. That has been urged on the companies very strongly that they should increase their rolling stock, but recently that has not been pushed to any extent because there is not a railway on the continent but has many cars on sidings not being used at all. I am not saying this in apology for the railways1 but am pointing out reasons that will be given by them. I think it wise to discuss these things before the House and give them the utmost publicity. I assure my hon. friends that I shall call the attention of the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway to this complaint and urge them, as far as practicable, to keep faith with the people of the Northwest wherever a charter has been given for the construction of a railway.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: While I did not hear the first part of the discussion and am not quite clear as to its purpose, it looks odd to me, that on Friday afternoon, when we generally expect to do a great deal of business, hon. members sitting behind the ministers should raise questions such as this and obstruct the Minister of Public Works in dealing with his estimates. It is apparently a concerted effort on the part of some of these gentlemen. The hon. member who first spoke (Mr. Knowles) a year or two ago opposed the renewal of the charter of this company.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: My hon. friend is all wrong, he is mistaken.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I do not think I am very far mistaken, not over seventy miles. There was a strong movement by some members from the west to oppose the extension of the time for the construction of this road and now they come here and complain that it has not been constructed. Is it any wonder that the Canadian Pacific Railway would hesitate about going on, knowing the influence of those gentlemen with the government, and knowing that 243
they might at any day cut their charter in two and hinder them from proceeding with the work. If I am making a statement that is not strictly correct, my information comes from a source which I think I can rely on, a gentleman equally interested with the hon. member for West Assiniboia * (Mr. Knowles). If he is serious in trying to get this road built, let him go to Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, to the Railway Commission or some one who has something to do with the building of the road and not come here. Governments do not build railways. It is true they are building the National Transcontinental, but they are not undertaking the construction of this road. I do not suppose they are granting an acre of land by way of subsidy or bonus or contributing a dollar towards it, and it is a matter of no moment to the government whether the road is built or not ; that is to say they are not a party to it.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I gave very distinctly my reasons for the special course I took and I think my hon. friend should at least be present to hear my statement before passing judgment on my conduct.

subtopic: THE MOOSEJAW-LACOMBE EXTENSION CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman should have given me an intimation before bringing it up. He cannot expect that we will be on hand at all times to discuss matters of this kind.
I think he should announce the day before at any rate and give hon. gentlemen notice that he is going to propose a great question, a question of prime importance to the west. I do not say but that it is a question of great importance to the west. I am not finding fault with the hon. gentleman in trying to get that road built because I think it is an important road. I understand it is constructed now from Moosejaw a certain distance, that it is constructed at the other end from Lacombe, and that there is a link in the middle which remains to be built. It is of great importance to the people in that country that the road should be built and I have no doubt that it will be built provided the hon. gentleman does not succeed in blocking a renewal of the charter. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman in his desire to have the road built, but I do protest against his wasting the time of the House in bringing a matter of this kind up when he knows perfectly well that the only thing that he could accomplish was to boom himself in West Assiniboia by making the people there believe that he is a great big man. I do not suppose that he had any other purpose. He knew perfectly well that it was no use. He could have gone to the Minister of Railways and Canals privately and asked him to assist him by urging upon the Canadian Pacific Railway to get that road built. He had the privilege of doing it because he is supporting the gov-



ernment and I will undertake to say that lie would have got just as good a promise from the minister and one which would have carried just as much weight if he had gone to him privately instead of taking an hour or two of the valuable time of the Minister of Public Works and instead of blocking the Estimates and keeping us perhaps sitting here until twelve or one o'clock in the morning

Minister of Public Works, (Mr. Pugsley) when he does get into the Estimates, will not inflict a penalty on this House and keep us here until three o'clock in the morning, knowing as he does that his political triends have been the cause very largely of the waste of time that has been going on.

speechtext: If the hon. gentleman thinks he will get through at two o'clock I will tell him that, as far as I am concerned, I have an intense objection to sitting and talking Estimates after twelve o'clock. I do not think there is any need for it. I think we should get through with our business at twelve o'clock at any rate and if the minister gives direct answers to the questions which are submitted to him and does not ask us to vote money for unreasonable things I have no doubt he will get along sufficiently well to enable the government to adjourn the House at twelve and let us go home, take our rest and be able to come back in the beginning of the week refreshed. speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
There is another obstructor coming.

I will just take two minutes of the time of the House to make a personal explanation. At the beginning of the discussion of the motion which is now before the chair, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) quoted from the report of the Civil Service Commission, at page 79, the following letter :
I have to inform you that if you consider that chemical fire extinguishers are necessary on hoard the vessels of the Quebec agency you are to purchase them from P. E. Perreault, 312 St. John street, Quebec. Mr. P.

has been advised to call upon you in connection with this matter.
The hon. gentleman stated that this letter had been signed by me. I was greatly surprised that he should make that statement.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) absolutely denied that. He said that he had never said that it was signed by the minister. He repeated that denial and, in the face of that, I do not think that the minister should repeat the statement.
At first he said that I had signed this letter.
No, he stated that he had not.
The record will show in regard to that.
Well, let the Minister of Public Works go on.

I think it is only right that I should be permitted to give a personal explanation. There are so many things being said against me that I think the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) should be willing to give me two minutes to make this explanation.
No, I do not think you ought to.

I understood the hon. member for Leeds to say that I had signed this letter. At all events I called his attention to that and I asked him where he had got his information that I had signed this letter. I sent over to the department for the file and I find that on the 20th July, 1906, Mr. Perrault applied to the department to sell some fire extinguishers, and on the 27th July, 1906, the letter which I have just quoted was written and was signed by the deputy minister.
Will my hon. friend read the letter ?
Yes. It is dated July 27, 3906.
No, Mr. Perreault's letter.

Yes, it is dated the 20th July, 1906 :
Quebec, July 20, 1906.

Spain, Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir,-The captain of the Canadian government steamer ' Minto ' was speaking to me about putting some chemical fire extinguishers aboard his ship the same as I put aboard of all the ships at this agency. The ' Minto ' has no chemical fire extinguishers whatever. You were present at a test I made on the King's wharf two years ago in competition with another make; mine proved itself far superior in every way. Inclosed please find cut giving information. The ' Minto ' would require eight machines owing to the way she is divided up; ordinarily

from four to six is all that is necessary- I would be pleased to receive an order for any other ships you would like to equip. Price, $14 each. Can place same on board on her return here. I am on the patronage list. Hoping to receive your esteemed orders, 1 remain,
Yours respectfully,
(Sgd.) P. E. PERREAULT,
312 St. John street, Quebec.
X do not remember having had any knowledge of this letter before I read it the other day in the report of the Civil Service Commission, but I find on the file another letter dated the 27th October, 1906. That letter was sent to me by the party named to the effect that Mr. Perrault had on his hands a certain number of extinguishers and that he would like to sell these to the government.	-
Who sent that letter ?

Mr. Lachance, M.P. Perhaps I had better give the letter :
Quebec, October 27, 1906. Hon. L. P. Brodeur,
Minister of Marine, Ottawa.
Mr. Minister,-Mr. P. E. Perreault had on hand a certain number of fire extinguishers when he was appointed to the Department of Marine and Fisheries at Quebec. He was then engaged as an agent in this trade. He has a certain number remaining on hand.
Could you not authorize Mr. Gregory to purchase them for the service of the lighthouses as well as- in the steamers. Their efficacy has been several times shown by various experiments made at Quebec and elsewhere.
Yours truly,

Then my answer follows which I will read in French and translate into English. It is dated November 6, 1906, and is as follows :-
My Dear Member,-I received your letter of the 27th of October last concerning the extinguishers that Mr. Perreault desires to sell to the department. I have had Mr. Gregory written to on the subject and when his reply reaches the department I will communicate my decision.
It appears that Mr. Perreault applied ' de novo ' to the department, and he received this answer :
I have to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 6th instant with reference to fire extinguishers and have to advise you that none are required bv the department.
That is the correspondence concerning that matter. I am exceedingly sorry that the member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) has tried to make a case against me without reason. Had he been kind enough to notify me that he would bring up this question I would have had the files ready to answer 243*
the insinuations he has made. The hon. gentleman did not think it advisable to do so, but I am nevertheless glad to put before the House the facts in connection with it.
I suppose the hon. gentleman would have no objection to lay the file on the table.

No objection at all. But I may say that some years ago the department brought before the House an original document, namely, the lease to Mr. Markey, and it was handed to an opposition member of this House and it has never -been returned to the House.
Does the hon. gentleman know it was handed to an opposition member ?	[DOT]
Yes, because it was read by him in the House.
Does he know that the opposition member did not return it ?
There has been no trace of it in the department since.
It may have been lost there. There was such confusion in the department that it may have been lost.
Oh, not at all; if my hon. friend wants to see this file I have no objection.
The minister having quoted from it, I suppose there is no objection to laying it on the table of the House.
I will of course put copies on the table.
That is not the point. The minister having sent to the department for the original file and having quoted it in the House. I suppose he will have no objection to lay it on the table.
I have no objection to have all these documents copied and laid before the House.
That is not what I ask.
Well, if the hon. gentleman does not take my word for it, here is the file and let him consult it. I will send it over by a page, but I must thank him for the courtesy he has extended to me.

I expect to give fair-play to my hon. friends opposite and I would expect the same from them in return. I made no suggestion that the minister would not do as he stated. There was no such thought in my mind. I was pointing out that the minister having sent for the de-partmelltal file and having quoted from it, it was only fair that he should lay it on the table of the House.

An lion. MEMBER. Well, you have It now.

After Recess.

House in committee on Bill (No. 151) respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company.-Mr. Crawford.
Mr. CRAWFORD moved that progress be .reported.

This Bill has been several times before the committee and I do not propose to object, but I may say to my hon. friend that I wish to deal with the matter by way of amendment at some time, and as I have been here ready on several occasions I hope that the Minister of Railways and the promoter of the Bill will concur in letting it stand over if it should happen that I shall not be here when it is called again.

House in committee on Bill (No. 151) respecting the Board of the Presbyterian College, Halifax.-Mr. Sinclair.
On section 1,
Is the promoter of this Bill present? I would like to have some explanation of it.
I do not think there is anything in the Bill of a contentious nature, and unless my hon. friend from Halton has some special reason for desiring it to stand, I hope he will not press his objection.

I will just say that this is a Bill which came before the Private Bills Committee. I had not an opportunity of being present, not being a member of that committee, and I know nothing about the Bill or the reason for it. I think we have been laying it down as a practice that a man is not expected to get his Bill through this committee unless he gives personal attention to it. I do not see why we should sit here promoting another man's legislation. If he does not see fit to come here and give reasons why the Bill should become law, I think we are perfectly justified in asking that it stand over. I would, there-Mr. BLAIN.
fore, enter my protest against further proceeding with this Bill. We have for some time laid it down as a distinct rule that a Bill should stand unless the promoter is present. I do ont see even the chairman of the Committee on Private Bills. We are legislating altogether in the dark, and I will ask the government to see that the rule, or at any rate the practice that we have adopted for some time back, is adhered to.

I do not know that the hon. member for Guysborough, in whose name the Bill stands, is any more its promoter than any other hon. member of this House. This Bill came from the Senate in the regular order and was placed in the name of the hon. member for Guysborough, who is probably more familiar with the legislation than a good many others, but who is in no special sense the promoter of the Bill. I am quite sure that the Bill has received careful consideration at the hands of those to whom it was committed, and that there is nothing in it that should not receive the assent of the House.

I think it is immaterial whether the promoter of a Bill is present or not when it comes before the House, particularly when it is a Bill that comes from the Senate. The hon. member for Halton with the Bill before him is able to look at its provisions, and, with his keen, incisive mind, I am quite sure that he could understand it as well as the hon. gentleman in whose name it stands. I do not know of any rule that requires a member whose name is attached to a Bill to be present in the House when it is under consideration. If there is such a rule, it is more honoured in the breach than in the observance.

There is no such rule, but there is no doubt that it is a satisfactory practice, unless there is somebody else who can give explanations which any member may desire to have. However, as the hon. member in whose name the Bill stands is now present, he will probably be able to give any explanations that are desired.

The hon. member for Halton did not mention any point on which he desired information. If he had asked for information which no hon. member present could give him, there would be a reason for allowing the Bill to stand over.

As the promoter of the Bill is now present, my objection of course falls to the ground, but I believe it is a good practice to insist that those in whose name any legislation stands should be present to answer for it. I admit that there is no rule, but I said that we had adopted a practice of that kind, and when the Minister of Finance was present I believe he endorsed it as a good practice. I think the

promoter of the Bill might tell us in a few minutes what is the purpose of it.

This Bill was sent to me by the secretary of the Presbyterian Board at Halifax, and he informed me that all the clauses of it had been before the Synod of the Presbyterian church, and were quite acceptable "to the parties in charge of the funds. This Bill is quite acceptable in every way to all parties concerned. I am not able to give the exact details but I understand that there are certain funds bequeathed to the different schemes of the church that are not supposed to be covered by the powers given the Presbyterian Board under former Acts. There are certain bequests which were made to the church in a general way, and it was held by some legal gentlemen that the board had not sufficient control over those bequests. I understand that the purpose is to make the Act so general that all bequests to the church can be dealt with by the board. I accepted the Bill on the recommendation of the secretary of the board, and I understand it was thoroughly threshed out by the members of the legal committee of the Synod of the Presbyterian church of the maritime provinces and is acceptable to them.
In what way does this differ from the clause we are appealing ? We are appealing paragraph ' 0 ' of section 3 of chapter 92 of the statutes of Canada, 1902. Is that a general or a special Act?

It was an Act to incorporate the board of the Presbyterian College of Halifax. The repealed section provided that the board should have power to receive, manage and administer property, real and personal, and titles and effects of every description then held or enjoyed by or under control of the board. The section was limited to what the board then had, and by this amendment the board has power to receive and administer property hereafter given to them as well. It applies not only to property they may now possess but which they may possess in the *(future.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.	-
