House in committee on Bill (No. 20) respecting the Belleville-Prince Edward Bridge Company.-Mr. Porter.

The hon. member for Belleville (Mr. Porter), who is the promoter of the Bill, is not present, and he asked me to explain it in his absence. The Bill has been before the Private Bills Committee and has been amended in some particulars. It was perfectly satisfactory to that committee.

I have a copy of the Bill, as amended by the Private Bills Committee, and it is satisfactory.
On section 1-tolls.
Why do you add that word ' driver ' in connection with a vehicle?
Each person passing over the bridge is charged a separate fee and they might undertake to tax the driver.
Suppose two people are in the rig.
There would be an extra fee for the extra person.
Are not the regulations of tolls on bridges in municipal rather than federal jurisdiction ?

I think the worst specimen is in the municipality of the city of Montreal. The Victoria bridge has a list of tolls, sanctioned by parliament, which is the most exorbitant I know of. I was surprised, when parliament voted so much for that bridge, that the list of tolls was not greatly reduced. I hope that parliament will be more careful in sanctioning toll charges, especially when they are as exorbitant as they are on that jubilee bridge in Montreal. That bridge has a tariff of charges six or eight feet high printed in small letters. Every jackass that crosses is taxed to an exorbitant degree.
You are not interested in that charge?
My hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) is the patron of that class of quadruped. All I say is that these tolls ought to be carefully revised by parliament, and somebody ought to be responsible for them.	'

I am glad the hon. gentleman (Mr. W. P. Maclean) has reached that conclusion now. I know that when this Bill was amended I fought very hard against the tolls, but I had little support in this House. I remember distinctly, when this was passed, the contention was put up that it was very difficult to raise money to build a bridge, and that when it was built it Would be very difficult to get means to keep it in repair, and these fees were agreed upon as reasonable at that time. I confess I looked with suspicion upon the proposal to increase that. In some instances they have been raised 100 per cent. Take, for instance, a bicycle and rider, ten cents. Ten cents for a bicycle and rider going across a bridge-that is exorbitant.
It is only five cents.
They have increased it to ten cents. ' Bicycle and rider, 10 cents.'

That is not as it was settled in committee. I was a member of

the sub-committee on the revision of these tolls. The hon. member for Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) was present, though I do not know whether he was a member of the committee. The representative of the township of Ameliasburg and also the representative of the board of trade and of the city council of Belleville were present, and tlie fees were practically agreed upon and a compromise made. I remember distinctly that the fee for bicycle and rider was fixed at five cents. Why it is given as ten cents in the Bill I do not know.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It was five cents and it is raised to ten cents in the Bill.
The tariff as submitted by the promoter of the Bill was : ' Bicycle 5 cents.' It was afterwards agreed to make it ' bicycle and rider 10 cents.'

Notwithstanding that that is in the Bill, my distinct recollection is that it was settled otherwise in the committee. I remember mentioning that, in my opinion, a bicycle going over a bridge did not cause very much wear and tear on the bridge, and that if the bicycle was charged five cents and the bicycle was ridden there should be no extra fee for the rider. I do not think it should be ten cents, and I am positive that it was arranged otherwise in committee.

The last clause provides that these tolls are to be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. These rates are maximum rates, and will not be reached if the Governor in Council does not approve.
In reference to the point raised by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), I think we may well ask what right we have to deal with such a Bill as this at all.
I think it was held that this was over navigable water.
That does not make incorporation in this parliament necessary.
But this parliament did incorporate the company.

I quite recognize that this is an amendment to an Act we passed in 1S99. But our attention was not at that time so particularly directed to the necessity of being careful about this matter as it is now. I do not know whether we can do anything in reference to that point now, but I would call the attention of the committee to the fact that, if this were a new matter, it is one that ought to be regarded as purely within the provincial jurisdiction, and, therefore, one that ought not to be dealt with in this parliament. I call attention to this because I wish to be consistent. Whenever I find an effort to in- * Mr. GALLIHER.
corporate here a company that ought to be incorporated by the provincial legislature, I endeavour to discourage it. This looks to me like a matter that would be within the jurisdiction of the local legislature.

If this parliament acknowledges-and I think it should be acknowledged-that a mistake was made in incorporating the company in 1899, the most this parliament could do now is to have a provision that the provincial governent of Ontario should have the right to regulate the tolls. On that point this parliament should not invade the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature. I think that the company should have been incorporated by the provincial legislature. Then, as the bridge is over a navigable stream, the company could secure permission of the Department of Public Works for the construction of the bridge. That is the course pursued in all the provinces so far as my experience teaches me. But that course was not pursued in this case. It seems to me this parliament should not undertake to regulate the tolls, but should have a provision in the Bill referring that matter to the abitrament of the provincial legislature of Ontario, or providing for the approval of the Governor in Council of Ontario.

This bridge has nothing to do with any international or interprovincial water. It is only to make a short way across from the county of Hastings to the county of Prince Edward in Ontario. This company was incorporated away back in 1S99 and tolls were then established for the traffic over this bridge. The county of Prince Edward being one of the real beauty spots of the Dominion is attracting a large number of tourists who go into the county both by land and water. On that account and to that extent we, as well as the inhabitants of the district, have an interest in this matter. Of course, if my hon. friend from Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) and the promoter of the Bill are perfectly satisfied, that must have great influence with the House, for they are the people most deeply interested. My only object is to get the Bill exactly as the committee want it. In the case of the bicycle there seems to be a little difference of opinion.
The Bill is now before this committee, I have no doubt, as it was passed by the subcommittee and the Committee on Private Bills. This matter of the toll on the bicycle was a matter of compromise.
That is disputed.

I think that the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Galliher) is mistaken; I have no doubt in my own mind that he is. I remember his making the observation to which he refers, but the same item came up a number of times and was the subject

of contention, and in conjunction with other items it was finally decided to leave it as it appears in the Bill.

I contend that no bicycle rider should be charged five cents for crossing this bridge. His bicycle weighs thirty pounds at the most. He crosses the bridge more rapidly by reason of that fact and wherever tolls are charged on roads they have not been imposed on a man because he happens to be on a bicycle.
I think it would be a bad precedent to establish if parliament should double the toll on a man because he happens to be riding his bicycle. He goes faster, gets off the bridge in less time and so useful a mode of travel as the bicycle should not be discriminated against in this way.

Does not a man driving a light sulky, weighing about the same as a bicycle, have to pay as if he were in another vehicle ? If you strike out the word ' bicycle ' altogether, the bicycle would pay nothing because it is only the things mentioned here on which toll is paid.
'Or other vehicles ' would cover that ?
No.

The more this is discussed the more positive I am that I am right. The very fact that we see the charge for each * person passing over the bridge five cents and then lower down for each bicycle five cents, shows that for the two the charge is ten ceflts, and what would be the sense of saying ' bicycle with rider ten cents ' because it would come to the same thing. I am positive that the arrangement in the special committee was that the bicycle, including its rider, was to pay only five cents, not ten cents. There is no doubt about that in my mind. I am sure the other members of the committee, if they were here would endorse my statement that we agreed to include the rider with the bicycle at five cents.

When the original Bill was passed the same question came up, does the charge for a vehicle include the driver ?-and it was agreed it did. If you put the bicycle separate from the rider and then charge for each, you are changing the whole principle and raising the toll one hundred per cent.
I say we do not, we leave it unchanged.

I say that if you agree to what we are told you agree, you do raise it. Who is the owner of the bridge now ? It is claimed that this was a public convenience, that it was hard to get money to keep it up and that it was expedient there should be some toll but to make it
as reasonable as possible so as not to prevent people from crossing the bridge or taking some other means of getting to their destination without crossing it. It was regarded as reasonable to charge the schedule brought down and agreed to, and I confess I do not see any ground for raising the charge. It may mean that some of those who desire to have it raised are the owners of the bridge. In the interest of the travelling public, I took the same ground with reference to the bridge at Montreal. I always think, in any of these bridges, you should make the lowest possible charge so that people may cross, may take produce and animals across with the least possible hinderance and not have the bridge holders make a big profit.

The more one studies this tariff the more he will be convinced that this matter should be left to the approval of the Governor in Council of Ontario because for instance it will be seen that children under six years of age, accompanied by parent or guardian, are free, but by another clause a lady with a baby in a baby carriage would have to pay five cents additional.
That is struck out.
I think that every principle of sound legislation leads one to the conclusion that it should be left to the approval of the Lieutenant Governor in Council of Ontario.

They could change it at any time. If Belleville suddenly developed into a large city, there is no reason why the tolls should not be reduced. It should be flexible and the Dominion parliament has more important things to attend to than adjusting these toll rates from time to time.

Conditions no doubt will change there. You are establishing a tariff of rates that will remain for all time unless that company chooses to come back to this parliament and have a reduced tariff substituted.
No, look at the last clause.
It is to be approved by the Governor in Council.
Of the Dominion. Why should the Governor in Council for this Dominion take charge of a matter that is purely provincial?

That is another argument.
Mr. EMMERSON'. That is the argument I am making and my objection to this Bill is absolutely from that standpoint.
Mr. FOWLER, I interrupted the hon. gentleman because he said that would have

to come to this parliament. It would be much more convenient to go to the Lieutenant Governor in Council than to the'Governor in council.

My observations have reference to the last clause. It seems to me to be self-evident that we were usurping the right of the province of Ontario with reference to the latter matter. It was done, no doubt, by mistake but having made the mistake I do not think that this parliament should ratify it. I think that this parliament should make an acknowledgment of the error and that a section stating that the tariff should be such a tariff as will be approved- from time to time by the Lieutenant Governor in Council of the province should be inserted.
Make a motion to that effect and I will support it.
I will accept that.

As the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) says it is a matter which certainly comes within the provision of the British North America Act with respect to property and civil rights within the provinces and, therefore, if the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals would move an amendment of that kind in reference to the last clause, I think we ought to support it.

I quite agree with the position taken by the hon. member for Westmoreland that this is no doubt a provincial matter which has been made a federal matter by reason of the Act passed in 1899. I see no reason why the parties interested in the Bill should not accept an amendment of that kind providing that the tolls should be approved from time to time by the Lieutenant Governor in Council.

The discussion has taken a somewhat wider range than might have been anticipated. The question of the rights of the provinces has been very well presented by my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson). We ought to have the Bill reprinted with the amendments in them and allow it to stand until the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter), the promoter of the Bill, is here to take part in the discussion. I think it would hardly be fair to insert a clause in his Bill when he was absent.
Progress reported.

House in committee on Bill (No. 153) to incorporate the Saskatchewan Power Company.-Mr. McCraney.
On section 1,

I received a communication in regard to this Bill from the muni-Mr. FOWLER.
cipality of Saskatchewan. I would like to ask if the objection has been withdrawn before the committee ?

As the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) explains, there were some objections made to the Bill in its original form by the corporation of Saskatoon. The objections have been withdrawn and I will read a letter that I have received from the clerk of the city in regard to the matter.
Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, April 24, 1908. Geo. E. McCraiiey, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons, Ottawa, Ontario. Sir,-Re Saskatchewan Power Company. I am in receipt of your letter, also your telegram April 15, and an reply would say that I have been instructed by the city council to write you thanking you for the interest which you have taken on the city's behalf in regard to the passing of the Saskatchewan Power Company's Bill.
The council are of the opinion that it would not necessitate the sending of a delegate to Ottawa *on Wednesday the 29th instant, as clause 3 seems to he in keeping with the petition that we forwarded to you some time ago.
I am, yours truly,
(Sgd.) A. H. TRUESDALE,
City Clerk.
The objections which the municipal corporation made are met by clause 3 of this Bill.

I would like to ask the promoter why he comes here to get this Bill crystallized into law instead of going to the legislature of Saskatchewan. From the slight information I have it seems -to me that it Is purely a local matter.
Mr. McCRAN'EY. I would be pleased to state to my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) the reason this company has come here for the incorporation for which it is asking. Under ordinary circumstances, in the province of Ontario, such a company would be incorporated and powers given to it by the local legislature, but hon. gentlemen will remember the question which arose in the discussion of the Saskatchewan Act and the fact that certain rights were reserved to -the Dominion parliament in regard to the lands.
1 will quote section 21 of the Saskatchewan Act:
All Crown lands, mines and minerals and royalties incident thereto and the interest of the Crpwn in the waters within the province under the Northwest Irrigation Act, 1898, shall continue to be vested in the Crown and administered by the government of Canada for the purposes of Canada.
Then the Irrigation Act which is chapter 61 of the Revised Statutes of Canada provides as follows :
Section 6. The property in and the right to the use of all the water at any time in any river, stream, water course, lake, creek, ra-

vine, canyon, lagoon, swamp, marsh or other boiy of water shall, for the purposes of this Act, be deemed to be vested in the Crown, unless and until and except only so far as some right therein, or to the use thereof, inconsistent with the right of the Crown, and which is not a public right or a right common to the public, is established.
That is the Irrigation Act? Mr. McCRANEY. Yes.
It says ' for the purposes * of this Act '. That is for the purposes of irrigation, is it not ?

But, the reference to the Irrigation Act is continued in the Saskatchewan Act.
It is a very bad principle to pass these water powers into the hands of private corporations. In addition to that my contention is that unless this is a navigable stream the province and not the Dominion has control over it. It may be that the Irrigation Act which the hon. gentleman has referred to gives authority to this parliament to deal with the matter but otherwise the province should own and control these powers and derive what revenue it can from them.

It would be desirable that the hon. gentleman in charge of this Bill should continue his explanation of it.
Progress reported.

What I want to suggest to the hon. gentleman is this : The hon. gentleman reads from the Irrigation Act and it says that the things that are enumerated are, ' for the purposes of this Act ' vested m the Dominion parliament. I would understand that to mean for the purposes of irrigation and matters incidental to it and not necessarily for the purposes of this Act which is an Act to incorporate a power company. Any thing that is referred to in the Acts which the hon. gentleman has quoted does not change the situation as far as I can see.
Mi\ SPROTTLE. I have here a copy of a letter sent by the Saskatoon city council I do not know whether the hon. member (Mr. MeCraney) has had a similar one and has dealt with it or not, but I notice that they oppose this Bill very strongly.

I have had a copy of the letter probably to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) refers and the objections which are contained in that communication are, the council say, met by the provisions of clause 3 as amended in the Senate I will send my hon. friend the letter which I have received from the city of Saskatoon.
The letter referred to by the hon. gentleman is with reference to the Draft Bill presented in the Senate and which was very considerably amended there so that we are considering it now.

The city of Saskatoon contends that there is a valuable water power there which they do not desire to get into the hands of a private corporation and which ought to be controlled by the city, and with regard to which they are making an application to the government. As I understand it this private company seeks by this Bill to get control of the water power and thus acquire the right to charge perhaps exorbitant prices for the supply of power and which would prevent the development of manufacturing industries.

Public Works, Buildings-Ontario-Belleville armoury, $75,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext:
At the last sitting of the committee I gave a full explanation of this item. I do not know whether any other gentlemen would like to have an explanation from the Minister of Militia or not.
Guelph armoury, $20,000.
What is the expected cost of this building ?

The total probable co^t of the armoury, with the heating, the electric wiring and fixtures, the fittings and furniture, including the site, is $114,537.30. We are now asking for $20,000, and will of course require a further amount later. In this cost is included the cost of a drill-hall which will be over the armoury. The building will be a very fine one.

When will it be
completed ?
During the present year.
Will it be at the disposal of the live-stock fair that is held at Guelph ?
I do not know. I have had no application for the use of it.

I would like to know the number of men the Belleville armoury is intended to accommodate. I would like also to know on what principle the siz,e and cost of these armouries are determined ; because they are becoming very costly. My desire was to have the Minister of Militia present, as he alone could give ns that information.

The 15th regiment, composed of eight companies, is the principal military unit that will occupy that armoury. That is about 400 strong. In addition to that, one company of a rural battalion, the 49th regiment, consisting of between forty and fifty men, will

have its headquarters iu this armoury. In arranging for an armoury the Militia Department makes an estimate of what ac-. commodation is required for the existing militia strength, and for some additional accommodation to provide for the natural growth of the place. I should say that Belleville has had for many years an armoury which was found to be insufficient, and it was torn down ; so that this new armoury is really taking its place. This and other city regiments do not go into camp annually, but do .their drill at headquarters iu the evenings. In most of the cities it is impossible to obtain the consent of the employers of labour to give the men of these corps the time to attend to their drill in the day time ; the consequence is that they do their annual drill, and give a great deal more of their time than the equivalent of twelve days, in the evenings ; and these armouries are the homes of these regiments during the long winter and spring months. I think they are an absolute necessity, and have been the means of doing a great deal of good to the militia. In fact, we could not get on without them.
There is a rural battalion in that county in addition to the city one ?
Yes, the 49th regiment. It has eight companies, one of which is situated at Belleville and will use a part of the armoury for storage of arms.
How many companies are there outside ?
Seven.
Where are they accommodated ?

There is a grant of money to each company of every rural battalion. The captain of the company receives this grant for the care of arms, and he keeps them in a building of his own or where he likes. That is not done in the cities to anything like the same extent, but there the money goes to pay a caretaker by the year for looking after the armoury and the stores.
What is to be the total cost of this building when completed ?
What is the size of it ?
The hall will be 175 feet by 80 with a range of armouries along the north side. The walls of brick on stone foundation. The centre portion three stories high.

I see that the specifications were prepared by the Architect Engineering Company at a cost of $1,755. Why Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
were not the plans prepared by the architects of the Public Works Department ?
At that time the staff was exceeding busy with other work.
What is the cost of the site ?

Why was the old armoury replaced ? It was a very commodious and convenient building, and I would have thought it would answer every purpose of the militia of Belleville and the vicinity for many years. Why was the site purchased so near the business centre ? It is on a street next the main street, and land could have been obtained further away at very much less price. The old building was one street further away from the main street.

The site is not under my control but as to why a new building is required I remember distinctly that strong protests were made that the old building was not sufficient, and strong pressure brought to bear to get a new one.
. Mr PUGSLEY. I would call attention to the fact that the lot Is a corner lot, 260 feet 6 inches on one street and 150 feet 6 inches on the other, and is quite close to the best business portion of the city.
From whom was it bought ?
From Mrs. Yonker and Mr. Richard Harnett.
What is the annual cost of keeping up an armoury such as you are building ?

The caretaker gets from $1 to $1.50 per day. Then there is the expense of fuel, which I do not think is very great because the whole building is not heated all the time. I should think the cost of keeping up the building, including heat, light and caretaker, would be from $1,200 to $1,500 per year.
Guelph armoury, $20,000.

This building is to be built of brick with stone dressing on stone foundation. The portion fronting on Has-sc'is street is 146 feet by 36. exclusive of projections. It is three stories high with a basement. In the rear there is to be an extension 80 feet wide and 190 feet deep, which will have two stories. The site cost $5,000, and the total cost will be $148,537.20, including the armoury and drill shed.
What is the strength of the force which will be provided for?

This armoury will accommodate two field batteries

of artillery, the 11th and 16th, also one com- Mr. SPROULE. When was the building pany of the 30th Regiment.	commenced ?
Where is the headquarters of the 30th ?
It is a Wellington county regiment.
Guelph would be the headauarters ?

It may be, but there is only one company resident there. The regimental headquarters will be there. Then there is a company of the Army Service Corps numbering 110, so that the number of men will be about 400, and these two batteries are among the most important in the country. There are six field guns in each battery. There will be accommodation there for these guns and harness and all the material connected with them. The same remark will apply to the Army Service Corps. There are wagons and a great deal of stores connected with a corps of that kind. Also, No. 1 company of the 30th Regiment keeps its stores and equipment in this armoury.

Were plans for this
armoury prepared in the jPublic Works Department ?
Yes, and tenders were called for as usual, and the lowest tender accepted.
Are plans for these armouries usually prepared in the department ?
Yes.

The hon. gentleman
gave us to understand that the reason this was not done in the case of Belleville armoury was that the architects in the department were very busy. I think he said twelve architects were employed in the department. That would seem to me a very good staff.
There is a great deal of work and it is more pressing at some times than at others.
Does the hon. gentleman think that twelve architects are insufficient for carrying on the business of the department ?
If I were to express an opinion, I would say they are not sufficient.
Twelve architects not sufficient to prepare the plans for the public buildings put up throughout Canada ?
They do more than prepare plans-there is the preparation of the specifications, the making of progress estimates and looking after a large number of buildings.
The contract was on June 1. 1900.
Then it has been going on ever since ?
Yes.
How long before it will be completed ?
We expect to finish It this year.
Who are the contractors ?
Nagel & Mills, of In-gersoll.
Is there a clerk of works on it all this time ?
It is in charge of a supervising architect, who is paid a commission of two per cent.
How were these troops previously accommodated ?

The batteries were accommodated in a building hired for the purpose. The company of the 30th Regiment, I suppose, had no special accommodation. I have explained that, in such cases, there is an allowance to the captain to provide accommodation such as he can. The Army Service Corps I think also was accommodated in a rented building, although it has not been very long organized and I could not be absolutely certain as to that.
Does the Minister of Militia himself decide, in cases of this kind, where new buildings should be erected?

As a rule, the military head of the district brings the matter to my attention, and I submit it to the proper officers of my department for a report. If that report is to the effect that the accommodation is needed, I asked for a statement as to exactly what is needed. When that information is procured, I forward the information to the Department of Public Works. Plans are prepared there, and, after they are prepared, they .are returned to me. I go over them again with the assistance of the officers of the department, and, if they are satisfactory, they are sent back to the Department of Public Works initialled by myself.

The items we have had this evening are very large amounts. The minister has stated the routine by which it is decided whether new buildings are necessary and desirable. Will he state the reasons which led to the decision that this was necessary ?
I hare not the correspondence before me.	,
Cannot the committee be informed what representations were made and by whom ?

I have a memo, here showing that this was strongly urged by the Department of Militia as early as January 15, 1903. The General Officer Commanding reported that it was absolutely necessary that the two field batteries, the city companies and the bands should be properly housed.
I think that was in Dundonald's time.
What is the estimated cost of this structure, completed in every respect ?
The estimate is $148,537.
The contract was something over $80,000. How is the rest made up ?

The amount paid for the site was $5,000-it was bought from the city council of Guelph, and formed part of the property known as the fair grounds. It is a corner lot. The survey of the site, printing, advertising, travelling expenses-
What is the amount of printing and advertising ?

I have it in a lump sum with other items which make a total of $3,139.21. Payment to the contractor up to 10th December, 1907, was $53,130, making the total expenditure to 10th December, $61,259.30. The amount due on the contract is $26,870, which makes the amount of the contract $80,000. Then, the amount due on the drill hall over the gun shed is $34,925.
Was there a contract for that ?
Yes.
The same contractor ?

Yes. The amount for heating and boilers is $5,000, electric wiring and fixtures, $2,500, fittings and furniture $7,000, sidewalks $3,000 ; contingencies and superintendence $7,983-making a total of $148,537.30.

Has the government reconveyed a portion of this land to the) city of Guelph or to the Guelph Fat Stock show people ? I understand a deputation came down for the pur-pose of asking a reconveyance. They wanted to purchase a portion of this land which was not required.
That has not been done, it is a large lot 178 by 467 feet.

What is the size of the building ?
Mr. PUGSLEi'. 146 feet on Huskisson street with a depth of 36 feet exclusive of projections and an extension of 88 feet in breadth by 190 feet deep. The building is of brick and stone with a stone foundation.
The former site of the Belleville building was on the next street. What became of the old site? Has it been sold by the government or what disposition has been made of it.
I do not know, I shall make inquiry.

It is a very valuable site and I think abuts on the present site. I would like to know whether it has been retained and will be used with the new site for the new building or whether it has been disposed of.
When we are in supply on Monday or Tuesday, I shall give the information.
What accommodation was there formerly ?

I think two buildings were hired for the two batteries, but I am not sure. The batteries as my hon. friend knows require good accommodation and it is difficult to get such buildings. They were rented prior to the time of constructing this building.

It seems to me there is a very large expenditure in connection with these military buildings. I made a rough calculation and find that out of the 46 items for Ontario public buildings, 18 are for military buildings and out of the $727,000 for Ontario about $390,000 is for these buildings. But that is not all, these are only preliminary steps in connection with most of these buildings. Take this Guelph armoury, you are asking a vote of $20,000, but the total cost will be $148,000, over seven times the amount you are asking to-day. On the same basis the total for the province would amount to $2,500,000. That would be hardly fair, but it will cost $1,500,000 at least to complete the buildings asked for this purpose. I question u bether such an expenditure can be justified under the circumstances, when so much money is required for purpose of greater importance than these drill halls and armouries. If Canada was amply supplied with transportation facilities and other facilities required for the business of the country it would perhaps then be quite proper to expend large amounts of money in erecting buildings for the accommodation of the troops. We seem to have got along very well in past times without all this tremendous expenditure, but it looks as though the Militia Department

wants to level up its buildings in accordance with its staff. It is like the man who put a cupola on his house, then had to furnish accordingly and wound up by putting on a big mortgage. It looks as though the Militia Department, having established a very large and particularly extensive staff, would wish now to have al the buildings throughout the country in connection with the militia in proper proportion to the staff they have created. I must for my part, protest against such a large expenditure. I do not think it is required or necessary in any sense. I do not think you will be able to enlist men any more easily by reason of these expensive building's than you would have been without them. Here is a building costing $150,000 to accommodate two batteries, and one company Qf infantry.
And an army service corps.

And you are spending $150,000 in buildings for them. It is not only the initial expenditure in connection with these, but the annual expenditure for repairs, caretakers, etc., which will be tremendous. I do not know what great influence the Minister of Militia must have in order to get these large votes passed through council. I wish to offer my protest against this tremendous expenditure, because I think it is entirely uncalled for and I do not believe it will increase in the slightest degree the efficiency of the militia of the country.

The whole question, of course, of the extent to which the government or parliament is justified in carrying the expenditure upon these buildings or upon the militia generally, is very important and interesting, but we can hardly take it up conveniently at this hour. I do not see much relevancy between the expenditure on the general staff and the expenditure upon these public buildings. I shall be prepared at the proper time to discuss the expenditure upon the staff and upon all branches of the militia and I am always anxious to hear fair criticism on these points.
I must differ from my hon, friend as to these expenditures in a general way. I am not prepared to say that the expenditure in some cases is not larger than is justified. I am rather inclined to agree that there have been cases in the past and in recent years and no doubt there will be cases in the future, where the same good results would be obtained with a smaller expenditure, but I believe in the principle of supplying the men who give their time and their money for the purpose of being prepared for the defence of the country with fair and reasonable accommodation, particularly in the large cities. Owing to the fact that employers of labour in those
large centres absolutely refuse, in many cases, to allow their employees to attend their annual drill or to give their time during the day towards perfecting themselves in drill, it is absolutely necessary to provide suitable buildings for these men to drill in comfort in the evenings. Some of the most efficient regiments in Canada are to be found in the cities. I do not care to mention any particular regiment, but, take the regiments of Toronto and of Hamilton ; take the 13th regiment of Hamilton and the other regiment there-they are -among the most creditable regiments in this country. No finer regiments are to be found anywhere. They could not have reached that pitch of perfection without reasonable accommodation and I do think that this country can well afford to give proper accommodation and that the country, when it understands the position of affairs, will be glad to give all reasonable accommodation to encourage these men to make themselves proficient in drill.
What is the cost of the Hamilton drill hall?
We are coming to that.

The minister has confirmed my argument, I think, because he has particularly mentioned the efficiency of the Hamilton regiment and they have arrived at that state of efficiency in a building very much inferior to the one which you propose to spend this money on. Do I understand that there is a vote for the Hamilton drill hall?
Hamilton has doubled and trebled its strength.

The expenditure of an additional $100,000 will not result in that regiment attaining a higher state of efficiency because the minister states that with inferior quarters they have reached a very high state of efficiency. Surely the efficiency of a regiment does not depend upon having a $150,000 or $200,000 building to drill in. Surely a building erected at a reasonable cost ought to do just as well. I quite understand that in cities it is necessary to have drill halls just for the reason that the minister has pointed out, that it is difficult for the employers of labour to allow their men to go out" for the length of time necessary to attend annual drill, not that these employers of labour are not as much actuated by the patriotic spirit as other people, but because it is a serious detriment to their business and therefore it is necessary for the men to drill at night. At the same time I think we have gone mad on the cost and style of these buildings. A very much cheaper building weuld answer the purpose just as well and the government could save the country a large sum and employ it in purposes which

would be more beneficial than in these expensive buildings.
I presume that the size of these buildings is to be accounted for by the fact that the space inclosed is used for the drill purposes?
Yes.

Does not the minister think that accuracy in ride practice is of more consequence than perfection in mere drill, and that the enormous sum, in the aggregate, expended on the large number of buildings which this government is now erecting would be better expended in the encouragement of rifle practice by some concrete scheme which would apply to the whole country. The constitutional objection which might be raised upon the ground that the subject of education is one coming within the purview of provincial authorities, could be overcome.
Rifle practice is carried on in all these buildings.
Not rifle practice with ordinary weapons?
Yes, with a minature cartridge.
The sub-target gun?
Yes, the sub-target gun is used in every armoury.

Would it not be possible to evolve some principle for teaching all young boys of a certain age to become experts in the handling of the rifle, and would it not be more useful than the effort to achieve perfection in the more costly and showy elements of drill?
I do not know.

I would like to ask the bon. Minister of Militia and Defence if he has had any demand or request from the citizens of Valleyfield to erect an armoury in that district. There are two companies there and I think they could form a good many more, in fact, a whole battalion if it were necessary. This place is very near the frontier and I would like to know if any demand has been made, how the minister would receive such a demand and what he would think about it?

There have been two deputations to wait upon me in connection with the matter. There has been some difficulty in connection with the old battalion at that point, part of which was recruited, I think, from Valleyfield, and which has been temporarily disbanded. The people of Valleyfield are * very anxious to organize a city battalion, to begin with four companies, and. of course, in that connection they would expect an armoury to be constructed at that point. No decision has Mr. FOWLER
been reached. The matter is still under consideration.
There are already two companies. I think there were four before, and there may be four yet.
I think there were eight companies altogether, but they were scattered all over that part of the country.

Yes. Referring to what my hon. friend said a moment ago, consideration must be given to the question of taking care of the arms, because the government would have to pay some person to take care of the arms and some place must be had for that purpose. It is a city of about 12,000 or 15,000 people and being near the frontier would it not be, in the opinion of the minister, a suitable place in which to establish an armoury? It could be done at a relatively small cost and it would be a very useful thing.

If my hon. friend will convince the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) as to the soundness of such a policy, personally, I should be very glad indeed to co-operate in having a. suitable armoury constructed at such an important centre as Valleyfield.

I would rather try to convince my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence than my hon. friend from Kings and Albert, because I understand that my hon. friend has not consulted the hon. member for Kings and Albert as to the building of armouries. I would rather address myself straight to the minister.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bergeron) asked for an armoury at Valley-field because that town is close to the frontier, but I would remind him that an armoury is not a fort. In Sussex, New Brunswick, where I live, we have an armoury there the contract price for which was $4,700 and that armoury suffices for storing the equipment of all the troops in the province.
Stores are kept in St. John and also in Fredericton.
The reserve stores are kept in St. John but the stores used by the militia of ~the province in camp are kept in this armoury the contract price for which was $4,700.
That was the mere building without fittings.

I suppose my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) wants to show his impartiality by criticising me as well as the government. X quite understand the difference between an armoury and a fortification, but knowing that it is the duty of the Minister of Militia to provide accommodation for the troops which most need it I brought before him the claims of Valley-field.
What is the population of Valleyfieid ?

Between 12,000 and 15,000. The volunteers in Valleyfieid belong to the battalions which distinguished themselves on the frontier during the Fenian Raid in 1866 and 1870 and also at the battle of Chateauguay in 1812 which saved Canada for the British Crown. The men in those battalions to-day are descendants of the men who fought in 1812 and in 1866. These historic battalions have always been ready to march to the call of duty and they deserve special consideration from the government of Canada. Anyway, on the basis of the policy laid down by the Militia Department an armoury should be built in that city. The Minister of Militia has admitted that a petition has been received for the erection of an armoury at Valleyfieid and I rose to endorse the prayer of that petition. I can tell the gallant member for Kings-Albert (Mr. Fowler) that there are np more historic battalions to be found in all Canada than are to be found in my constituency, and when he rises again to criticise the government I trust he will not turn his criticism on the member for Beau-harnois who knows perfectly well the difference between an armoury and a fortification.

The hon. gentleman first wanted an armoury at Valleyfieid because it was near the frontier which would indicate that it was a fortification he was thinking of. Now he gives as a reason that these battalions are filled with veterans of the Fenian raid which took place 42 years ago.
They are the descendants of these men.

I understood my hon. friend to say that they were the descendants of the men who fought at Chateauguay. Now, if these men were 20 years of age 42 years ago at the time of the Fenian Raid they would be 62 years old now and it is a hospital they wanted instead of an armoury.

There are none so deaf as those who do not wish to hear. What I said was that these battalions fought at Chateauguay and during the Fen-iain Raid and I know that in England different regiments are proud of their history and of their brave deeds in years gone by.

I am not rising to ask the Minister of Public Works to erect a drill hall in any part of the county I have the honour to represent notwithstanding that we have in that county a battalion eight companies strong and numbering possibly 400 men. In that regiment, the Lome Rifles, the 20th battalion, 400 men have to be provided for ; and if you took all the drill halls in the county, and put them up at auction or sold them at private sale, you would not realize more than $10,000 for them ; whereas in the adjoining county of Wellington, where 400 men are to be provided for, the Minister of Public Works at the request of the Minister of Militia is going to spend $148,000. Does the Minister of Militia not see that this is discriminating against the rural battalions? If he is going to maintain the force at full strength and give encouragement to the young men to connect themselves with the militia of the country, he should see that there is a more equal division of the expenditure. I am not going to complain of the amount that is being expended in Guelph, nor am I going to ask at the present time that any money be expended in my county, because the expenditure of this country has grown so enormously that practically we are not at liberty to ask that it be increased to any extent. We are getting on very well ; I see no signs of war in the near future ; our battalion is held together very well ; they go out to drill in good force and I dare say that if they were called out for any other purpose they would be equally at the command of the minister. But the minister is a little more particular about building up the city corps than the rural corps, and I am going to give him a concrete case. Some time ago a troop of cavalry called the Massassaga Horse was formed with headquarters in the city of Toronto. The minister permitted one squadron of that troop to be raised in the county of Halton, right at the corner of the county which was the headquarters of N'o. 1 company of the 20th battalion. What was the effect ? The captain of that company found that his men were being decoyed away, because they were more willing to join a cavalry troop. It was a little more pleasant, and when they went out to drill, each man received pay for his horse as well as himself, so that tnere was a little more money in it; and the captain of No. 1 company at Oakville found it a difficult matter to keep his men. I think an invasion of that kind should not have beeD

allowed, as it may hare the effect of injuring or wiping out that company. The minister mgy tell me that he had nothing to do with it, that somebody in Toronto controlled it. It is strange to me if the minister cannot dictate where a squadron shall have its headquarters, and prevent recruiting for one branch of the service where it will interfere with that of another. I shall be glad if the minister can tell me that he has taken steps to prevent that sort of thing in the future.

My hon. friend is quite correct in supposing that I am not directly responsible. I am responsible, of course, for the administration of the Militia Department, but this particular case I never heard of before. The officer commanding western Ontario, General Otter, one of the ablest officers in Canada, had that matter under his control, and what he did he no doubt did with the best intentions, however it may have worked out. I would suggest to my hon. friend that very likely the individuals who are objecting are not the young men themselves who have had the privilege of joining this cavalry regiment, but the infantry officers who find it more difficult to get recruits.
I grant that is the case.

I am disposed to think that I shall favour the majority, and if the young men, who own their own horses and are ambitious to belong to a cavalry squadron, want to do so, and the officer commanding thought it was wise to meet their wishes, while I am sorry that the captain of the infantry company should be put to any inconvenience, the lesser must suffer for that which is of greater importance. I know that that difficulty does happen in my own county. I represent a purely rural constituency where we have an infantry regiment and I think two or three squadrons of cavalry, and the officers of the infantry regiment tell me that it is absolutely impossible for them to keep their regiment up to its strength because of the extension of the cavalry regiment. It is a question which is the better of the two. In my own county the farmers' sons are well to do and own their own horses, and there is no better place in the world in which to recruit cavalry regiments than in localities of that kind. My hon. friend from Kings (Mr. Fowler) knows that the same conditions exist in his county. Wherever there are districts in which the young men are ambitious to form cavalry regiments and where cavalry regiments are needed, I should be disposed to give every facility to their organization-I do not think it is necessary to put the rural militia in opposition, so to speak, to the city militia. I think it is quite possible to do full justice to both, and I do not think that because Mr. HENDERSON
a city regiment, or two or three regiments, secure handsome drill halls or armouries, it necessarily follows that we should neglect the rural regiments. In my county there is a regiment of infantry with eight companies and a regiment of cavalry with, I think, three squadrons, and yet I can tell my hon. friend that during the whole time I have been Minister of Militia, not more than .|1,200 has been spent in my county. In fact there is only one armoury there where all the arms are kept. It is an old armoury which was built fifty years ago, and two or three years ago I spent $1,200 on it to put it into proper shape. My hon. friend will see that I at any rate have not abused my position by spending large sums on my own regiment. This question has been discussed on many previous occasions and I would like to say this. I believe that we should gradually, but as rapidly as possible, supply armouries for all the different companies throughout the country. This can be done at a very reasonable cost. An armoury for one company, which would be a building with a good lecture room and accommodation to hold the stores, could be constructed for some $2,500, perhaps less. A larger building where there are two or three companies together, at a place where the commanding officer of the regiment lives, could be constructed for perhaps $4,000 or $5,000. During the last three or four years $50,000 to $75,000 has been voted each year. I regret that some of the armouries will cost more than we expected, but we have constructed a number in British Columbia and the Northwest, a few in Ontario, one or two in the province of Quebec and two or three in Nova Scotia. My intention is to continue constructing such armouries and to give them in order of merit to the different rural battalions throughout the country.
Hamilton drill hall-addition, $100,000.

There has been a drill hall in Hamilton for sime time which will continue to be occupied. The new building will be a very fine One. It will be built on a site with 100 feet frontage and 300 feet deep. The main drill hall will be 128 feet by 220. There was paid for the site $29,000, and this $100,000 is required to complete the building. The tota cost is estimated at $315,089.76, inclusive of the site. It will accommodate the 13th Regiment consisting of 600 men, the 91st Highlanders with 500 men, the 4th Field Battery with 115 men, the Army Service Corps, 106 men. The 7th company, 36 men. will occupy the old drill hall.
Is this under contract ?
Yes.
What is the size of the present building and how much did it cost ?
The old building measures 250 feet long by 116 wide.
Of what material is it built ?
Brick with stone dressings.
What about the new building ?	'
It is to have a frontage of 367 feet by 300 feet in depth. Its main hall is to be 128 feet wide by 336 long.
Was the new building found too small ?
Yes, the strength of the militia in Hamilton has been doubled within the last four or five years, and they could not drill properly in the old hall.
The 13th Regiment has its headquarters there. And what are the others ?
The 90th Regiment, the 44th Field Battery, with a strength of one hundred odd, and the 19th Army Service corps, with 110 and No. 12 Field Ambulance, and the band.
About one thousand men altogether.
More, for these regiments are about 500 men each.
Well, say 1,200 men. None of these regiments or corps have been created within the last five years ?

I have not the record before me, but I think it was within the last five years there has been an increase in the numerical strength of both regiments, and I think the Field ambulance company has been started within that time.

As a matter of fact, these different corps do not have to drill on the same night ? The matter could be arranged so that one would use the drill hall one night and another the next night, and so on. In that case, there would be room enough in the old building. You are going to spend $315,000 additional for this building. The original building, I suppose, cost $200,000-that is, you will have spent over half a million to accommodate 1,200 men. It seems to me this is altogether unjustifiable. The minister should have resisted the pressure put upon him by the members from Hamilton or-if they were not together in this matter-from the member for Hamilton. The only real necessity for this great expenditure was the re-election of the ministerial member for Hamilton (Mr. Zimmerman). However useful a man that hon. gentleman may be-and I say nothing about that,-this is a very large price to pay for the pleasure of having him here. I protest most strongly against this 244
expenditure as absolutely uncalled for-a waste of public money.

I am glad to hear a military man say that, for I have entertained much the same opinions for a length of time, but have usually concluded that my judgment would not carry much weight, as I take so little interest in military affairs. I have often wondered whether some of the money that we spend in these palatial buildings for military purposes could not be spent to much better purpose in some other line. I do not pretend to be competent to judge as to the efficiency of a militia force. But many years ago the force seemed to me much more active in our country than it is to-day-I mean in the case of the rural battalions. They have dwindled until now you can hardly get a company together. The last few days before they go to camp the officers are doing their best to get recruits, while a few years ago there was no trouble to keep the companies up to their full strength. There was comparatively little trouble to keep them for the full length of time, and now they go in for a year and then drop out- no one seems to have any interest in it. But while this retrograde process is going on, we seem to be enormously increasing the expenditure. I dislike to seem captious in regard to these expenditures, for I believe every country should make reasonable provision for its own defence, and to keep its citizens in military training. But it seems to me that we are not spending our money in the best way. Nor can I say that I am prepared to give suggestions as to how to spend it better, not being sufficiently informed in military affairs to outline a system. An hon. member made the remark the other night that we had one officer for every two and a half men on the average. That being the case, the force is evidently topheavy. It seems to me that not sufficient encouragement is given to the rural battalions. But our experience is the same as that of other countries, that, when it is necessary to put a force in the field for the defence of the country, the rural battalions are superior to those of the city. They have a better physique and are of a higher type of self-reliant manhood, making them a most valuable force in trying circumstances. Yet, these rural corps do not seem to be given due encouragement, but all the eclat of military life is afforded the towns and cities.

I am glad the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has spoken as he has. I entirely agree that the rural battalions do not receive the consideration to which they are entitled. I repeat what I said before, that I am not going to advocate larger expenditures, but I do desire to emphasize the idea that there should be some equitable distribution of



this money, less for the cities and more for the country. I believe that the bone and sinew of the militia of this country is in the rural districts. One of the best regiments that served in putting down the Northwest rebellion was the York Rangers made up practically altogether of farmers' sons, men capable of enduring greater hardship than those drawn from mercantile shops, banks and other business houses. In time of trouble I believe it would be found that the most reliable forces were the rural battalions. I am an advocate of reduced expenditure but I do contend there should be a more equitable distribution and that the rural battalions should receive something more than they have received, even if it is to be taken away from the city battalions.

I regret that it seems to be my fate to disagree with my colleagues as to military matters. I do not believe that the rural corps require any further consideration than they receive. I think the rural battalions are very well taken care of so far as expenditure is concerned and I do not think they, require any more. I contend that altogether too much money is being spent on the city corps and that too much money is being expended on armouries and everything of that sort. One would think to listen to the hon. member (Mr. Henderson) that it was necessary to take a lump sum and spend it on the militia. I say that the expenditure on the militia is many times greater than it should be in this country. Years ago when less money was spent we had quite as efficient a militia force as we have to-day. If there is any trouble about enlisting men in the rural battalions it is due to the manner in which they are officered at the present time. In the olden time the officers were taken from the rural community itself and farmers sons were in command and the officers and the men were of the same social grade and they worked in harmony. But to-day the conditions are different and the reason is on account of the prohibitive expense of the outfit necessary for an officer. There is too much gold lace, too many frills, too many feathers ; the officers are drawn from the cities and there is no fellowship between them and the men. If the regiments to-day are not composed of the same class of men as formerly-and that is truer of the infantry than of the cavalry-it is due to the reason I have stated. I have before expressed these views in the House and the minister has agreed with me but nothing has been done. My contention is that we should have a system like the Boer system. an inexpensive system where the men would be taught fewer of the frills and more of how to shoot. There should be more money spent on teaching the men rifle practice than on teaching them how to march past with grace. You don't have Mr. HENDERSON.
much of that sort of things to do when yon get into active service. At all events no war would come so rapidly, that after you have your enrolment you cannot give your men sufficient drill to fit them for active service. If you simplify the uniform of the officers so as to make it possible for men of small means to become officers you will have the officers drawn from the same community as the men and you will have a better class of men going into the ranks.
Hamilton post office-addition to buildings, $7,000.
This is the complete altei'ations to the rear of the Hamilton post office. The total estimated cost is S20,-033.37.

This is another instance in which the money of this country is not equitably distributed. In the county of Halton which I represent there has not been one dollar expended in the way of furnishing post offices and yet in the adjoining counties, because they contain towns and cities of considerable dimensions, very large sums of money have been expended. In the city of Guelph something over $40,000 was spent in the improvement of the post office although it is a puzzle to the people of Guelph when they look at the building to know how they managed to put away all that money. The government, in these appropriations, should take the rural districts into consideration as *well as the cities and larger towns. I am contending for a more equitable distributing of public money and even if a county has no towns and villages exceeding 1,500 or 2,000 population they should not be ignored whilst large expenditures go to the cities.
You and I agree exactly.

Some years ago after making a very careful calculation in my own county I estimated that if $30,000 was set apart it would at that time have erected a building in each of five incorporated towns and villages at a cost of $0,000 in each place, and would have provided a good post office containing a residence for the postmaster. I do not say you could erect buildings now at the same cost, but I know that when I made my suggestion it was endorsed by Sir Louis Davis then a minister, who said the thing could be done for even less money. My plan was not accepted. It seemed that the government could not erect a building of such small dimensions as would call for an expenditure of $6,000. I made a calculation to show that there would be a saving to the government that the interest on the whole $30,000, provided the government borrowed the money at 3 per cent would be less than the rentals that were paid by the government for the various post offices. Then an advantage would be that in every case

the post office in these five towns and villages would be in a brick building where a vault could be put in for the protection of the valuable letters passing through the mail, and exit as well as an entrance could be provided which would prevent the very congested condition that we find in a great many of our village post offices in the morning and evening just after the arrival of the mails. I am going to show you how we get post offices in Halton. I picked up a local newspaper and I found an item under the following heading :
New post office for Burlington.
Burlington is in the county of Halton. It is about seven miles from the city of Hamilton. It may be a surprise to the Postmaster General or the Minister of Public Works, to find that the village of Burlington is to have a new post office. It is provided in this way :
Burlington will have a new post office this summer. Mr. William Kerns has decided to build a substantial brick structure on the site occupied by the present post office. The figures are being obtained from local contractors, and the contract will be awarded in a few days. Mr. Kerns is to be congratulated upon his step to improve our beautiful village, and the change should be appreciated by the public generally.
I have no doubt it will be appreciated by the Postmaster General.
What is the population?
1,400 or 1,500. I know very well the building where the post office is now kept. It is a small place and, I think, belongs to the gentleman whose name is mentioned here.
Is it a private residence ?

No, the postmaster lives in his own home, but this gentleman who owns the present building, with that enterprise which characterizes him as a leading citizen of the town, proposes to remove this building and erect a substantial brick building and have it used as a post office. I have no doubt the Postmaster General will appreciate the change. It will not change the location of the post office. It is left exactly in the same place, but it will be a more substantial and a more commodious building. That is the way we get post offices in Halton. I regret however, that in all the towns and villages we have not men of the same enterprise and consequently we have in many cases very inferior buildings, crowded and congested in the morning and evening when the mails come in and not at all equal to the requirements of these places.

I think I will have to take a step up into your constituency.
244J
I would be delighted and you will see one of the most beautiful counties in western Ontario.
There are many beautiful counties in western Ontario.
If the hon. gentleman should come some time in the month of June we will regale him with the finest strawberries that you can find anywhere in the Dominion.
No.
The hon. gentleman may say 'no.'
Not better than Sussex Bay ?
I never heard of Sussex Bay. Oakville strawberries were known forty vears ago throughout this country.
Sussex Bay strawberries were known a century ago.

And you will find
every kind of fruit almost-peaches, pears, plums, gooseberries-
That is enough ; I will come.
He cannot go until the session is over.

There will be lots of delicious fruit after the session closes. We have it the whole summer through and the hon. gentleman can come at any time. I hope his coming will be of some advantage and that it will result in the levelling up of these expenditures. I do Dot mean that you should increase the expenditure.
Just a readjustment.

Just a readjustment. It will simply take a little from Hamilton, Guelph, Brampton and Toronto and give it to the county of Halton and other rural counties. I am satisfied that that is sound policy and that is a policy that will be appreciated by the rural sections of the country. That is all I have to say about the matter, and I hope I am not misunderstood.
Kinoar.dine public building, $7,000.
The total cost, including everything, is $29,000. The original contract was $17,000.
Is that building completed ?
No the contract was only let last fall.
You did not spend any money last year at all?
The town gave the site so that there was no site to buy. and there was no money expended last year.
How much have you paid to the contractor ?
Nothing has been paid yet.
Have you a clerk of works ?
No.
Nothing has been done on the contract at all ?
The contract was let last November.
What is the population ?
In 1901 it was 2,077, and^ the population of the township was 2,855. Kincardine is in North Bruce.
$12,000 seems a large amount in addition to the contract.

In these days the cost of fitting up a public building is considerably greater than it formerly was. It has to be wired for electric light and electric fixtures and heating apparatus have to be provided.
What kind of heating apparatus ?
Hot water heating.

This is another illustration of the unwisdom of the course we are following. I notice that at Kincardine the revenue was $3,053 last year and that we paid an allowance towards rent and fuel of $150. That is practically the full cost.
It must have been changed since because the Postmaster General's Report for 1907 which I have before me gives the amount which I have stated.
It is $200 for the Post Office, and $60 for the Customs, and this building will provide for the Customs, Post Office and Inland Revenue Departments.

Interest on the money for the erection of the building, the cost of caretaking, insurance, repairs and taxes, if there are any, will amount to somewhere about $1,600 or $1,700 a year, while we are getting the accommodation to-day for $150. If that is good business policy, I do not understand business.
This is for a post office and customs house I suppose ?
Custom house and examining warehouse and inland revenue office.
Is the policy of the government in erecting these buildings the
same as in former years ; are vaults erected in these buildings or does the government supply safes in the offices ?

Kingston Royal Military College-new servants' quarters, $10,000.

This is to make provision for the erection of new servants' quarters. They are called servants' quarters, but they are for the non-commissioned officers at the Royal Military College. These are to consist of two buildings, 167 feet long by 33 feet broad. They are to be placed on two opposite sides of a square, with yards in rear. Each building consists of eight dwellings two stories high, of brick with stone facings, and with stone basement. The contract is let for this work; the amount of the contract being $77,939. What are you doing with non-commissioned officers' quarters in the college except among the cadets?
They consist of sixteen different dwelling houses.
That is $6,000 to each house. I think it is a pretty good job to be a servant in the Royal Military College, to be housed in a $6,000 house with steamheating, electric lighting and ail the rest.
I understand that they are non-commissioned officers.
What are non-commissioned officers doing there?
They are teachers and instructors in connection with the college.

In rented houses.

I want to protest strongly against this expenditure. The greater part of the expenditure on this institution is money thrown away. From what we have seen in the public press and have heard elsewhere, the gentleman who is at the head of that institution is absolutely unfit to have charge of the instruction of young men. His habits, his methods of instruction, his ideas of proper conduct are entirely at variance with those ordinarily accepted; yet he continues to occupy the position of head of this school. We are now told that there are some sixteen noncommissioned officers, drill, instructors, for this school. How many pupils are attending the school ?
About 100.

It evidently is as much over-officered as the militia. There is about [DOT] one instructor to every six cadets. The thing is absurd. We ought to have more information before we allow this item to pass. I do not know for whom these buildings are intended, but it is absolutely impossible that sixteen drill instructors should be required to instruct one hundred cadets.

When the plans were submitted to me and I saw the class of buildings, and when I read the statement that they were for servants' quarters, it struck me that these buildings were altogether too expensive for persons occupying that position. I sent to the Militia Department. and either the deputy minister or Mr. Jarvis called upon me and informed me that these persons composed the subordinate staff of the institution and that this accommodation was absolutely required, and that this class of dwellings was not at all more than was reasonably required for the staff.

We have them now called the staff, a while ago they' were servants, and then they were called drill instructors. Now it appears they are the staff. I have no doubt that the average dwelling of members of this House does not cost $6,000. and Mr. PUGSLEY.
yet we are authorizing a vote for this amount to house non-commissioned officers. I do not think that they deserve better housing than we ourselves get, and I would ask tne minister not to press this item until we have more explicit and more detailed information
I will bring a list showing exactly who these people are, and what are their duties.
What is the average salary and allowance which these drill instructors receive ?

Perhaps I used the term drill instructors improperly. I know that one man teaches gymnastics and some of them take charge of the horses and are servants connected with the college generally. I do not say they are all teachers.
We ought to have full explanation from the Minister of Militia regarding what is done at that institution and the number of graduates turned out before we pass these items.
The best time to give that would be when the estimates for the Militia Department are up and when I shall make my statement and have all the papers necessary.

But should we then reach the conclusion that the military college should be done away with, we will have voted the money for these buildings. We ought to have a full explanation before we vote a dollar. We have heard of some very absurd things that have transpired in that institution. For instance a young man was asked if he had shaved off the down on his upper lip. If he had said he had not, no one would have been any the wiser because it was not visible, but he was manly enough to say he had done so, and he was put in close custody for four days. Did any one hear of anything so absurd ? Young men go their of the highest moral and religious ty'pe, and there they learn to play cards and gamble and smoke cigarettes and cigars and learn other vices of that kind. That is not the kind of training which parents desire their young men to have.
Many splendid men have come out of that institution.
Yes, but sometimes the institutions degenerate. They are good or bad according to the class of men who control them and carry on the work of tuition.
I would like to ask the minister if he could not give us within $20,000 to $30,000 an estimate of the cost of those buildings.
It would not be fair to me nor to the committee if I should guess at the cost.

I want to enter my protest against expenditure of tills kind. It ought to be an object lesson to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) to see the paltry amount he gets for his department when so much is expended on the militia. The statement made by the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) is perfectly correct when we are asked to vote such sums as these for the militia compared with the votes for agriculture.

Before we pass from that item, have any steps been taken for the capture of the man who murdered one of the officers who was taking a course of instruction in this school ? And how was it that nothing was done until next morning- as I understand to have been the case- by the 150 officers and men who were there? These seem to be the facts as published; and they are, as they stand, a reflection upon the force. Has the Minister of Militia, as the responsible head of that department, any explanation ?
I cannot give an answer. I will ask for the report in the morning and give it to the House or to my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler).
I understand that the provincial authorities have been searching for this man.

It has always been the boast of our people that a murderer was hunted down, no expense necessary to that end being spared. There was a case in the Klondike where $30,000 was spent in order to trace and capture a murderer there. It was a splendid object lesson. But this seems to be an object lesson the other way. It is a very unfortunate thing that this man should be murdered in the city of London, and nothwithstanding that the country thereabouts is thickly settled the murderer-
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) suggest that the provincial authorities have not done their duty ?

I suggest that all the authorities have not done their duty. As soon as the murder was known, every one of these men should have been turned out in search of the murderer and the search should not have been remitted until he was captured. A reward should have been offered and everything necessary done.
The authorities here hare not even a report yet, for the minister (Sir Frederick Borden) has told us that he will ask for one to-morrow morning.

The hon. gentleman, (Mr. Fowler) knows that the administration of the criminal law is in the hands of the provincial authorities. The offering of a reward would be the proper duty of those authorities.

It is true that the enforcement of the criminal law is in the hands of the provincial authorities.. It is true also that an officer attending a course of instruction in the military post at London was murdered by one of the members of the force, and yet no effort was made-

How does the hon. gentleman know ?
MV. FOWLER. It is so stated in the newspapers and not denied. As a matter of fact, if they had turned out at once they could have caught him.
It does not follow.
It certainly does.

I did not say that I would ask for a report to-morrow morning. I have no doubt the report is in the department here, and I have promised to get it; to-morrow morning-at least that is what I intended to say.
Then, I misunderstood the hon. minister.

There is no doubt that this is a serious matter. It seems very strange that, with the number of soldiers about when this crime was committed, this man should have been allowed to get away. There seems to be a feeling abroad in this country in favour of shielding the criminal. I have heard several people, in conversation about this man, express the hope that he would get away.
I do not think any such spirit should be encouraged in the country. Many people are in the habit of allowing these things to go along the lines of least resistance, as when in the old days, if train robbers entered a ear every one would hold up his hands, until once in a while they would meet a man who would not and then everything was turned the other way. A few instances like that would have a good effect. I think it is the duty of the government to press on the people that they should not shield this man, because he must get food and shelter, and some steps should be taken to impress on the officers and non-commissioned officers at London that it was their duty to arrest that man, dead or alive, within 15 seconds. I see reports of jealousy between the London de-
Mr. FOWLER,
tectives and the rural police. A little instruction to the people of Canada in the treatment of criminals is required.

I would not be prepared to say that any person is in fault. I would rather assume that the officers do their duty. That is the experience I have had in the enforcement of the criminal law and I prefer to believe that until there is evidence to the contrary. The mere fact that the murderer is at large is not positive proof that the authorities are neglectful.
With regard to the London post office, we are asking a revote of $3,000, of which $1,475 is for vault fittings, and $500 for paving the streets.

The chief architect does not know but he tells me the prices run in different parts of the country from 11 cents to 20 cents. The average, I think, is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 16 cents. It is IS cents a square foot in Ottawa.
A price of 26 cents was mentioned the other day.
That was at Antigonish but that included some things unusual. The street was not level and had to be filled up to make it level.

Perhaps he did better and more substantial work for the govern-' ment.
You can get it in some parts of the country from 9 cents a foot.' Take the cases of Flesherton and Dundalk.
We have had it done for 11 cents.
