That depends on how accustomed to laying them the people are. I know in the village where I have a summer home, where we have no persons experienced in this class of work, I would have to pay a great deal more than I would in Ontario where a great deal of this work is done.

The building is 55 feet 6 by 90 feet, two stories high over basement, built of brick, stone fittings and a stone foundation. It is intended for post office, customs and inland revenue. North Bay is an important and rapidly growing town.
When the Canadian Pacific Railway runs to Sudbury instead of North Bay, North Bay will be merely a crossing on the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario.
I doubt that; I think it will grow.
What is the total cost of the buildings?
The total cost of the buildings, including site, is $61,375.
What is the population of North Bay?
In 1901 it was 2,530, but I think it has grown considerably since that time.
What is the cost of the site?
It would appear to be expensive, it cost 88,100.

From Mrs. William Doran.' It is a valuable lot and is well situated on the corner of Main and Fraser streets; it is 66 feet on one street and 132 feet on the other.

Mr. PUGSLEY'. I cannot say.

The minister should consider the importance of having these buildings isolated.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. It is a good idea.

I have had the pleasure of being in North Bay several times and I think it deserves a reasonable building, but to spend 867,000 in a town of 2,500 population and to spend nothing in other larger towns is not treating the latter fairly. I approve of public buildings in any town of reasonable size in the Dominion provided the money is properly spent, because it is important for strangers coming into a town to see ornamental buildings. But I will not approve of spending so much money in a small place and neglecting larger places. A 825,000 building in a town of that size would be sufficient.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. I am not prepared to say that I would approve of erecting such an expensive building, but I presume the minister was impressed with the importance of North Bay and considered it was for customs purposes as well as for post offices.
It is a distributing centre for all that country.
When was the site purchased?
The 31st March, 1905.
Taking the cost of the lot at 88,000 and the total cost at 861,000, that would leave 853,000 for the building. which is 813.000 more than Mr. Hv-man, when minister, said it would cost.
He probably did not include the fittings, which cost 86,000, and the heating and boilers.
88,000 is an unconscionable price to pay for a lot 66 feet by 132 in a town like North Bay.

My information is that the lot could be sold to-day for considerably more than the government paid for it. Everything depends on the location of a lot and the possibility of securing other suitable lots. Under the circumstances I think 88,100 was nothing excessive.
By what means, under what conditions, and from whom was the site purchased?
It was purchased from Mrs. Doran and I have nothing here to show that it was not a direct purchase.
Who recommended the site ?
An officer of the department was sent up to examine it.
Of course, that would be after the site was offered. Was it taken on the recommendation of a member ?

I do not know as to that; I have no information. I know that the minister interested himself very much in securing the erection of the building. There was a petition from the citizens of the town and also from the board of trade.

I understand that the population of this town is about 2,000. and this is at the rate of about 845,000 an acre for the land, which seems to me to be a very unreasonable price for land in a little village.
North Bay is not a village.
The minister has not not yet given any information as to how the department came to purchase the site.
I have no information whether any other lots were offered or not, but the department sent up an expert on land values, and on his report they authorized the purchase.
Has the minister the name of that expert ?
I have not this evening.

I must say that the price of this lot is to my mind altogether out of keeping with the value of property in that section of the country. Land is not so scarce there. There is abundance of it; and as to location, I do not think it is absolutely necessary that the post office should be in the centre of the town. You may put it in the centre of the town to-day, and in five years it may be in the suburbs. If an expert was sent to value the lot. he must have been misled terribly by the people who were pressing the sale of this lot on the government. It is now ten minutes past twelve ; we sat late last night, till about half-past two ; the House is very thin, and I would recommend the minister to allow us to go home and get a rest. I promise the minister that between twelve o'clock and two, if he insists on our remaining here, he must not expect to get any estimates through. I do not think it is reasonable to ask us to sit after twelve o'clock on Friday night in a thin House. The

business of the House will go on much better if the minister will give us time to rest.

Most of us have Saturday as a holiday and then Sunday. I really think we ought to get along with the business ; I think both sides of the House ought to bend their energies to that. We have had every opportunity for discussion. I do not want to keep the House unduly, but suppose we go on and pass a few more items.

The minister talks about bending our energies. The government have been holding back ail the important measures. The Northwest Land Bill and the Election Bill are going to take up considerable time, and these estimates will be passed more quickly after we are apprised of those measures.

Surely it is unreasonable, after the late hour that we were here last night, to keep us here longer to-night.

Surely my hon. friend will not suppose that the government could tire out the opposition. They look as fresh as anybody could wish. All I ask is that we shall be reasonable and show the country that we know how to work and are prepared to work in the public interest.

The minister talks about what is reasonable, but I say it is not reasonable to keep us here longer in view of the fact that we were here one night till half-past two and another night till three. I think there is a great deal of reason in the contention of. the hon. member for Dalton and other members who say that considering the lateness of the hour to which we sat in the last three or four nights, we should adjourn at this hour of the morning.

Perhaps the hon. minister will allow me to point out a matter that has some bearing on the present situation. No doubt we did sit up until about two o'clock yesterday morning. I do not myself desire to see any obstruction to the passing of the estimates, but the four or five following items are of a very general character that will be discussed probably at length. The next item is that of public buildings for Ontario.
Mi-. PUGSLEY. Small items only.

Yes, but small items become in the main big items. There are four or five of them and these are the items probably the hon. gentleman wants to go on with. We have passed $200,000 or $300,000 to-night after a very long tedious sitting. I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that he should show a little good nature and that if he does it will perhaps bring to him a little indulgence and assistance later on. I have listened to the discussion and I am quite sure that, from the nature of the following items, they will take more time than he thinks.

That stands. But this item for the Ontario public buildings fire escapes, $5,000 we ought to pass. These public buildings are at Belleville, Goderich, Guelph, Hamilton, Orillia, Petrolia, Paris, Port Arthur, and a large number of others, and the items are all for fire escapes aggregating $5,000.
Now that the minister has given the names of these places, we will find them on ' Hansard ' and tomorrow we shall be able te look into the matter.
These cannot be at all controversial. Anything that is at all controversial I will let stand over.

I trust the minister will regard these as controversial. I would supplement what was said by my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) a short time ago. I do think that ail the sessions of parliament that I have attended, the government has this session shown the least disposition to go on with business.
Yet when I am trying my level best, you will not let me get along.

The hon. gentleman is very anxious to get his money, but there are measures on the Order Paper we never hear of and it seems to me he should advise his colleagues to bring some of those forward before he exhausts his estimates. To my mind there are important measures that ought to be dealt with before we deal with those estimates. I do not believe in leaving those to the end of the session when every one is anxious to get home and when proper consideration cannot be given them.
There will be the fullest opportunity to consider them.

Provided we remain here, but I do not think the government has shown a disposition to advance business this session as they have done in former years. I have no hesitation in appealing to the minister to adjourn the House now and let us go home. I do not consider that we are responsible if the estimates are not put through. The government have been delinquent and have allowed business to stand too long.

If you will consider the Ontario public buildings, I will pass* over the military building and the Printing Bureau and the Ottawra departmental buildings and we will adjourn You are in such a pleasant mood that we might get through the items that are not controversial.
Well, suppose we allow the minister to escape on his fire escape, then we can go home and will come back here even in better humour than to-night- and I think we have been in pretty good humour.
Oh, work a little longer; it is early.
Early in the morning, but rather late too.
Carried.

No, it is not carried. And I do not propose it shall be carried so soon as that. I do not know whether these fire escapes have been provided for the public buildings before or not. Where is it intended to purchase them ? Are they to be Iron stairways outside the buildings?
Yes.
The minister cannot get an iron stairway for $120. It must be only an iron ladder.

Have they a landing at
each story ?
Yes.

Prom whom are they purchased ?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. Very often they can be purchased in the town in which the building is situated. It is ordinary blacksmith work, you know.
Very few can be got that way. These are made by people with special machinery for that purpose.
Prom whom has the department been purchasing the fire escapes which have been in use ?
There is a firm in Ottawa named Smith which made quite a number and also a firm in Toronto.
How much was spent in fire escapes last year ?
I have not the figures.
Do I understand that this fire escape has a special name ? Is it a patent contrivance?	[DOT]
No, I speak of the Shipway Iron and Bell Co., of Toronto.
This is not a contrivance controlled by anybody ?
No.
What did that firm receive from the department last year ?
There was a vote of $3,000 last year, principally spent on fire escapes for the Printing Bureau.
Did the same firm supply them and put them up.
Yes.
What was the average cost ?
From $150 to $175.
Have the government been in he habit of providing fire escapes for public buildings ?

Only in some cases. But on account of some of the dreadful accidents that have happened, there is a general disposition throughout the country to require that public buildings should be provided with fire escapes and by-laws have been passed in many places to that effect.
For instance, we have no fire escapes on this building in which we meet ?
No.
Or on the other public buildings in Ottawa ?
I think not. We have started in by putting them on the printing building.
Did one firm supply all the fire escapes for the Printing Bureau ?
Yes.

Is it intended to purchase fire escapes for other places from the same firm ?
Mr. 'PUGSLEY. There is no intention one way or the other.
What change has necessitated this sudden determination to supply fire escapes where they were not supplied before ?
I gave the explanation -the calamities that have happened in Canada and the United States in public buildings.
Not more in recent years tii a a formerly ?

Yes, there was the dreadful fire in Montreal only last year. Bylaws have been passed in a number of places, and the chief architect is of opinion that fire escapes should be placed upon public buildings.
He has come to that conclusion lately ?
Yes. In fact, requests have been made by various authorities.
Are tenders to be asked for the supply of these fire escapes ?
Yes, prices will be asked.
From specified firms?
If they can be got locally, they will be got in that way.

I do not think that any one objects to the expenditure suggested by the minister. Personally, I think it most desirable. But the minister need not talk about securing these locally. I have had a little to do with fire escapes, and I have learned that you must get them from some one in that particular business. A local man would scarcely know how to measure a building to supply a fire escape. Who had the contract for putting fire escapes on the Printing Bureau building, and at what cost ?
The Ottawa Brass and Scale Company, at $4,200.
Were tenders asked for?
Yes.
How many tenders were received ?
The chief architect does not remember.
Does he know whether more than one was received ?
He is not able to say.
Does he know whether tenders were really asked for publicly, or was notice sent out to those on the patronage list ?
They were not advertised for.
Notice simply sent out to friends of the government ?
To those engaged in the business.
Especially friends of the government ?
Oh. no.

I think we would be disposed to let this item pass, together with two more, Parkhill and Peterborough. It was suggested that we might take the Owen Sound buildings, but it would have to be opened up again and I think it better, instead of taking Owen Sound, to take Peterborough which is of much the same character and would not elicit much discussion.
Sir. CLES1ENTS. On the item of fire escapes I would suggest that a great deal of money can be uselessly spent on fire escapes. On buildings like the Printing Bureau it is quite proper to have them, but I do not see why a small building should require a fire escape, for instance a post office. They are built practically fire proof and it is not necessary.
What would be the total cost of the Parkhill buildings the cost of land and the amount necessary to complete the building ?

It is on a site 50 by 150. We have been for a good while negotiating with regard to a lot and as a result of the negotiations, in which we were very materially assisted by Sir.
